abstract_original: Organ cross-talk refers to the bidirectional communication between different organs that enables the body to maintain physiological homeostasis, respond and adapt during dynamic states. Disturbances to these inter-organ communication networks may result in inappropriate physiological responses, thereby compromising systemic function. This proposal will leverage a unique publicly available large-scale, multi-organ, multi-omic dataset comprising 18 solid tissues from rats subjected to an endurance exercise training program. Our hypothesis is that organ-specific signaling hierarchies will determines the coordinated multiorgan responses that drive systemic adaptation. Following organ-specific multi-omic vertical integration, we will determine 1) the predictors of phenotypic adaptations, and 2) the cross talk between organs via horizontal integration. The computed networks will provide the foundation to generate a digital twin rat which will serve as a valuable tool to model organismal responses to physiological, environmental and pharmacological challenges. This comprehensive, temporally resolved analysis will offer unprecedented insights into how molecular interactions are coordinated across organs and levels of organization to determine whole-organism physiological function.

title: Conserved Disorder: Learning Sequence Conservation from Functional Constraints in Intrinsically Disordered Regions
title_norm: conserved disorder learning sequence conservation from functional constraints in intrinsically disordered regions
abstract_text: The fields of protein biophysics and bioinformatics investigate evolutionary conservation patterns in intrinsically disordered regions, which contain sequence features like short linear motifs and charge patterning that encode vital molecular functions. This project will define conserved intrinsically disordered regions by integrating human and viral proteomic data through AIUpred disorder prediction, explicit solvent all atom molecular dynamics simulations, sequence descriptors over moving windows, and machine learning. The study will integrate UniProt, Eukaryotic Linear Motif, IDRome, MaveDB, and GISAID databases by filtering sequences for disorder thresholds and cross referencing them with deep mutational scanning and post translational modification data. This research will provide a unified map of conserved disordered regions, establishing essential baselines for functional annotation and creating reference points for future sequence alignments and comparative analyses.
full_text: This protein biophysics and bioinformatics project investigates how evolutionary sequence variations of intrinsically disordered regions encode functional specificity. Subsets of intrinsically disordered regions contain functional motifs but current annotations favor folded protein domains over these flexible segments. The team asks how sequence features generate conserved functions to establish reference points for analyzing the disordered proteome. The core strategy integrates evolutionary and structural data across human and viral proteomes to identify patterns of functional conservation. Key methods include structural predictions using the AIUpred algorithm and explicit solvent molecular dynamics simulations alongside machine learning models. The team validates all analytical results by measuring sequence conservation across diverse species using independent databases of orthologous proteins. Researchers utilize primary databases like UniProt and MaveDB alongside supplementary resources including OrthoDB and the Eukaryotic Linear Motif repository. The team synthesizes datasets by cross referencing filtered sequences with scanning data and predicted motifs to construct unified maps. Because current functional annotations favor structured domains the researchers mitigate missing information by utilizing alternative data repositories like MobiDB. The two year project timeline progresses from infrastructure setup and structural investigations to concluding database releases and manuscript submissions. This broad scope requires cross disciplinary collaboration to unite expertise in bioinformatics and biophysical modeling across three independent laboratories. The project guarantees open access by hosting a public database of conserved regions on the CyVerse computational infrastructure. The team incorporates members from three distinct laboratories and provides robust training opportunities in computational and experimental analysis techniques.

While folded domains exhibit clear conservation of structure and function, IDRs evolve rapidly and appear sequence diverse, obscuring how they encode functional specificity. Bridging the sequence function relationship in IDRs and even their reliable functional annotation remains a major challenge. Emerging evidence, however, suggests that subsets of IDRs harbor conserved sequence features such as short linear motifs (SLiMs), charge patterning and aromatic clustering that give rise to transient structural elements and encode critical molecular functions. This project aims to systematically identify and characterize the most conserved IDRs across proteomes by integrating large-scale sequence alignments, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, and experimental functional annotations from publicly available databases. By combining resources such as UniProt, Eukaryotic Linear Motif (ELM), IDRome, and MaveDB, we will quantify the interplay between evolutionary, structural, and functional signatures of conservation in disordered regions. Our multidisciplinary Working Group unites computational and experimental biophysics to build a curated, open-access database of conserved IDRs. This synthesis effort will reveal how dynamic, flexible protein regions maintain specific and evolvable functions, an emergent property at the mesoscale interface between sequence evolution, molecular structure, and cellular regulation.

title: Integrative Multi-Omics Synthesis to Identify Shared Molecular Mechanisms of Mammalian Hibernation
title_norm: integrative multiomics synthesis to identify shared molecular mechanisms of mammalian hibernation
abstract_text: Mammalian hibernation is a distinct physiological state involving decreased metabolism, lowered body temperature, and fasting, making the investigation of its underlying gene expression mechanisms crucial for understanding metabolic adaptation across taxa. To identify conserved molecular processes controlling metabolic suppression, this project will map gene orthology and model longitudinal gene expression changes between active and hibernating states using custom bivariate Ornstein Uhlenbeck trait evolution models. The study will integrate Sequence Read Archive RNA sequencing datasets and reference genomes across multiple tissues by processing raw reads through a uniform mapping pipeline and cross referencing species data via orthology maps. Identifying these conserved differentially regulated genes will clarify mammalian metabolic evolution and establish a biological foundation for downstream research concerning human metabolic regulation, ischemia tolerance, and organ preservation.
full_text: This project investigates mammalian hibernation to determine if metabolic suppression relies on shared or lineage specific transcriptional mechanisms. Although transcript data exists for individual hibernating mammals the field lacks comparative analyses of expression across multiple species. The proposed study identifies conserved genes for metabolic suppression to clarify mammalian evolution and inform human organ preservation. The team integrates RNA sequencing data from multiple tissues to model changes of gene expression using phylogenetic frameworks. The analytical pipeline incorporates transcript quantification with featureCounts alongside phylogenetic analyses using custom bivariate models of trait evolution. The proposed study will validate the custom bivariate models of trait evolution through the use of simulation tests. The project uses public RNA sequencing data from the Sequence Read Archive alongside published genomes and sequence alignments. The team integrates distinct datasets through uniform processing pipelines and maps of gene orthology derived from genome alignments. The team will mitigate sparse sampling of tissues across species by developing phylogenetic tools to handle missing data. The two year timeline begins with transcript processing and concludes with data synthesis and preparation of academic manuscripts. Managing these diverse variables requires a cross disciplinary team with distinct expertise in molecular biology and computational phylogenetics. The team will distribute project findings through primary literature alongside open source software and datasets of hibernation studies. This diverse research group spans multiple career stages and provides technical mentoring for support personnel in the laboratory.

Despite decades of study, the shared molecular and cellular regulatory mechanisms that drive and sustain hibernation remain largely unresolved. This project aims to unify existing omics-scale datasets, mostly transcriptomic, from numerous hibernating mammals to identify conserved pathways and molecular signatures underlying this extreme phenotype. Our project will leverage publicly available datasets and apply cutting-edge computational tools that are developed in the context of this project to analyze transcriptional variation underlying hibernation in a phylogenetic context.

title: Revealing the Ontology of Allostery through Community-Scale Synthesis
title_norm: revealing the ontology of allostery through communityscale synthesis
abstract_text: Protein biophysics and molecular evolution research investigates allosteric regulation in transporter proteins including the P type ATPase superfamily, utilizing existing databases and algorithms to catalog regulated proteins and predict binding sites. This project will identify amino acid sites controlling allosteric mechanisms and determine their evolutionary origins by statistically comparing transporter families using tools including AlphaFold, Direct Coupling Analysis, and Adaptive Steered Molecular Dynamics. The study will integrate data from UniProt, InterPro, the Protein Data Bank, and the Allosteric Database to build an augmented allosterome database combining sequence alignments, protein structures, and molecular dynamics trajectories. Identifying these allosteric control sites will enable the annotation of uncharacterized allosteric systems, the interpretation of disease associated mutations, and the experimental design of synthetic allosteric proteins.
full_text: Existing databases catalog regulated proteins and algorithms predict binding sites but lack curated negative examples of non regulated proteins. The proposed study compares transporter homologs to uncover allosteric mechanisms and enable the experimental design of synthetic allosteric proteins. The team will assemble a comparative database of transporter families and map evolutionary landscapes through statistical comparisons of properties. The methodology utilizes AlphaFold and PyTorch alongside established methods for direct coupling analysis and adaptive steered molecular dynamics. The team will benchmark results by testing the ability of models to categorize proteins and propose functional point mutations. The study draws data from the Protein Data Bank (PDB) and the Allosteric Database (ASD) alongside the UniProt repository. The team will build an augmented database by combining structural data and sequence alignments for fifty distinct protein families. The team will mitigate the known lack of negative examples by utilizing domain insertions as proxy markers for allosteric regulation. The two year timeline progresses from data curation and analysis to the final evaluation of models and manuscript preparation. This project requires multi lab collaboration to combine diverse expertise in machine learning and the computational modeling of molecular evolution. The team will publish their evolutionary findings and host the augmented database publicly on the CyVerse platform for community access. The research group features principal investigators and staff scientists specializing in machine learning and the biophysics of chemical materials.

abstract_original: Allostery is a fundamental property of proteins wherein perturbations at one site can influence another distant site. Understanding the sequence, structural, and dynamic determinants of allostery is critical to engineering new biosensors, designing allosteric modulators, and predicting the functional impact of mutations. For many proteins, allostery allows control of protein activity in response to external stimuli, such as ligand binding, protein or nucleic acid interactions, post-translational modifications, light, and redox state. There are proteins, though, that do not clearly exhibit such regulatory mechanisms, and are thus rarely included in publicly available allosteric databases. Consequently, it remains unclear what features distinguish regulated systems and regulatory sites from their non-regulated counterparts. To this end, we will focus our work on a specific class of proteins—namely transporter proteins—and assemble a database that is, on the one hand, very specific—restricted to all such proteins, and broad because it includes proteins for which there is a lack of evidence for allosteric regulation. This augmented allosteric database will provide a basis for identifying the degree of allostery in proteins. Through these databases, and associated computational interrogations, we will reveal the determinants of allostery in transporter proteins, a large and diverse family of membrane proteins comprised of allosteric and non-allosteric members.

title: SynEvo: Discovering Evolutionary Principles of Molecular Organization through Cross-Species Data Synthesis
title_norm: synevo discovering evolutionary principles of molecular organization through crossspecies data synthesis
abstract_text: Evolutionary systems biology studies the intermediate scale organization of gene regulation and metabolism in humans and mosquitoes, demanding the integration of population genetic variation with cross species multi omics data through biochemical models. Currently, no analytical framework connects population level genetic variation with isolated cross species multi omics data to explain how evolution structures regulatory and metabolic networks. This project will develop a machine learning framework using graph neural networks, variational autoencoders, and genome scale metabolic models to merge population genetics with multi omics data, determining the rules that govern cross species network adaptation. A standardized pipeline will integrate datasets from GTEx, TOPMed, Ag1000G, and VectorBase with databases like Reactome and BiGG through metadata harmonization and cross species feature alignment based on orthology frameworks and pathway scaffolds. This research will yield a novel framework that maps physiologically plausible network modules, providing fundamental knowledge directly applicable to evolutionary theory, human health, and vector biology.
full_text: Evolutionary systems biology lacks frameworks connecting population level genetic variation with intermediate scale organization for humans and mosquitoes. Systems biology models network dynamics using isolated datasets while integration with population genetics through biochemical models remains incomplete. The proposed study develops machine learning frameworks to determine network adaptation rules benefiting human health and vector biology. The study design utilizes hybrid machine learning models and cross species manifold alignment to identify conserved network modules. Key methods incorporate variational autoencoders and graph neural networks alongside genome scale metabolic models and orthology mapping tools. The team validates results through cross validation and benchmarks findings against flux balance analysis and curated pathway databases. The study utilizes population datasets from GTEx and All of Us alongside pathway databases including Reactome and BiGG. A standardized pipeline integrates these distinct datasets through metadata harmonization and cross species feature alignment using orthology frameworks. The team mitigates data sparsity for mosquito variants by prioritizing human datasets and developing adaptable transfer learning models. The two year timeline progresses from data harmonization and model training toward the final release of comprehensive toolkits. This project requires cross disciplinary collaboration to merge specialized expertise spanning machine learning and genome scale metabolic modeling. The project distributes version controlled workflows and interactive atlas data through open access repositories alongside comprehensive training materials. The team features principal investigators and staff scientists who provide mentorship for students and host specialized instructional workshops.

abstract_original: Living systems exhibit emergent organization that bridges molecular and evolutionary scales. Genetic variation, regulatory control, and metabolic dynamics interact across levels of complexity to produce coordinated cellular behavior, yet most datasets capture only one layer at a time. Despite vast genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, and metabolomic resources across species and environments, no synthesis framework connects these data to reveal how evolutionary forces shape the mesoscale—the intermediate level where genes, proteins, and metabolites assemble into adaptive networks. The SynEvo Working Group will develop a machine-learning–driven synthesis framework that unites population-genetic and multi-omics data to uncover conserved and divergent axes of molecular organization. Using well-characterized human and mosquito datasets, we will identify how genetic variation, regulatory control, and metabolic flux interact to produce conserved mesoscale modules reflecting evolutionary constraint and innovation. These contrasting systems serve as testbeds for uncovering evolutionary design principles of molecular coordination—how selection and constraint shape regulatory–metabolic organization across life. SynEvo integrates interpretable machine learning with genome-scale metabolic (GEM) and MiReN (Minimal Regulatory Network; MILP-based regulatory inference) approaches, producing an open SynEvo Atlas hosted within NCEMS infrastructure—a reusable resource for evolutionary systems biology. By revealing both species- specific adaptations and conserved mesoscale design principles, SynEvo will advance conceptual and computational frontiers, providing fundamental insight into how life organizes itself across molecular, physiological, and evolutionary dimensions, with applications to human health, malaria transmission, and environmental resilience.

title: A Unified Framework for Analyses of Proteome Turnover Dynamics
title_norm: a unified framework for analyses of proteome turnover dynamics
abstract_text: The proteostasis domain focuses on protein turnover rates across species and kingdoms of life, recognizing that degradation signals and protein stability mechanisms exhibit broad conservation throughout evolutionary history. This project will construct the Protein Stability Database to analyze protein turnover conservation by standardizing public data, refitting measurements using uniform kinetic models, and applying deep neural networks and protein language models to correlate biophysical traits with degradation rates. Dynamic labeling mass spectrometry data from the PRIDE repository will be integrated with structural and thermodynamic databases by reanalyzing raw intensity data using uniform kinetic models and controlled vocabularies for experimental metadata. This research will produce a standardized metadata resource connecting protein half lives to molecular features, enabling comprehensive cross kingdom comparisons of biophysical properties that govern protein turnover across species.
full_text: This proteostasis research investigates rates of protein turnover to understand how molecular mechanisms determine protein stability across different evolutionary contexts. Eukaryotic degradation signals exhibit broad conservation but unstructured existing datasets obscure how sequence properties and proteostasis networks determine protein lifetimes. This project builds a standardized database to analyze evolutionary conservation and identify biophysical properties governing cross kingdom protein turnover. The study design standardizes public data regarding turnover by refitting measurements with uniform models and applying machine learning to orthologs. Methods involve exponential decay modeling and Bayesian sampling combined with deep neural networks and protein language models including ESM2. Validation of model performance requires calculating reconstruction loss for proteins with fast turnover and measuring prediction accuracy against established databases. Primary sources feature mass spectrometry data from PRIDE alongside structural predictions from AlphaFold and repositories of genomic sequences including OrthoDB. Data integration involves reanalyzing raw intensities with uniform kinetic models and combining resulting rates with corresponding structural and omics variables. The team mitigates incompatible formats of data and physiological variations by correcting enrichment kinetics and applying unified models with metadata. The two year timeline spans initial development of the database during the first year and subsequent validation of models. The project requires cross disciplinary collaboration because harmonizing quantitative mass spectrometry data with computational modeling exceeds individual laboratory capacity. The project provides open access to the resulting database and analytical code through established repositories including CyVerse and GitHub. The research team includes principal investigators from proteomics and computational biology working alongside staff scientists to provide training opportunities.

abstract_original: Proteins vary widely in how long they persist within cells, from minutes to years, and this variation plays a central role in regulating biological function and maintaining cellular homeostasis. Decades of research have revealed several mechanisms that influence protein half-lives across the kingdoms of life. However, the differential impact of these mechanisms on protein half-lives within and between species remains incompletely understood. This knowledge gap can be addressed by comprehensive analyses of global proteome stability datasets enabled by recent advances in mass spectrometry-based proteomics. However, these datasets are currently fragmented across heterogeneous studies that are not easily amenable to meta-analysis. This Working Group will bring together complementary expertise in proteomics, computational biology, systems biochemistry, and evolution to systematically harmonize and integrate publicly available datasets on protein turnover across four representative species across two kingdoms of life - E. coli, S. cerevisiae, M. musculus, and H. sapiens. By reanalyzing existing data using consistent approaches and unifying metadata standards, we will generate a comprehensive, comparable, and publicly accessible resource, the Protein Stability Database (PSD). This database will enable us to identify the molecular and evolutionary principles that govern protein stability and assess how turnover patterns vary across different cell types and organisms. Beyond addressing these core questions, our Working Group aims to establish best practices and a shared vocabulary for measuring and reporting protein turnover, enabling seamless incorporation of future datasets and integration with other NCEMS data resources.

title: Predictive Synthesis Framework for Elucidating Biophysical Cell State from Spatial Transcriptomics and Proteomics
title_norm: predictive synthesis framework for elucidating biophysical cell state from spatial transcriptomics and proteomics
abstract_text: The spatial omics field evaluates how subcellular molecular location influences cellular function, making the integration of spatial transcriptomics and spatial proteomics essential because bulk RNA and protein levels correlate poorly. Current analytical methods evaluate molecular abundances separately because the technical difficulty of aligning adjacent tissue sections restricts the ability to measure how subcellular organization determines cell behavior. This project will build a computational framework utilizing STalign diffeomorphic mapping, SEraster grid harmonization, and SubCell deep learning models with contrastive multimodal embedding algorithms to extract spatial relationships and predict cell fate decisions. The study will integrate human cancer datasets from the Spatch database by registering adjacent spatial transcriptomics and spatial proteomics sections into a common coordinate framework rasterized onto a shared pixel grid. This framework will shift spatial omics from abundance only observations to predictive models that link spatial molecular patterns directly to biophysical mechanisms and cellular phenotypes.
full_text: The field of spatial omics analyzes subcellular organization and lacks tools to integrate RNA and protein spatial locations. Subcellular location influences cellular function while difficult alignment of adjacent tissue sections limits comparisons of RNA and proteins. This computational framework tests whether integrated spatial relationships predict cell states better than abundance to uncover biophysical mechanisms. The strategy maps adjacent tissue sections onto a shared grid to train models for classification of cell states. Key tools include mapping algorithms like STalign and SEraster alongside deep learning models like SubCell for contrastive embedding. The team will benchmark results against models of abundance and validate the alignments using root mean square errors. The project utilizes the public Spatch database of human cancers and additional cohorts containing transcriptomic and proteomic data. The team will integrate distinct datasets by registering tissue sections into a common coordinate framework to generate patches. Adjacent tissue sections undergo non rigid distortions during imaging and the team will apply non linear alignment algorithms. The project spans two years and includes intermediate milestones for data harmonization before final release of a toolchain. The scope requires cross disciplinary collaboration to combine expertise in machine learning and biophysics with scalable computing infrastructure. The team will release code and harmonized datasets under permissive licenses alongside a peer reviewed publication of findings. The collaborative team includes principal investigators specializing in artificial intelligence and staff scientists with expertise in cloud computing.

abstract_original: Cell states reflect not only molecular abundance but also where molecules reside. Public spatial omics (Spatch) now provide high-plex RNA (Xenium/CosMx) and protein (CODEX) maps, yet cross-modal synthesis at subcellular scales remain fragmented. We will develop an open, end-to-end synthesis framework that (i) registers adjacent-section spatial RNA-Protein images at subcellular resolution using diffeomorphic alignment (STalign), (ii) harmonizes RNA features into protein-scale rasters (SEraster) to create a one-to-one correspondence of patches to be compared (iii) quantify membrane/nuclear proximity, polarity, local density, and other features (iv) trains RNA-to-protein predictors and learn a unified biophysical fingerprint of cell state. Using the paired Xenium/CosMx-CODEX cancer atlas as a validation set and curated public cohorts as application sets, we will benchmark against abundance-only baselines. Framework performance will be assessed by overall registration quality, verified patch correspondence, and cross-modal predictive accuracy, with appropriate positive and negative controls to rule out leakage and spurious structure. We will test the hypotheses that RNA-protein spatial relationships yield predictive signals for cell state beyond abundance and that low- dimensional biophysical fingerprints precede and predict cell fate decisions. All code, trained models, and harmonized datasets generated from this work will be released under permissive licenses with containerized, reproducible workflows and scheduled public snapshots. This community-scale synthesis will convert dispersed spatial imaging datasets into predictive, interpretable models of cell state, while leveraging NCEMS (CyVerse compute, data harmonization, and project management) for scalable analysis and dissemination.

title: A Cross-Crop Data Synthesis of Circadian-Gated Vesicle Trafficking Nodes That Constrain Cytokinesis Under Heat Stress
title_norm: a crosscrop data synthesis of circadiangated vesicle trafficking nodes that constrain cytokinesis under heat stress
abstract_text: Plant cytokinesis depends on cell plate biogenesis via the phragmoplast and vesicle trafficking system, which represent critical developmental processes that are regulated by circadian timing and frequently disrupted by heat stress. This project will determine if time of day influences the thermal sensitivity of trafficking genes across annual and perennial plant species by applying computational pipelines and network frameworks to build context specific gene expression models. The study will integrate public sequencing and live cell imaging repositories by standardizing metadata, processing raw RNA sequencing data into comparable expression matrices, and connecting distinct species datasets through genome anchored orthology maps. This research will identify novel regulatory genes that connect endomembrane trafficking with thermal physiology to inform future agricultural strategies for mitigating heat induced yield loss in essential crops.
full_text: This project investigates plant cytokinesis to determine if circadian timing modulates impacts of heat stress on regulators of trafficking. The proposed study connects distinct physiological fields to evaluate thermal sensitivity of genes and mitigate loss of crop yield. The analytical strategy builds networks of gene expression from public omics data to compare annual and perennial plant species. Analytical workflows process RNA-seq data while Knowledge Independent Network Construction (KINC) frameworks build networks using models of covariates. The team will benchmark analytical pipelines against held out data and validate candidate genes using live cell imaging. Datasets include the Sequence Read Archive (SRA) and Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) alongside repositories for live cell imaging. The team will process raw sequencing data through a unified pipeline and connect species data using orthology maps. Confounding variations in public data will be mitigated by incorporating models of covariates to remove spurious statistical relationships. Project milestones include curation of data followed by harmonization and construction of networks prior to cross modal validation. This project requires cross disciplinary collaboration across five laboratories to integrate expertise in cell biology and network construction. The team will deposit code in GitHub and release analysis notebooks alongside preprints to ensure open science practices. The team includes a postdoctoral researcher and graduate students who will receive training in cross institution data integration.

abstract_original: Plant cytokinesis depends on the coordinated delivery of Golgi- and trans-Golgi network (TGN)-derived vesicles to the phragmoplast midzone, where they fuse to build the new cell plate. Heat stress destabilizes this process, but it remains unclear whether thermal sensitivity of cytokinesis is a fixed molecular property or is instead modulated by the time of day at which heat occurs—an interaction long documented for other stress-responsive pathways but never examined at the level of membrane trafficking machinery that builds the mesoscale structures underlying cell division. This project will synthesize publicly available transcriptomic, proteomic, and genomic datasets across a phylogenetically diverse panel of species (Arabidopsis, maize, sorghum, wheat, and perennial crops such as apple, pear, and peach for which chromosome-scale genomes already exist) to test whether circadian gating of heat-responsive gene expression converges on a conserved, tractable set of endomembrane trafficking regulators required for cell plate biogenesis. We will assemble a curated compendium of RNA-seq experiments that vary time-of-day and temperature treatment, reprocess them through standardized, reproducible pipelines (e.g., GEMmaker/Nextflow) to generate harmonized gene expression matrices, and construct context-specific gene co-expression networks that explicitly model and remove confounding technical and biological variables. The project directly targets a mesoscale emergent property (how sub-organellar trafficking coordination scales up to determine whether a cell successfully divides under stress) and cannot be addressed by any single dataset or lab alone. All harmonized expression matrices, network models, and analysis workflows will be released as an open, versioned resource, and the project will train graduate students and postdocs in reproducible multi-species network biology, cross-institution data integration, and comparative genomics, building a template for future mesoscale synthesis efforts linking gene regulatory dynamics to subcellular structural outcomes.

title: From Nucleosome Mechanics to Cell-Type Identity: A Multiscale Synthesis of Chromatin Polymer Physics, Condensate Biochemistry, and Single-Cell 3D Genomes to Explain Disease-Relevant Genome Folding in the Human Brain
title_norm: from nucleosome mechanics to celltype identity a multiscale synthesis of chromatin polymer physics condensate biochemistry and singlecell 3d genomes to explain diseaserelevant genome folding in the human brain
abstract_text: Mesoscale chromatin organization links nanometer nucleosome interactions and biomolecular condensates to megabase compartments across brain cell types, representing a critical mechanism underlying cell type specific diseases including schizophrenia and Alzheimer's disease. Current high resolution structural and population datasets remain disconnected, leaving a gap in mechanistic models that connect nucleosome biophysics to cell type specific chromatin folding and genetic disease risks. This project will build a multiscale chromatin simulation framework by parameterizing coarse grained polymer models with structural data, executing mesoscale simulations to test condensate forming mechanisms, and mapping genetic variants using statistical colocalization analyses. The research will integrate cryo EM structures and single cell diploid 3D genomes to parameterize polymer interactions, subsequently overlaying the predicted physical chromatin states onto brain wide eQTL atlases and GWAS summary statistics. This framework will provide a mechanistic explanation for why specific variants cause cell type restricted phenotypes, converting correlative genetic associations in psychiatric and neuroimmune conditions into testable structural hypotheses.
full_text: The domain of mesoscale chromatin organization requires models linking the biophysics of nucleosomes to large scale folding in brains. Current studies detail structural physics and genomic architectures but these distinct fields remain disconnected from datasets of population genetics. This study builds a simulation framework to provide structural explanations for how specific genetic variants cause restricted human diseases. The core strategy parameterizes models of polymers and benchmarks simulated structures against single cell genomes before overlaying physical states. Key methods include simulations of mesoscale chromatin and comparisons of nested models alongside approaches for stratified enrichment and colocalization. Results undergo validation against empirical single cell structures and orthogonal datasets using specific protocols that are registered in advance. Datasets feature single cell genomes and cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structures from public repositories like the Sequence Read Archive. The team will harmonize structural measurements to parameterize interaction terms before overlaying predicted annotations onto datasets of population genetics. The team addresses incompatible resolutions and formats through structural integration sessions and the collaborative development of bridging computational pipelines. The timeline involves two workshops per year and virtual sprints to achieve three phases of parameterization and genomic mapping. This project requires cross disciplinary collaboration because no single laboratory possesses the required expertise across structural biophysics and genomics. The team will deposit harmonized data into public repositories and publish software featuring containerized environments under open source licenses. The team spans multiple career stages and offers trainees funded workshops alongside educational modules that pair biophysics with genomics.

abstract_original: A central unsolved puzzle in molecular and cellular biology is how nanometer-scale nucleosome-nucleosome interactions and biomolecular condensate formation give rise to megabase-scale chromatin compartments and loop domains that differ systematically across human cell types—and how these emergent architectures channel genetic risk into cell-type-specific disease phenotypes. This gap sits squarely at the mesoscale NCEMS prioritizes: it cannot be resolved by structural biology, polymer physics, or population genetics alone, but requires their synthesis. This Working Group proposes to integrate four classes of existing public data that have never been jointly modeled: (1) single-cell diploid 3D genome structures (Dip-C/scHi-C) spanning dozens of human and mouse brain cell types; (2) nucleosome- and chromatin-fiber-resolution structural and simulation data (cryo-EM structures of pioneer-factor–nucleosome complexes, mesoscale oligonucleosome models, cohesin-loop Hi-C perturbation datasets); (3) biochemical and structural characterizations of chromatin-associated condensate components (corepressor oligomers, histone-modifying enzyme complexes, RNA-binding proteins undergoing liquid-liquid phase separation); and (4) population-scale functional genomics linking genetic variation to cell-type-specific gene expression and disease risk (brain-wide eQTL atlases, GWAS summary statistics for schizophrenia, multiple sclerosis, and Alzheimer's disease). Our central hypothesis is that cell-type-specific genome folding emerges from a hierarchy of physical rules—entropic and electrostatic steric pressures generated by intrinsically disordered chromatin regulators at the nucleosome scale, cooperative condensate formation by transcriptional corepressor/coactivator complexes at the sub-domain scale, and loop-extrusion/compartmentalization dynamics at the topologically associating domain scale—and that this hierarchy is a mechanistic intermediate between GWAS variants and their cell-type-restricted phenotypic effects. We will build coarse-grained, mechanistically grounded polymer models of chromatin fibers parameterized from structural and biophysical data, validate emergent compartment and loop predictions against single-cell Dip-C structures across neuronal and glial subtypes, and test whether condensate-forming regulatory complexes (e.g., corepressor tetramers, methyltransferase-associated assemblies, RNA-binding phase-separating proteins) quantitatively explain observed heterochromatin/euchromatin partitioning differences between cell types. We will then map disease-associated eQTL and GWAS loci onto these physically resolved chromatin states to ask whether variants disrupting predicted condensate-nucleation or loop-anchor regions preferentially explain the cell-type specificity of psychiatric versus neuroimmune disease associations already reported in public datasets. This effort requires collaboration across structural biophysics, polymer theory, single-cell genomics, and population-scale systems immunology/genetics—expertise that no single lab possesses, but that our team collectively spans. Deliverables include an open, versioned multiscale chromatin simulation framework linked to public single-cell 3D genome and eQTL/GWAS resources, reproducible pipelines for condensate-informed loop-domain prediction, and training modules pairing biophysical modeling with population genomics for graduate students and postdocs across participating institutions. By unifying nucleosome-scale biophysics with population-scale genetics through existing data alone, this project exemplifies community-scale synthesis: resolving how physical emergence at the mesoscale of chromatin organization constrains and explains cellular identity and disease susceptibility in the human brain.

title: Functional Redundancy as a Mesoscale Buffer: Synthesizing Ancient and Modern Metagenomes with Host Proteo-Genomic Atlases to Test the Stability of Microbiome-Host Molecular Modules
title_norm: functional redundancy as a mesoscale buffer synthesizing ancient and modern metagenomes with host proteogenomic atlases to test the stability of microbiomehost molecular modules
abstract_text: Microbial ecology investigates how microbial functional modules couple to host molecular physiology, a critical phenomenon because microbiome associated host phenotypes remain highly stable despite extensive variation in underlying microbial taxonomy. To determine if functional modules associate with host circulating proteins and metabolites independently of taxa over evolutionary time, this data synthesis project will apply DIAMOND, MEGAN, and Mendelian randomization to diverse metagenomes. Data from the Human Microbiome Project, UK Biobank, and ancient metagenome archives will be standardized into a cross cohort functional module abundance atlas and linked to host proteogenomic profiles using statistical genetics methods. This research will provide a novel framework to differentiate between emergent functional properties and taxon specific correlations, significantly improving the prioritization of biomarkers and therapeutic targets for microbiome related conditions.
full_text: This microbial ecology project studies microbial functional modules to address gaps in testing across modern and evolutionary timescales. Host phenotypes associated with microbiomes remain stable but understanding of this functional stability across different eras is incomplete. The primary research question explores if these functional associations remain conserved over time to prioritize biomarkers for therapeutics. The overall study design utilizes a data synthesis approach to construct indices of redundancy and integrate host data. Key methods include algorithms for taxonomic binning and models of statistical genetics such as Mendelian randomization and colocalization. The proposed study will validate results by testing findings against independent modern cohorts and datasets of ancient genomes. The project utilizes datasets from the Human Microbiome Project (HMP) and the GWAS Catalog alongside archives of ancient metagenomes. The team will integrate distinct datasets by standardizing information into an atlas of abundances for linkage with genetics. Known limitations of DNA damage and exogenous contamination will be mitigated using established protocols for authentication and screening. Proposed milestones consist of four consecutive stages including the harmonization of metagenomes and integration of host genetic data. The project scope requires cross disciplinary collaboration to synthesize specialized fields like theory of phylogenetic networks and statistical genetics. The team will release datasets under open licenses and containerize analytical code for public availability on platforms like GitHub. The team includes two postdoctoral researchers and one graduate student receiving cross disciplinary training in analysis of ancient DNA.

abstract_original:
A central puzzle in microbial ecology is why host phenotypes associated with the microbiome often remain stable despite enormous taxonomic turnover in microbial communities across individuals, populations, and evolutionary time. One resolution is that functional modules—conserved sets of microbial genes encoding metabolic pathways such as short-chain fatty acid synthesis, bile acid transformation, and tryptophan/indole metabolism—represent an emergent, mesoscale level of biological organization that buffers taxonomic variability and directly couples to host molecular physiology. This project will synthesize publicly available shotgun metagenomic data spanning contemporary human cohorts (Human Microbiome Project, MetaHIT, curatedMetagenomicData, MiBioGen) and ancient microbiomes (dental calculus, paleofeces, and archived shotgun datasets from Paleolithic through historical periods) with large-scale human proteogenomic and metabolomic resources (UK Biobank Pharma Proteomics Project, plasma cis-pQTL maps, NMR metabolomic panels) to test whether specific microbial functional modules show consistent, genetically anchored associations with host circulating protein and metabolite networks, independent of which taxa or strains carry them, and whether this coupling is stable across evolutionary timescales.

We will reprocess all metagenomes using a standardized DIAMOND+MEGAN-based taxonomic and functional binning pipeline to build a harmonized cross-cohort, cross-era atlas of functional module abundance, explicitly accounting for degradation and contamination artifacts characteristic of low-biomass ancient samples using established authentication and decontamination frameworks. Strain- and gene-family-level phylogenetic network methods (NeighborNet and related split-decomposition approaches) will be used to quantify the degree of taxonomic substitutability underlying each functional module, generating a quantitative 'redundancy index' per pathway. In parallel, we will mine existing microbiome-host GWAS summary statistics and cis-pQTL/metabolite-QTL resources to identify host genetic variants associated with both circulating protein/metabolite levels and microbiome functional module abundance, applying Mendelian randomization and genetic colocalization to test causal or bidirectional relationships between microbial functional capacity and host proteomic/metabolomic states. Modules showing robust host-molecular coupling in modern cohorts will then be evaluated in ancient samples paired with available ancient human genomic data, providing a natural, deep-time test of whether these host-microbiome molecular relationships are evolutionarily conserved or population/era-specific artifacts of recent lifestyle change.

This synthesis requires integrating expertise unavailable within any single laboratory: metagenomic algorithm development and phylogenetic network theory, ancient DNA authentication and low-biomass contamination control, and human proteogenomic/statistical genetics analysis at biobank scale. The resulting open-access resource—a versioned, reproducible workflow and 'Microbiome Functional-Host Proteome Atlas' spanning contemporary and ancient timescales—will provide the field with a principled, falsifiable framework for identifying which microbiome-associated molecular phenotypes represent robust emergent mesoscale properties versus incidental, taxon-specific correlations, directly informing biomarker and therapeutic target prioritization in microbiome-related disease research. All code, intermediate outputs, and harmonized datasets will be deposited under FAIR principles, with structured training modules for graduate students and postdocs spanning computational metagenomics, paleogenomics, and human genetics.

title: Mapping the Coupling Between Regulatory Cell-State Transitions and Mesoscale Condensate Architecture Across the Bacterial Kingdom
title_norm: mapping the coupling between regulatory cellstate transitions and mesoscale condensate architecture across the bacterial kingdom
abstract_text: The research domain of bacterial cell biology and biomolecular condensate biophysics examines phase separated mesoscale protein assemblies, which are important because bacteria utilize these structures for cellular compartmentalization. The critical scientific gap is whether gene regulatory networks systematically encode the spatial reorganization and phase assembly of bacterial mesoscale structures during physiological transitions. The primary objective will create a cross species atlas linking bacterial regulatory states to phase separation propensity by applying sequence based biophysical predictors, associative polymer models, and mixed effects regression to synthesize transcriptomic and proteomic data. This project will integrate PRECISE, COLOMBOS, PaxDb, ALEdb, and isolate repositories by harmonizing metadata with controlled vocabulary ontologies and mapping matched transcriptomic and proteomic data to genome wide phase separation propensity scores. The resulting cross species atlas will establish whether bacterial spatial organization represents an actively programmed regulatory output rather than a passive biophysical byproduct.
full_text: This project merges bacterial biology and condensate biophysics to determine if regulatory networks encode phase separated assemblies during transitions. The team will build a cross species atlas to determine if spatial organization represents an actively programmed regulatory output. A three phase computational strategy will integrate transcriptomic and proteomic data with polymer physics models of condensate phase behavior. The researchers will apply sequence based biophysical predictors (catGRANULE) alongside associative polymer models and mixed effects regression techniques. Transcript level inferences will be cross validated against protein abundance data and model predictions will undergo benchmarking against experimental literature. The study will utilize established RNA-seq collections (PRECISE) and the PaxDb proteomic database alongside the ALEdb evolution dataset. The team will integrate datasets by harmonizing metadata with controlled vocabulary ontologies and mapping information to phase separation scores. The researchers will mitigate technical batch effects and phylogenetic dependencies by controlling for these variables within mixed effects models. Milestones include completing an expression to propensity atlas and conducting biophysical translation alongside the execution of evolutionary genomic integration. This project requires cross disciplinary collaboration because simultaneous expertise across network biology and condensate biophysics exceeds single laboratory capabilities. The team will share data and code via public repositories (Zenodo) while openly distributing all scientific findings through preprints. The research group includes principal investigators and trainees who will receive cross disciplinary training across evolutionary biology and biophysics.

abstract_original:
Bacteria lack membrane-bound organelles, yet an increasing number of proteinaceous mesoscale assemblies—BR-bodies, PopZ microdomains, ParB/parS partition complexes, cold-shock and stress granules—are now recognized as functionally important, phase-separated or phase-separation-like structures. What remains unknown is whether the assembly and disassembly of these structures is systematically encoded in the transcriptional and regulatory logic of the cell, such that physiological transitions (growth phase, stress, quorum-sensing state, biofilm commitment) predictably reorganize the mesoscale proteome. This project will synthesize three classes of public data that have never been jointly analyzed at scale: (1) large bacterial gene-expression compendia spanning thousands of conditions and dozens of species (e.g., PRECISE, COLOMBOS, SRA-derived RNA-seq collections, proteomic abundance databases such as PaxDb), (2) sequence-based biophysical predictors of phase-separation propensity and intrinsic disorder (catGRANULE, PScore, FuzDrop) applied proteome-wide, and (3) curated experimental catalogs of known bacterial condensate components together with comparative genomic and evolution-experiment data (ALEdb, clinical isolate genome collections, long-term evolution lineages) documenting mutations in regulatory circuits such as quorum-sensing systems and efflux pumps.

The working group will first build a cross-species atlas linking condition-specific transcriptional/proteomic states to the predicted phase-separation propensity of the expressed proteome, testing whether physiological transitions (e.g., entry into stationary phase, quorum-sensing activation, envelope stress) are consistently accompanied by co-regulated shifts in the abundance of high-propensity, disorder-rich proteins relative to their low-propensity partners. This addresses a mesoscale question central to NCEMS's mission: does gene-regulatory network architecture function, in part, as a control layer for mesoscale self-organization, translating discrete transcriptional states into emergent, spatially organized biomolecular assemblies? Second, using biophysical/polymer-based condensate models—of the associative-polymer type used to explain multiphase architecture and viscosity tuning in reconstituted systems—the team will translate measured or inferred stoichiometric shifts in expression atlases into predictions of condensate composition, phase boundaries, and internal architecture, generating testable hypotheses about which regulons are poised to nucleate or dissolve specific mesoscale structures under specific conditions. Third, the team will exploit existing evolution-experiment and clinical-isolate genomic datasets to ask whether naturally occurring or experimentally evolved loss-of-function mutations in regulatory genes (quorum-sensing regulators, efflux pumps, two-component systems) shift the expression balance of condensate-forming proteins, thereby altering emergent mesoscale organization as a byproduct of adaptive evolution—paralleling known cases where regulatory mutations have unexpected downstream physiological consequences.

This synthesis requires integrating expertise in bacterial evolutionary genomics and regulatory network biology with quantitative condensate biophysics and polymer theory, a combination not resident in any single laboratory. It leverages exclusively existing public datasets, produces an open, versioned, and queryable atlas linking transcriptomic state to predicted mesoscale organization across bacterial diversity, and provides trainees hands-on experience integrating heterogeneous omics, evolutionary, and biophysical modeling data—directly building the data-science workforce NCEMS aims to cultivate while addressing a fundamental, previously unaddressed question about the origins of mesoscale order in cells lacking organelles.

title: Nonlinear Collapse of Protein Interaction Networks at Stability Thresholds: A Cross-Kingdom Synthesis of Deep Mutational Scanning and Interactome Data
title_norm: nonlinear collapse of protein interaction networks at stability thresholds a crosskingdom synthesis of deep mutational scanning and interactome data
abstract_text: Molecular systems biology explores how interaction networks buffer destabilizing mutations, a phenomenon crucial for understanding proteome scale robustness in human membrane proteins and plant cytosolic immune regulators. This project will determine whether network connectivity dictates mutation tolerance by harmonizing stability and topology data to model nonlinear functional collapse thresholds using changepoint detection, percolation simulations, and single cell transcriptomic coexpression via a modular Python pipeline. Stability measurements from MaveDB and ProteinGym, interactomes from BioGRID and STRING, and evolutionary data from gnomAD will be synthesized by standardizing variant coordinates and linking them to unified graph representations. This research will yield a quantitative framework predicting when mutations become pathogenic or adaptive, informing variant effect interpretation in human diseases and clarifying plant immune network robustness.
full_text: This molecular systems biology project investigates if interaction network positions predict phenotypic tolerance to biophysically destabilizing protein mutations. Large independent datasets demonstrate nonlinear mutational effects but lack integration to explain phenotypic robustness across proteome scale networks. The study asks if network connectivity dictates mutation tolerance thresholds to establish predictive frameworks for disease and adaptation. The design harmonizes datasets to model interactions of thermodynamic stability and network topology using single cell transcriptomic profiles. A modular Python pipeline will execute network centrality calculations and changepoint detection and percolation simulations for robustness analysis. The simulated network collapse points will undergo validation against independent phenotypic measurements of surface trafficking and immune signaling. Data sources incorporate thermodynamic measurements from MaveDB and interaction networks from BioGRID alongside public single cell transcriptomic atlases. Synthesis involves standardizing thermodynamic units and mapping evolutionary annotations to unified graph representations of interactomes with centrality metrics. The team will mitigate heterogeneous data structures and curation biases through rigorous data harmonization and statistical sensitivity analyses. Proposed milestones sequentially encompass initial data harmonization and computational modeling before the integration of single cell transcriptomic datasets. The massive analytical scale necessitates cross disciplinary collaboration combining distinct expertise in protein thermodynamics and network systems biology. The researchers will share harmonized datasets and open source code through public repositories to ensure transparent open access. Graduate students and one postdoctoral researcher from three institutions will receive cross disciplinary training in biophysical network modeling.

A central puzzle in molecular systems biology is why some mutations that destabilize a protein produce negligible phenotypic consequences while others trigger abrupt, disproportionate loss of cellular function. We propose that this threshold-like behavior is an emergent property of the coupling between a protein's biophysical stability and its position within interaction networks, rather than an intrinsic property of the mutation itself. This working group will synthesize three classes of publicly available data that have never been jointly analyzed at scale: (1) proteome-wide thermodynamic stability measurements from deep mutational scanning and mega-scale stability assays (e.g., MaveDB, ProteinGym, Tsuboyama et al. stability atlas, deep receptor scanning datasets for GPCRs), (2) protein-protein and protein-DNA interaction network data from curated interactomes (BioGRID, STRING, IntAct, the Arabidopsis interactome AtPIN, and plant immune signaling networks), and (3) evolutionary and population-genetic datasets capturing selection on protein variants (gnomAD, ClinVar, dN/dS estimates, experimental evolution fitness landscapes).

Our central hypothesis, motivated by prior observations of threshold-like fitness relationships in antibiotic resistance enzymes and by the differential trafficking behavior of destabilized membrane proteins such as CFTR and GPCRs, is that network connectivity buffers the phenotypic consequences of destabilizing mutations up to a critical free-energy threshold, beyond which interaction networks undergo sharp, nonlinear rewiring or collapse. We predict that highly connected hub proteins exhibit wider stability buffering zones due to redundant or cooperative binding interfaces, while peripheral proteins collapse at smaller perturbations, and that this relationship generalizes across kingdoms despite divergent protein architectures (human membrane-embedded receptors and channels versus plant cytoplasmic immune regulators).

To test this, we will build a unified computational pipeline that maps ΔΔG values from deep mutational scanning onto network centrality metrics (degree, betweenness, clustering coefficient) and models how progressive destabilization propagates through interactome topology using percolation and network robustness frameworks. We will compare human disease-relevant systems (CFTR, GPCRs, KCNQ1-type ion channels) with plant immune signaling hubs (e.g., NPR1-centered networks) to ask whether energetic-topological coupling constitutes a conserved organizing principle of cellular systems or is contingent on compartment-specific biophysics (membrane insertion energetics versus cytosolic folding). Single-cell transcriptomic data will be incorporated to test whether cell-type-specific expression of interaction partners modulates the effective stability threshold in situ.

This project requires integration of expertise that no single lab possesses: membrane protein folding thermodynamics and pharmacological chaperone biophysics, network-based systems biology and plant immune signaling, and evolutionary protein biophysics and fitness landscape modeling. The resulting open-source framework, datasets, and reproducible workflows will be released publicly, and the project will train graduate students and postdocs in cross-disciplinary skills spanning biophysical modeling, network science, and comparative genomics, directly addressing NCEMS's mission to reveal mesoscale emergent principles connecting molecular energetics to cellular network behavior.

title: Sequence-to-Structure-to-Condensate: A Multi-Scale Synthesis Framework Linking RNA Secondary Structure Ensembles to Protein-RNA Condensate Composition and Emergent Material Properties
title_norm: sequencetostructuretocondensate a multiscale synthesis framework linking rna secondary structure ensembles to proteinrna condensate composition and emergent material properties
abstract_text: This research investigates biomolecular condensates, specifically stress granules, nucleoli, and paraspeckles, to understand how interactions between RNA binding proteins and RNA structural ensembles drive phase separation beyond conventional linear sequence motifs. The role of RNA structural conformations in dictating protein recruitment and condensate material properties remains unresolved because existing large scale datasets lack integration to test these structural hypotheses. The primary objective is to determine if RNA structural ensembles systematically control protein recruitment and condensate states by harmonizing datasets and applying structural energy modeling, gradient boosted trees, and neural networks. The study will integrate ENCODE, POSTAR3, RNAct, and structural probing datasets by mapping interaction, structure, and composition data onto a common GENCODE based genome build to compile a unified relational database. This work will yield a predictive framework introducing RNA structure as an independent variable, advancing the field beyond existing protein centric and sequence only models of biomolecular phase separation.
full_text: This project investigates biomolecular condensates during phase separation to resolve how RNA structural conformations govern recruitment of proteins. Current models attribute formation of condensates to protein disorder and sequence motifs while large independent datasets remain unintegrated. The proposed study asks if RNA structural ensembles systematically control recruitment of proteins to establish new predictive frameworks. The overall study design executes a computational synthesis of public datasets and structural descriptors to train supervised models. Key methods include calculation of base pairing probabilities and structural energy modeling alongside gradient boosted trees and neural networks. The team will validate findings against independent datasets and benchmark new algorithms against baseline models of sequence motifs. The project analyzes public databases including POSTAR3 and GENCODE alongside chemical probing information from the RNA Mapping Database. abstract_original:
Biomolecular condensates that concentrate RNA and RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) — stress granules, nucleoli, paraspeckles — display emergent material properties (viscosity, interfacial tension, multiphase architecture) that cannot be predicted from single-molecule biophysics alone. A major unresolved question is how the structural ensemble of RNA itself (not just its sequence composition or RBP motif content) shapes which proteins are recruited into a condensate and what physical state results. Despite an explosion of public data relevant to this question — large-scale RBP-RNA interactome datasets (CLIP-seq, eCLIP across ENCODE), condensate proteomic/transcriptomic atlases, high-throughput condensate-forming sequence screens, and computational RNA secondary/tertiary structure prediction tools — no existing resource integrates RNA structural information with condensate composition and biophysical outcome data at scale. This gap exists precisely because closing it requires expertise spanning RNA structural modeling, condensate biology/proteomics, and large-scale data integration — capabilities distributed across our two labs and beyond, and unattainable within a single lab's toolkit.

We propose a Working Group that assembles a harmonized, multi-database resource linking three previously siloed data types: (1) genome-wide RBP-RNA binding data (eCLIP/PAR-CLIP repositories, RNAct, POSTAR3), (2) predicted and experimentally-derived RNA structural ensembles (using established structure prediction and SHAPE/DMS chemical probing datasets deposited in the RNA Mapping Database and GEO), and (3) condensate composition and material property datasets, including proteomic/RNA-seq atlases of stress granules, nucleoli, and paraspeckles, plus recently published high-throughput pooled condensate-propensity screens covering thousands of protein sequences. We will further apply Rosetta-based structural energy modeling to characterize how RNA structural stability and flexibility relate to the multivalency principles known to govern phase separation, generating a predictive framework that goes beyond current sequence-only phase-separation predictors.

This synthesis requires reconciling incompatible experimental formats, resolving differing genome builds/annotations, and building shared computational pipelines across RNA structural biology and condensate proteomics — work far beyond any single lab's scope, and ideal for a distributed working group including trainees who will gain cross-disciplinary data science skills. Deliverables include an open-access integrated database and analysis pipeline (RNAstruct-Condensome), a set of testable structural determinants of RNA-driven condensate assembly, and machine-learning models predicting condensate partner recruitment from RNA structure. All workflows, code, and harmonized datasets will be released under open science standards, providing the community a reusable resource and establishing RNA structural context as a previously underappreciated axis of emergent mesoscale organization in the cell.

title: Decoding Environmental Selection Pressures on Condensate-Forming Sequence Grammars: A Multiscale Data Synthesis Across the Prokaryotic-to-Eukaryotic Thermal and Salinity Continuum
title_norm: decoding environmental selection pressures on condensateforming sequence grammars a multiscale data synthesis across the prokaryotictoeukaryotic thermal and salinity continuum
abstract_text: Biomolecular condensation and mesoscale self assembly rely on sequence encoded sticker and spacer interactions within intrinsically disordered regions, enabling predictive liquid liquid phase separation models and biological architecture visualization. It remains unclear whether these condensation prone sequences undergo adaptive tuning under environmental selection pressures like thermal and osmotic gradients because multidimensional data lack large scale integration. To determine if sequence parameters systematically differ across environments and alter phase behaviors, this project will extract sequence features, execute physics based coarse grained simulations utilizing Mpipi class models, and cross validate predictions against structural datasets. The project will integrate UniProt, MobiDB, DisProt, PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, EMDB, PDB, and EMPIAR by cross referencing proteome wide annotations with taxonomic metadata to map optimal growth temperatures onto specific sequences. This framework will link molecular sequence variations to organism level phenotypes, contextualizing biomolecular condensates within evolutionary adaptation and providing foundational data for engineering environmentally stable proteins in biotechnological applications.

abstract_original:
Intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) drive biomolecular condensation through sequence-encoded 'sticker-and-spacer' grammars, yet whether these grammars are themselves products of environmental selection remains unknown. Organisms spanning psychrophiles, mesophiles, thermophiles, and halophiles have evolved proteomes under vastly different physicochemical constraints (temperature, ionic strength, crowding), but no systematic effort has linked these environmental gradients to the biophysical 'rules' governing mesoscale self-assembly. This project will synthesize four classes of publicly available data that, to date, have never been integrated at scale: (1) curated proteome and IDR annotation databases (UniProt, MobiDB, DisProt) spanning thousands of species with documented optimal growth temperatures and salinities; (2) condensate-associated protein catalogs (PhaSepDB, CD-CODE, DrLLPS) identifying known or predicted phase-separating proteins and their partners; (3) parameterized coarse-grained simulation frameworks (e.g., Mpipi-class models) that translate sequence composition and patterning into predicted phase diagrams, saturation concentrations, and critical solution temperatures; and (4) structural/ultrastructural datasets from cryo-electron tomography, cryo-EM, and SAXS repositories (EMDB, PDB, EMPIAR) that reveal in vivo or in vitro condensate architecture for a subset of these proteins, particularly in bacterial systems where mesoscale organization has been directly visualized.

We will computationally extract sequence-grammar features (aromatic/cationic sticker density, charge patterning, spacer composition and length, net charge per residue) from IDRs across organisms occupying extreme versus moderate environmental niches, then apply existing coarse-grained simulation engines to predict each sequence's phase behavior (critical temperature, droplet viscoelasticity, salt/temperature sensitivity) without generating new experimental data. These predictions will be statistically correlated with organismal growth conditions to test whether specific grammatical features (e.g., increased spacer flexibility or altered stickers valence) systematically track thermal or osmotic adaptation, analogous to known compensatory strategies in folded-protein stability. Where cryo-ET or structural data exist for homologous condensate-scaffolding proteins (e.g., bacterial polar organizing proteins, RNA-binding stress granule components), we will cross-validate simulation-derived phase behavior against observed ultrastructural features (filament versus droplet morphology, interfacial properties) to determine whether sequence-encoded adaptations manifest as predictable changes in mesoscale architecture.

This synthesis requires integrating expertise in structural/mesoscale bacterial biology, physics-based coarse-grained modeling of condensates, and sequence-to-function mapping of disordered regions—capabilities distributed across our three groups and not achievable within any single lab. The project will produce an open-access, queryable atlas linking environmental parameters, IDR sequence grammar, predicted phase behavior, and (where available) structural ground truth, providing a resource for the community to test hypotheses about evolutionary constraints on emergent mesoscale organization. Findings will illuminate whether phase separation itself is an evolvable, selectable trait shaped by environmental pressure, offering a new framework for understanding how molecular-scale sequence features generate cell-scale adaptive phenotypes. All code, curated datasets, and simulation outputs will be released under FAIR principles, and the working group will train graduate students and postdocs in cross-disciplinary integration of genomics, biophysical simulation, and structural data analysis.

title: From Copy-Number Amplicons to Proteostatic Stress: A Multiscale Synthesis of 3D Genome Reorganization, Protein Complex Stoichiometry, and Cellular Fitness in Cancer Cell Lines
title_norm: from copynumber amplicons to proteostatic stress a multiscale synthesis of 3d genome reorganization protein complex stoichiometry and cellular fitness in cancer cell lines
abstract_text: In cancer cell biology, genomic amplifications including extrachromosomal DNA and focal copy number gains drive oncogene expression and tumor adaptation, representing critical alterations that profoundly affect cellular systems. This project will determine whether extrachromosomal DNA amplifications alter chromatin architecture and induce proteostatic stress to dictate genetic dependencies, applying a computational synthesis utilizing probabilistic graphical models, positive unlabeled classifiers, and network based exposure diffusion models. Datasets from DepMap, ENCODE, and public single cell repositories will be integrated by reconciling cell line identities to create a matched cohort table aligning amplicon status, proteomic data, and functional readouts. This framework will link molecular genomic events to higher order cellular phenotypes, providing novel mechanistic knowledge to identify new biomarkers and therapeutic targets for cancers with genomic amplifications.
full_text: Researchers know that genomic amplifications drive tumor adaptation but isolated datasets require integration to explain specific phenotypic outcomes. The primary question explores how extrachromosomal DNA alters chromatin architecture to cause protein imbalances and uniquely explain tumor heterogeneity. The project utilizes data from the Encyclopedia of DNA Elements (ENCODE) and the AlphaFold Database and public repositories. Researchers will integrate datasets by reconciling cell line identities and mapping protein identifiers to create a matched cohort table.
