abstract_original: A central unresolved question in cancer cell biology is how genomic amplification events—particularly extrachromosomal DNA (ecDNA) and focal copy-number gains—propagate through intermediate, mesoscale layers of cellular organization to produce emergent phenotypes such as drug resistance or engineered fitness dependencies. Existing studies typically examine single layers in isolation: genomic amplicon structure, 3D chromatin architecture, protein complex stoichiometry, or CRISPR-based fitness screens. No public synthesis has yet connected these layers into a coherent multiscale model linking DNA-level amplification to chromatin domain reorganization, to protein-level stoichiometric imbalance and misfolding stress, to cell-level dependency and drug response. This project will integrate five classes of publicly available data across matched or overlapping cancer cell lines: (1) CCLE/DepMap genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, CRISPR dependency, and drug-response datasets; (2) Hi-C and related 3D genome architecture data from the 4D Nucleome and ENCODE consortia; (3) ecDNA amplicon structural catalogs (e.g., ecDNA Atlas, AmpliconArchitect outputs); (4) structural proteomics resources including limited-proteolysis and cross-linking mass spectrometry datasets, PDB and AlphaFold structural models, and CORUM protein complex annotations; and (5) public single-cell CRISPR/Perturb-seq datasets probing regulatory and proteostatic responses to genetic perturbation. Our central hypothesis is that copy-number amplification—especially via ecDNA, which decouples genomic loci from native chromosomal 3D context—triggers characteristic reorganizations of chromatin domains and looping architecture that produce transcriptional dosage imbalance among interacting protein complex subunits. This imbalance generates measurable proteostatic stress, detectable as elevated misfolding-prone or entangled conformational states in structural proteomics data, which in turn constrains cellular fitness landscapes captured by DepMap dependency scores and drug sensitivity profiles. We will build a statistical and machine-learning integration framework—combining probabilistic graphical models for cross-layer dependency structure, positive-unlabeled learning to handle sparsely annotated misfolding/entanglement states, and network-based approaches adapted from epidemiological exposure modeling—to quantify how amplicon-driven 3D genome perturbations transmit through the proteome to shape emergent cellular vulnerabilities. This effort requires collaboration well beyond any single laboratory: expertise in cancer multi-omics and ecDNA biology, 3D genome organization and single-cell regulatory genomics, protein folding/misfolding biophysics and statistical fitness-landscape modeling, and machine-learning frameworks for heterogeneous multi-omic and network data. No new experimental data will be generated; the project synthesizes and harmonizes existing public repositories into a unified analytical pipeline and predictive model, released as open-source workflows and annotated multiscale integration datasets. Deliverables include a public database linking amplicon architecture to chromatin domain shifts, protein stoichiometric imbalance scores, and dependency/drug-response outcomes across hundreds of characterized cell lines, alongside trainee-led modules teaching multi-omic data harmonization, structural bioinformatics, and cross-scale statistical modeling. By formally connecting genomic, chromatin, and proteomic mesoscale phenomena to whole-cell phenotypic emergence, this work will resolve a long-standing gap in understanding how structural genomic instability manifests as exploitable cellular vulnerability, offering a generalizable template for multiscale synthesis in molecular and cellular biosciences.

title: Cross-Scale Morphodynamic Grammar of Membrane-Bound Organelle Shape Change: Integrating Whole-Cell Volumetric Imaging with Cytoskeletal Agent-Based Simulations to Learn Generalizable Rules of Mesoscale Shape Transitions
title_norm: crossscale morphodynamic grammar of membranebound organelle shape change integrating wholecell volumetric imaging with cytoskeletal agentbased simulations to learn generalizable rules of mesoscale shape transitions
abstract_text: The shape transitions of membrane bound organelles are driven by known molecular components of the cytoskeleton, but extensive volumetric imaging and simulation data on these processes remain systematically unintegrated. To determine if common physical rules dictate how cytoskeletal organization translates into shape changes, this project will extract morphometric features and reconstruct simulations using deep learning volumetric segmentation, Markov Chain Monte Carlo sampling, and transfer learning. The study will integrate public imaging datasets from EMPIAR and the Cell Image Library with biophysical models by projecting empirical and synthetic trajectories into a shared morphodynamic embedding space using optimal transport distance metrics. This research will link molecular scale cytoskeletal mechanics with cell scale phenotypes to determine whether distinct organelle shape changes represent convergent physical solutions across unrelated biological systems.

The relevant molecular components are known but existing volumetric imaging and simulation data lack systematic integration across organelle types. This study asks if cytoskeletal organization dictates changes of shape through convergent physical solutions to link molecular mechanics with cellular phenotypes. The analytical strategy extracts morphometric features from imaging data and reconstructs simulations to compare resulting trajectories through transfer learning. Applied methods include volumetric segmentation through deep learning and Markov Chain Monte Carlo sampling alongside comparisons using Gromov-Wasserstein distances. Researchers will validate results using held out sets and generalization tests alongside joint sessions to verify biological plausibility of outputs. The project utilizes imaging databases including EMPIAR and the Cell Image Library alongside supplementary data from published biophysical models. The proposed study integrates empirical and synthetic datasets into a shared embedding space using distance metrics based on optimal transport. abstract_original:
Organelles such as cilia, mitochondria, and the nuclear envelope undergo characteristic, reproducible shape transitions—elongation, curvature inversion, budding, shedding—that emerge from the interplay of cytoskeletal forces, membrane mechanics, and motor activity. Despite decades of organelle-specific study, it remains unknown whether a common, quantitative 'morphodynamic grammar' governs how mesoscale cytoskeletal organization is translated into organelle shape across otherwise unrelated systems. Testing this requires reconciling two data types that are rarely combined: high-resolution static and time-resolved whole-cell volumetric imaging (soft X-ray tomography, cryo-electron tomography, lattice light-sheet, and correlative EM datasets now populating public repositories such as CIL, EMPIAR, and the Cell Image Library) and biophysical simulation outputs from agent-based and continuum models of cytoskeletal self-organization (actomyosin cortices, microtubule bundles, septin scaffolds) deposited in supplementary archives and modeling repositories. No single lab possesses both the breadth of curated whole-cell image datasets across organelle types and the diversity of validated cytoskeletal simulation frameworks needed to ask whether shape-change trajectories are governed by shared low-dimensional physical rules.

This working group will assemble and harmonize (1) publicly available 3D/4D organelle imaging datasets spanning cilia, mitochondria, nuclear envelope, and cortical actin systems, extracting standardized morphometric descriptors (curvature spectra, surface-area-to-volume trajectories, topological transition events) using automated segmentation and shape-quantification pipelines; and (2) simulation-derived shape and force trajectories from published agent-based and continuum cytoskeletal models, re-parameterized where necessary from reported model specifications to generate comparable synthetic morphodynamic time series. A central methodological innovation is the use of optimal-transport-based time series comparison (building on Gromov-Wasserstein type distances) to align organelle shape trajectories from disparate imaging modalities, temporal resolutions, and organelle identities into a shared morphodynamic space, and to compare these empirical trajectories against simulated trajectories from mechanistically distinct cytoskeletal models. We will then apply transfer learning: representations learned from the better-sampled, mechanistically well-characterized systems (e.g., ciliary shedding, actomyosin ring constriction) will be used to predict and interpret shape transitions in less-characterized organelle systems, testing whether cytoskeletal-force signatures inferred from simulation generalize across biological contexts.

The expected outcome is a data-derived taxonomy of mesoscale shape-transition classes and their associated cytoskeletal force signatures, clarifying whether phenomena such as whole-organelle shedding, curvature inversion, or symmetry-breaking site selection reflect convergent physical solutions to shared mechanical constraints rather than organelle-specific evolutionary innovations. This directly addresses the Center's mesoscale emergence mandate by linking molecular-scale cytoskeletal mechanics to cell-scale organelle phenotypes purely through synthesis of existing image and simulation data. The project requires collaboration between imaging-data curation expertise, biophysical modeling expertise, and time-series/optimal-transport methodology—capacities distributed across our team and beyond what either lab could assemble alone. All harmonized datasets, segmentation pipelines, distance metrics, and trained transfer-learning models will be released as open, versioned, reproducible workflows, and the project will train graduate students and postdocs at the interface of quantitative imaging analysis and biophysical simulation, building the data-savvy workforce NCEMS aims to cultivate.

title: Transposon-Seeded Cooperativity: Synthesizing Cross-Species Epigenomic Atlases to Test Whether Transposable Elements Drive the Emergence of Mesoscale Chromatin Hubs
title_norm: transposonseeded cooperativity synthesizing crossspecies epigenomic atlases to test whether transposable elements drive the emergence of mesoscale chromatin hubs
abstract_text: Within computational epigenomics and evolutionary biology, research examines how transposable element insertions influence the formation of higher order regulatory structures, a vital process for supplying new transcription factor binding sites. To determine if transposable element insertions drive cooperative regulatory hub formation, this research will analyze mammalian datasets utilizing domain adaptation neural networks, joint epigenome segmentation algorithms, and phase separation propensity scoring tools. The project will integrate multi species datasets from ENCODE, modENCODE, and the 4D Nucleome project through standardized pipelines, utilizing joint segmentation models to merge chromatin records with 3D genome architectures. Identifying whether transposable elements seed chromatin hubs will provide mechanisms for regulatory evolution and inform the interpretation of disease linked reactivation and species specific gene regulation changes.

abstract_original: Transposable elements (TEs) have long been recognized as raw material for new transcription factor (TF) binding sites, but it remains unclear whether TE insertions merely add isolated binding events or actively seed the higher-order, cooperative assemblies—TF hubs, super-enhancers, and phase-separated condensates—that constitute mesoscale regulatory architecture. This proposal assembles a working group spanning computational epigenomics, TE evolutionary biology, chromatin biophysics, and comparative genomics to synthesize publicly available ChIP-seq, ATAC-seq, Hi-C, and RepeatMasker/TE annotation datasets across multiple mammalian species (human, mouse, and available primate/rodent epigenomes from ENCODE, modENCODE, and comparative consortia) to test the hypothesis that TE-derived binding motif clusters nucleate emergent, cooperative regulatory hubs whose properties—size, TF composition, chromatin accessibility, and 3D contact frequency—are not predictable from single-motif occupancy alone. Building on prior work using domain-adaptation neural networks to correct for species-specific repeat content when predicting TF binding, we will extend these architectures to explicitly model TE subfamily identity as a covariate, asking whether specific TE families (e.g., SINEs, ERVs, LINEs) are statistically enriched at loci showing multivalent, cooperative TF co-occupancy versus loci with single-TF, sequence-driven binding. We will integrate this with IDEAS-style multi-species epigenome segmentation to define chromatin states genome-wide and identify 'emergent' regulatory domains—regions where TE insertion coincides with the transition from sparse to dense, multi-factor chromatin states across evolutionary time. Publicly available Hi-C and ChIA-PET datasets will be mined to test whether these TE-seeded hubs correspond to loop anchors, TAD boundaries, or contact domain reorganization, linking sequence-level TE insertion events to mesoscale 3D genome architecture. title: Beyond Binary Interactions: Synthesizing Public Crosslinking Mass Spectrometry Data to Map Emergent Mesoscale Protein Assemblies Across Human Tissues
title_norm: beyond binary interactions synthesizing public crosslinking mass spectrometry data to map emergent mesoscale protein assemblies across human tissues
abstract_text: The research domain of cellular biology and proteomics focuses on mesoscale protein associations, including metabolons, signaling condensates, and assembly intermediates, which are crucial for understanding dynamic in cell protein interactions. Current databases primarily capture stable complexes, leaving transient mesoscale contacts poorly understood because inconsistent processing methods and error models hinder reliable comparisons of public crosslinking mass spectrometry data. The objective is to determine whether harmonized crosslinking data reveal reproducible mesoscale associations that explain genetic pleiotropy; this computational synthesis will apply containerized search pipelines, target decoy error modeling, AlphaFold2 predictions, and permutation based enrichment testing. This project will overlay PRIDE and ProteomeXchange datasets, tissue specific co fractionation atlases, and AlphaFold2 structures to categorize physical contacts, mapping these integrated networks onto Reactome pathways and genome wide association statistics. This synthesis of isolated datasets will output a novel mechanistic framework linking molecular scale protein interactions to phenotypic outcomes, which explains genetic pleiotropy and penetrance variability for downstream research.
full_text: The fields of cellular biology and proteomics underutilize crosslinking mass spectrometry datasets to evaluate mesoscale associations of proteins. Current databases capture stable complexes through laboratory assays and literature curation while transient interactions of proteins remain uncharacterized. The proposed study harmonizes isolated datasets to determine if these associations of proteins explain genetic pleiotropy and penetrance. This project utilizes a computational synthesis of public data to construct a consensus network of contacts among proteins. The analytical strategy applies structural predictions by AlphaFold2 and statistical modeling of background rates alongside containerized search workflows. Results will be validated through statistical null models and Universal Spectrum Identifiers to trace the provenance of spectra. The study will utilize mass spectrometry datasets from PRIDE and ProteomeXchange alongside fractionation atlases and the Reactome database. The team will integrate datasets by overlaying networks of crosslinks with structural models to categorize the physical contacts. The team will mitigate inconsistent chemistries across studies by reprocessing data through a unified false discovery rate framework. The proposed project encompasses four sequential milestones from the harmonization of data to the integration of genetic pathways. This scope requires cross disciplinary collaboration among three groups with expertise in chemistry and the engineering of data. The team will release open source code and analytical notebooks in public repositories alongside preprints of the findings. The team includes postdoctoral and graduate researchers who will receive specialized training in structural modeling and network genetics.

abstract_original:
Protein-protein interaction (PPI) databases are built overwhelmingly from binary, often in vitro, assays and curated literature, capturing stable, well-defined complexes but systematically missing the transient, low-affinity, and multivalent contacts that organize the cellular mesoscale—metabolons, signaling condensates, and co-translational assembly intermediates. In-cell crosslinking mass spectrometry (XL-MS) uniquely samples these fleeting proximities inside their native molecular crowding context, yet thousands of public XL-MS datasets sit underutilized in repositories such as PRIDE/ProteomeXchange, processed with inconsistent search engines, scoring schemes, and false-discovery-rate (FDR) models that make cross-study comparison unreliable. Meanwhile, orthogonal large-scale resources—tissue-specific co-fractionation/abundance-correlation PPI atlases, curated pathway knowledgebases (Reactome), and GWAS-derived network-expansion modules linking genetic variants to pleiotropic phenotypes—offer independent, structurally agnostic views of cellular organization. This project asks: do reproducible, harmonized crosslinking contact networks reveal a distinct class of 'mesoscale-only' associations—reproducible across independent cells, tissues, and studies, yet absent from canonical stable-complex databases—that correspond to emergent higher-order assemblies, and do these assemblies help explain otherwise unexplained genetic pleiotropy and variable penetrance of disease variants?

We will assemble a working group spanning crosslinking-MS method development and standardization, proteomics data infrastructure, and network/systems biology to: (1) systematically reprocess and harmonize thousands of publicly deposited in vivo and in-organello XL-MS datasets using unified FDR models and open pipelines, building on recently proposed community standards for crosslinking data reliability; (2) construct a consensus, confidence-weighted 'contact network' spanning multiple cell types and organisms, distinguishing reproducible crosslinks recurring across independent studies from stochastic, single-dataset artifacts; (3) integrate this network with existing tissue-specific protein co-fractionation atlases and AlphaFold2-based structural models to classify contacts as (a) consistent with known direct/stable interfaces, (b) plausible but previously undetected direct interactions, or (c) proximity-only signatures suggestive of condensate-like or metabolon-like mesoscale clustering; (d) cross-reference the resulting assembly modules against Reactome pathway architecture and GWAS network-expansion pleiotropy maps to test whether mesoscale-only clusters disproportionately explain shared genetic associations, disease gene modules, and variable variant penetrance not accounted for by canonical PPI networks.

This synthesis is infeasible for any single lab: it requires simultaneous expertise in crosslinking chemistry and error modeling, proteomics repository engineering and standardized data access (universal spectrum identifiers, ProteomeXchange harmonization), and large-scale network/genetic integration—expertise distributed across the three participating groups. Outputs will include an open, versioned mesoscale contact network resource, standardized reanalysis workflows deposited as community pipelines, and a public catalog of candidate emergent assemblies prioritized for experimental follow-up. Graduate students and postdocs will be trained across proteomics informatics, structural modeling, and network genetics, directly building the cross-disciplinary, data-savvy workforce NCEMS aims to cultivate, while advancing a mechanistic, testable framework for how mesoscale protein organization gives rise to cellular and organismal phenotypes.

title: Closing the Genotype–Metabolite Gap: A Cross-Repository Synthesis Linking Microbial Genomic Potential to Untargeted Mass Spectrometry Signatures of Chemical Novelty
title_norm: closing the genotypemetabolite gap a crossrepository synthesis linking microbial genomic potential to untargeted mass spectrometry signatures of chemical novelty
abstract_text: Molecular and cellular biosciences investigate the critical interface between genome encoded enzymatic potential and realized chemical output using large independent databases of untargeted mass spectrometry and genomic sequencing. A significant discrepancy exists between genomic predictions and observed chemical diversity, because most mass spectrometry features remain unannotated and few predicted biosynthetic gene clusters link to validated chemical products. The primary objective will map where genomic biosynthetic potential is chemically realized, silent, or exceeded by applying unsupervised spectral embedding, alignment free Siamese neural networks, and canonical correlation to align mass spectrometry features with functional sequence embeddings. This project will computationally integrate untargeted tandem mass spectrometry repositories and microbial genomic sequence databases by aligning spectral feature neighborhoods with sequence based functional neighborhoods using shared sample identifiers and ecological metadata. This research will establish an analytical framework for discovering undiscovered enzymes, determining ecological constraints on metabolic expression, and supporting host microbiome interaction studies and natural product discovery.
full_text: This project in molecular and cellular biosciences investigates discrepancies between genome encoded enzymatic potential and observed chemical diversity. Independent databases hold vast sequencing and mass spectrometry data but lack annotations and links to validated chemical products. The proposed study aligns spectral and genomic sequence data to map biosynthetic potential and support natural product discovery. The study design extracts features from matched genomic and metabolomic samples to align sequence embeddings with spectral embeddings. The analytical approach utilizes spectral networking and joint embedding techniques alongside canonical correlation and alignment free neural networks. Results will undergo validation against manually curated case studies of modified metabolite families to calibrate false discovery rates. Datasets include public sequence databases and untargeted tandem mass spectrometry repositories such as MassIVE and MetaboLights and PRIDE. The proposed study integrates datasets by aligning spectral feature neighborhoods with functional sequence neighborhoods using shared ecological metadata. The project mitigates uneven sampling depth and biases in database representation through the application of permutation based models. Project milestones progress from establishing matched sample sets and extracting spectral features to genomic functional inference and synthesis. The scope necessitates cross disciplinary collaboration to integrate required expertise in mass spectrometry data standards and functional genomics. The project releases code under open source licenses and deposits derived data embeddings into version controlled public repositories. Postdoctoral researchers and graduate students will receive joint training in mass spectrometry informatics and microbial functional genomics methodologies.

abstract_original: A central puzzle in molecular and cellular biosciences is why the chemical diversity actually observed in biological systems vastly exceeds what can be predicted from genomic annotation alone, and conversely, why so much predicted biosynthetic potential is never detected as an actual molecular product. This mismatch is a quintessential mesoscale emergence problem: it arises at the interface between genome-encoded enzymatic potential (biomolecular scale) and the realized chemical repertoire of cells, tissues, and microbial communities (subcellular/cellular scale), and it cannot be resolved by genomic or metabolomic data alone. We propose a working group that synthesizes two massive, independently curated public data ecosystems—untargeted tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS) repositories (GNPS, MassIVE, MetaboLights, PRIDE) and microbial genomic/metagenomic sequence databases (IMG, GTDB, human/animal microbiome metagenomes)—to systematically map where genomic biosynthetic potential is realized, silent, or exceeded by unpredicted chemistry. Leveraging spectral networking, MassQL-based pattern queries, and large-scale reference library matching, we will identify families of modified small molecules (building on known cases such as bile acid and lipid modifications) and cluster them by shared substructural motifs using unsupervised spectral embedding. In parallel, we will apply alignment-free, sequence-based functional inference (extending Siamese neural network approaches developed for divergent bacterial gene function assignment) to genomes and metagenome-assembled genomes from the same or ecologically matched samples, predicting candidate biosynthetic gene clusters and modifying enzyme families independent of homology to characterized reference enzymes. The core synthesis task is to computationally align these two independently generated feature spaces—spectral neighborhoods representing chemical modification logic, and sequence-based functional neighborhoods representing enzymatic potential—to detect (1) 'orphan chemistry': recurrent, structurally coherent MS/MS features with no plausible genomic explanation among co-occurring organisms, signaling either undiscovered enzymology or non-biological/exogenous origin; and (2) 'silent potential': biosynthetic gene clusters or enzyme families with strong predicted modifying activity that are never represented in matched spectral data, suggesting regulatory, ecological, or expression-level constraints on realization of genomic potential. This effort is beyond the scope of any single lab because it requires simultaneous mastery of MS data standards, spectral library curation, sequence-based functional genomics, and network-based cross-domain data integration at a scale spanning millions of spectra and genomes. We will build open, reproducible computational pipelines and shared ontologies linking spectral and sequence identifiers, released as community tools compatible with existing GNPS and genome database infrastructures. Graduate students and postdocs will be trained jointly in mass spectrometry informatics and microbial genomics, gaining fluency across historically siloed subdisciplines. By characterizing systematically where and why genomic potential succeeds or fails to manifest as chemical reality, this project will generate a generalizable framework for studying emergence at the genotype–metabolite interface, with direct relevance to host–microbiome chemistry, natural product discovery, and the broader question of how molecular-scale information gives rise to unpredictable chemical phenotypes.

title: A Cross-Family Atlas of Emergent Allosteric Order Parameters: Synthesizing Structural Ensembles, Deep Mutational Scans, and Ancestral Sequence Data to Discover Universal Rules of Protein Regulation
title_norm: a crossfamily atlas of emergent allosteric order parameters synthesizing structural ensembles deep mutational scans and ancestral sequence data to discover universal rules of protein regulation
abstract_text: Molecular biophysics investigates allostery and protein dynamics across different protein folds, an important pursuit for identifying common physical signatures that standardize mechanisms currently understood only within isolated families using distinct metrics. Current approaches cannot determine whether allostery represents a fold specific phenomenon or if a universal physical order parameter governs these mechanisms across evolutionarily unrelated protein folds. To determine if coarse grained dynamical parameters predict allosteric site identity across unrelated folds, this project will compute standardized flexibility indices, elastic network strain fields, and correlated motion networks to train uncertainty aware machine learning models. The research will integrate GPCRmd trajectory repositories, MaveDB mutational datasets, and ASBench allosteric databases using standardized computational pipelines to resolve source discrepancies in structural numbering, trajectory length, and force fields. Identifying a generalizable parameter will yield a novel predictive framework that resolves a conceptual molecular biophysics question and provides a basis for engineering allosteric communication in proteins.
full_text: This project in molecular biophysics examines whether a universal physical order parameter governs allostery across unrelated protein folds. Researchers currently understand allosteric mechanisms within isolated protein families using distinct metrics that lack standardization across unrelated folds. The proposed study asks if coarse grained dynamical parameters predict allosteric coupling to enable the engineering of protein communication. The data synthesis project integrates public datasets to compute standardized dynamic metrics for use within machine learning models. Methods include the calculation of dynamic flexibility indices alongside the application of uncertainty aware machine learning and interpretability models. The team will validate predictions against ground truth labels from allosteric databases and mutational fitness data using family level holdouts. The project utilizes molecular dynamics repositories (Folding@home) and mutational scanning datasets (MaveDB) alongside allosteric site databases and structural ensembles. Standardized computational pipelines will integrate these sources to resolve discrepancies in structural numbering and trajectory length across the different datasets. The team will mitigate a lack of data for certain protein families by deploying uncertainty aware machine learning models. The scope of this project requires extensive collaboration to combine expertise in protein dynamics and nuclear receptor allostery. This cross disciplinary team supplies the large scale simulation and machine learning infrastructure that no single laboratory possesses. The team will share data and code through a versioned database alongside open source repositories and public preprints. The project supports a postdoctoral researcher and two graduate assistants to provide training in molecular simulation and data science.

abstract_original:
Allostery is a hallmark of mesoscale emergence: local perturbations at a ligand-binding or mutation site propagate through a protein's conformational ensemble to alter function at a distant site, yet no unifying physical order parameter has been identified that predicts this behavior across unrelated protein folds. Individual labs have generated fragmented pictures of allostery in specific systems—kinases, nuclear receptors, PDZ domains—using distinct metrics (dynamic flexibility/coupling indices, mutual information from MD ensembles, correlation networks), making it impossible for any single group to test whether a shared mechanical or informational signature underlies allosteric regulation broadly. This project synthesizes four large, independently curated public resources—(1) multi-microsecond MD trajectory repositories (Folding@home public projects, GPCRmd, DE Shaw Research/MoDEL archives, MDDB), (2) deep mutational scanning datasets (MaveDB, ProteinGym) spanning kinases, nuclear receptors, and enzymes, (3) curated allosteric site databases (ASD, ASBench) and PDB ensembles of apo/holo/mutant structures, and (4) ancestral sequence reconstruction datasets and phylogenetic alignments for allosteric protein families—to ask whether a small set of emergent, coarse-grained order parameters (e.g., rigidity/flexibility gradients, strain propagation fields, or coupled fluctuation modes) can predict allosteric coupling strength and site identity across evolutionarily unrelated folds, independent of sequence or topology.

We will harmonize dynamics-derived metrics (flexibility indices, correlated motion networks, strain/stress fields computed from elastic network and all-atom ensembles) across thousands of publicly deposited structures and trajectories, then align these physical signatures with functional readouts from deep mutational scanning (fitness/activity changes at distal sites) and evolutionary conservation/covariation patterns from ancestral reconstructions. Machine learning models—including uncertainty-aware architectures for sparse, heterogeneous biological data—will be trained to test whether mesoscale dynamical order parameters generalize as predictors of allosteric hotspots across families never seen during training, and whether evolutionary trajectories (ancestral-to-modern transitions) systematically reshape these parameters in predictable ways. A key deliverable is an open, versioned allostery atlas linking structural dynamics, mutational fitness landscapes, and evolutionary history for hundreds of protein families, enabling community-wide hypothesis generation about design principles for engineering or rewiring regulatory communication in proteins.

This effort requires integration of expertise that no single lab possesses: quantifying protein dynamics and evolutionary flexibility landscapes, mechanistic understanding of ligand-induced allosteric transitions in nuclear receptor systems, and large-scale simulation/ML infrastructure for harmonizing heterogeneous, high-volume trajectory and screening data. The working group will pair graduate students and postdocs with complementary backgrounds (biophysics, structural biology, machine learning) to build shared open-source pipelines for ensemble analysis and predictive modeling, directly training a next-generation workforce fluent in both molecular simulation and data science. By testing whether allostery is governed by universal emergent mechanical order parameters rather than family-specific idiosyncratic pathways, this synthesis directly addresses NCEMS's core mission: understanding how coordinated mesoscale organization—here, in the fluctuation and strain dynamics of a single macromolecule—gives rise to functional properties not evident at the level of individual residues or static structures.

title: Entanglement as an Emergent Design Constraint: Cross-Scale Synthesis of Protein Topology, Translation Kinetics, and Proteostasis Networks
title_norm: entanglement as an emergent design constraint crossscale synthesis of protein topology translation kinetics and proteostasis networks
abstract_text: Within structural biology and bioinformatics, protein topological entanglements including knots and lassos represent important phenomena whose relationships with translation kinetics and cellular maintenance pathways remain obscured across independent databases. It remains uncharacterized whether protein topological entanglement constitutes a systemic structural constraint that cells manage through coordinated co translational and post translational mechanisms. This project will test if entanglement operates as a multi scale constraint by building a cross referenced dataset and comparing entangled sequence windows to length matched controls using polymer physics algorithms and logistic regression. The study will integrate KnotProt, Protein Data Bank, AlphaFold DB, BioGRID, and ClinVar into a unified relational schema by standardizing protein and residue identifiers using UniProt accessions alongside sequence and structural coordinates. The resulting framework will connect genetic sequence features to topological outcomes and evaluate structural topology as a novel metric for predicting missense variant pathogenicity.
full_text: This structural biology and bioinformatics project investigates whether complex topological entanglements operate as systemic constraints requiring coordinated cellular management. Existing databases catalog complex structures and metrics of translation separately without illuminating relationships between topology and cellular maintenance pathways. This study tests whether entanglement constitutes a multi scale biological constraint and evaluates structural topology for predicting variant pathogenicity. The study synthesizes public datasets across four phases to compare sequence windows with entanglements against length matched control regions. The team will apply algorithms from polymer physics alongside graph analytic network metrics and models of logistic regression. Results will undergo internal validation through statistical comparisons against decoy regions and independent replication of key analyses by trainees. Data sources incorporate structural repositories like the Protein Data Bank and AlphaKnot alongside genomic databases including ClinVar and OrthoDB. The project integrates these distinct datasets into a relational schema by standardizing protein identifiers with unified sequence coordinates. The team will mitigate coordinate limitations using a standardized relational schema and address structural confounding using logistic regression. The timeline of two years encompasses four sequential phases of data integration alongside two in person working group workshops. This project requires cross disciplinary collaboration because data integration demands simultaneous expertise in structural bioinformatics and coevolutionary genomics. The resulting unified database and statistical code will be hosted in a public repository utilizing containerized computational environments. The team unites biophysics specialists with postdoctoral researchers and graduate students who will receive training in network biology.

abstract_original: Knotted, lassoed, and slipknotted proteins represent rare but functionally persistent topological outcomes of evolution, yet why certain folds tolerate or exploit such non-trivial entanglement while others avoid it remains unresolved. Existing structural databases (KnotProt, LassoProt, AlphaKnot, the Genus database for biomolecules) now catalog topological complexity across tens of thousands of experimentally solved and AlphaFold-predicted structures, while independent community resources capture the cellular machinery and kinetic context in which these proteins are synthesized and maintained: ribosome profiling datasets reporting codon-level translation elongation rates, genome-wide chaperone-substrate interactome maps (BioGRID, HumanNet, chaperone-specific interactomes for Hsp70/Hsp90/GroEL systems), evolutionary conservation and dN/dS databases, and disease-variant repositories such as ClinVar and gnomAD. No existing effort has integrated these disparate, single-domain resources to ask whether topological entanglement constitutes a systematic, mesoscale-level constraint that cells manage through co-translational and post-translational mechanisms. This project proposes exactly that synthesis. We will build a unified cross-referenced dataset linking each cataloged knot, slipknot, lasso, and theta-curve motif to its corresponding gene's local codon usage bias and predicted translational pausing near the entanglement-forming region, its documented chaperone dependencies and interactome connectivity, its evolutionary rate and conservation depth across orthologs, and its representation in pathogenic missense variant catalogs. Using polymer-physics-based knot/lasso detection algorithms alongside statistical closure methods already developed within the team, we will first establish a high-confidence, proteome-wide map of entangled regions, extending beyond human proteins to bacterial, archaeal, and viral proteomes with divergent translational and chaperone systems. We will then test specific mesoscale hypotheses: that entanglement-forming segments are enriched for rare, slowly translated codons that create co-translational folding delays permitting topological threading; that entangled proteins disproportionately depend on specific chaperone classes (e.g., GroEL/GroES-type cavities versus Hsp70 holdases) identifiable through interactome connectivity patterns; and that residues within or adjacent to knot/lasso cores show distinct signatures of purifying selection and human disease mutation enrichment relative to matched non-entangled controls. This effort requires combining expertise in knot-theoretic structural analysis, coarse-grained polymer and coevolutionary modeling of macromolecular assemblies, and biophysical protein-folding mechanism, none of which alone can resolve translation-, chaperone-, and evolution-scale correlations from static structural catalogs. The resulting open, versioned database and analysis pipeline will let the community query any protein for its topological status alongside its translational and proteostasis context, generating testable predictions about chaperone requirements or disease risk for uncharacterized entangled folds. Graduate students and postdocs will be trained across topology algorithms, ribosome-profiling bioinformatics, and network biology, producing a genuinely transdisciplinary dataset and workforce capable of reasoning about how molecular-scale geometric complexity propagates into cellular-scale regulatory demands, directly addressing NCEMS's mesoscale emergence mandate.

title: Nucleolar Condensate Scaling Laws as a Mesoscale Determinant of Ribosome Biogenesis Capacity and Skeletal Muscle Hypertrophy: A Multi-Omic, GPU-Accelerated Synthesis
title_norm: nucleolar condensate scaling laws as a mesoscale determinant of ribosome biogenesis capacity and skeletal muscle hypertrophy a multiomic gpuaccelerated synthesis
abstract_text: Skeletal muscle biology investigates mechanical overload induced hypertrophy, where the nucleolus functions as a phase separated biomolecular condensate regulating ribosome biogenesis, a process that predicts tissue growth more accurately than mTORC1 signaling. Independent studies document nucleolar components and hypertrophy multi omics, but a quantitative link connecting organelle level condensate biophysics with tissue scale growth remains unachieved. To determine whether nucleolar parameters control ribosome biogenesis and hypertrophy, this computational project will use GPU accelerated comparative genomics, graph neural networks, and free boundary partial differential equations to construct a cross scale model. The research will integrate GEO, ArrayExpress, MetaMEx, and nucleolar atlases with PScore and catGRANULE metrics, utilizing graph neural networks to combine transcriptional and interaction data to parameterize the differential equation model. This work will deliver a quantitative cross scale framework testing how organelle scale condensate dynamics constrain organismal traits, providing an approach generalizable to other biomolecular condensates and cellular phenotypes.
full_text: The proposed study explores skeletal muscle biology to link parameters of nucleolar condensates with hypertrophy at the tissue scale. Current models emphasize mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1) but lack integration of organelle and tissue scales. This research asks whether parameters of nucleolar condensates control ribosome biogenesis to provide a framework for cellular phenotypes. The team designs a purely computational synthesis to harmonize public datasets and build models of growth in nucleolar droplets. Key methods include the alignment of genomes and graph neural networks to support a model of partial differential equations. The researchers validate predictions of translational capacity and nucleolar size against independent measurements from public datasets of imaging. Data sources include Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) and MetaMEx alongside atlases of the nucleolar proteome and propensity scores. Graph neural networks integrate data of protein expression with structural data to parameterize the model of partial differential equations. The researchers mitigate the fragmentation of data and computational costs of alignment through cross disciplinary collaboration and parallel computing. Milestones for the project include the harmonization of data and the integration of networks alongside modeling of free boundaries. The synthesis requires cross disciplinary collaboration to provide concurrent expertise in quantitative physiology of muscles and mathematical modeling across multiple scales. abstract_original:
A long-standing puzzle in skeletal muscle biology is why increases in ribosome biogenesis capacity—rather than acute changes in mTORC1 signaling alone—best predict the magnitude of mechanical-overload-induced hypertrophy across species and individuals. Ribosome biogenesis is orchestrated within the nucleolus, a biomolecular condensate assembled through liquid-liquid phase separation of rRNA, ribosomal proteins, and assembly factors. The nucleolus is a canonical mesoscale structure: it sits between individual macromolecules (Pol I machinery, ribosomal proteins, rRNA) and the organelle-level output (mature ribosomes), and its size, number, and phase behavior are hypothesized to nonlinearly determine translational capacity and thus cellular growth outcomes. We will assemble a synthesis dataset from public repositories including: (1) transcriptomic and proteomic time-course data from human and rodent resistance-exercise/mechanical-overload studies (GEO, ArrayExpress, MetaMEx), (2) curated nucleolar proteome atlases and condensate phase-separation propensity scores (e.g., PScore, catGRANULE-derived annotations) for rRNA transcription/processing factors, (3) ribosome profiling datasets quantifying translational output across hypertrophy models, and (4) comparative genomic assemblies spanning human, mouse, and rat rDNA loci and regulatory regions. Graph neural network models will integrate multi-omic layers—transcriptional regulatory networks, nucleolar protein-protein interaction networks, and phase-separation-relevant sequence/structural features—to predict emergent nucleolar assembly states and infer stoichiometric bottlenecks controlling ribosome output.

Model parameters will be fit and validated against independent public datasets capturing nucleolar size dynamics and fiber-level hypertrophy trajectories, generating testable scaling laws relating molecular-scale condensate parameters to cellular and tissue-level growth outcomes.

This effort requires convergent expertise no single lab possesses: quantitative muscle physiology, high-performance computational biology, and multiscale mathematical modeling. Deliverables include an open-access cross-species nucleolar-hypertrophy multi-omic database, reproducible GNN and PDE modeling pipelines, and a generalizable framework for linking biomolecular condensate emergence to organismal phenotypic outcomes, with direct training opportunities for graduate students and postdocs in data integration, GPU computing, and multiscale modeling.

title: A Cross-Species Physical Grammar Atlas: Testing Whether Conserved Polymer Physics, Not Conserved Sequence, Governs Emergent Condensate Material Properties
title_norm: a crossspecies physical grammar atlas testing whether conserved polymer physics not conserved sequence governs emergent condensate material properties
abstract_text: The research domain encompasses intrinsically disordered regions in biomolecular condensates, a critical biological phenomenon where sequence features including charge patterning and aromatic valence predict phase behavior. A critical open question is how condensate material properties remain functionally stable across evolutionary divergence and whether evolutionary selection targets physical parameters rather than primary sequence identity. This project will test if evolutionary selection targets physical parameters by constructing a cross species database through computational data synthesis, applying sequence to parameter mappings, coarse grained models, ancestral state reconstruction, and gradient boosted machine learning. The approach will synthesize databases including PhaSepDB, DisProt, UniProt, and ClinVar by cross referencing disorder annotations and ortholog groupings to build a sequence corpus linked with structural, evolutionary, and clinical annotations. This research will produce a cross species database that establishes mechanisms explaining sequence divergence, identifies disease associated variants, and provides physical parameters for synthetic biology design.
full_text: This project investigates intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) in biomolecular condensates to explain functional stability despite rapid evolutionary sequence divergence. Charge patterning predicts phase behavior but understanding is incomplete regarding whether evolution selects physical parameters instead of sequence identity. The primary question investigates whether selection targets physical parameters to explain functional conservation and identify novel pathogenic variants. The computational study design converts public sequences into vectors of physical parameters for evaluation via phylogenetics and machine learning. Key methods feature coarse grained models and ancestral state reconstruction alongside Gaussian process regression and gradient boosted trees. The team will benchmark machine learning against baselines for sequence conservation and validate statistical models using bootstrapped confidence intervals. Data sources feature sequence repositories like DisProt and UniProt alongside evolutionary databases like OrthoDB and clinical datasets including ClinVar. Researchers will synthesize ortholog groupings to build a corpus of sequences and link vectors of physical parameters with clinical annotations. The project mitigates data leakage by stratifying cross validation and reduces confounding sequence variations by matching variants on conservation scores. Project milestones include assembling an open access atlas and developing pathogenicity scores alongside models for the demixing of condensates. The cross disciplinary scope necessitates collaboration to integrate data across polymer physics and evolutionary genomics beyond single laboratory capabilities. The team will share data via Zenodo and distribute open source code using software containers alongside preprints of intermediate results. The multidisciplinary team includes principal investigators and graduate students receiving training in database curation and coarse grained biophysical modeling.

abstract_original: Intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) drive biomolecular condensate assembly through sequence-encoded interaction 'grammars'—charge patterning, aromatic valence, stickers-and-spacers architecture—yet these regions are notoriously poorly conserved at the residue level across orthologs and paralogs. A long-standing puzzle is how condensate-relevant emergent properties (viscosity, interfacial tension, multiphase demixing, client/scaffold partitioning) remain functionally robust across evolutionary divergence despite this apparent sequence plasticity. We propose that selection acts not on primary sequence identity but on a lower-dimensional set of physical parameters—compaction (Rg, scaling exponent), charge patterning (kappa/SCD), aromatic/proline patterning, and derived stickers-and-spacer valence—that map onto condensate material properties. This project will assemble a cross-species, cross-paralog 'physical grammar atlas' by synthesizing publicly available biophysical measurements (SASBDB small-angle scattering profiles, published single-molecule FRET transfer efficiencies, NMR-derived secondary structure propensities), condensate proteomics/composition databases (PhaSepDB, CD-CODE, LLPSDB, DrLLPS), disorder and ortholog annotation resources (MobiDB, DisProt, UniProt/OrthoDB), evolutionary conservation scores (PhyloP, GERP, ConSurf), and disease-variant repositories (ClinVar, ALSoD, dbSNP) for IDR-containing proteins central to condensate biology (TDP-43, tau, α-synuclein, FUS-family, prion-like transcription factor domains). Using previously validated sequence-to-parameter mappings and coarse-grained model parameterizations (e.g., HPS/Mpipi-type frameworks) already established by the team, we will computationally translate thousands of orthologous and paralogous IDR sequences into physical parameter vectors without generating new experimental data, then apply phylogenetic comparative methods and machine learning to ask: (1) Do physical parameters show significantly higher evolutionary conservation than sequence identity across orthologs spanning yeast to human? (2) Do disease-associated mutations and ALS/FTD-linked variants disproportionately perturb conserved physical parameters relative to matched non-pathogenic polymorphisms, even when they fall outside classically conserved residues? (3) Can physical-parameter conservation predict which condensate systems are prone to pathological intra-condensate demixing (as observed for TDP-43) versus those that tolerate sequence divergence while preserving liquid-like behavior? (4) Do synthetic biology design rules for engineering condensate-based gene circuit robustness generalize across the natural parameter space uncovered by the atlas? This effort requires integrating polymer physics expertise (single-molecule and scattering-based conformational analysis), condensate materials science and coarse-grained simulation frameworks, and quantitative sequence-structure-function modeling with disease-variant and synthetic-biology design perspectives—expertise distributed across the team but unify-able only through a dedicated working group with computational, evolutionary genomics, and biophysics specialists. The resulting open-access atlas, reproducible workflows, and predictive parameter-conservation models will provide a generalizable framework for interpreting IDR variation, prioritizing disease mutations for mechanistic follow-up, and guiding rational design of synthetic condensates. Graduate students and postdocs will be trained in cross-database curation, phylogenetic comparative statistics, and biophysical parameter modeling, building a pipeline transferable to other mesoscale emergence questions in molecular and cellular biology.

title: Emergent Mesoscale Regulation of Torpor: A Cross-Species Synthesis of Biomolecular Condensates and Mitochondrial Reorganization in Independently Evolved Hibernators
title_norm: emergent mesoscale regulation of torpor a crossspecies synthesis of biomolecular condensates and mitochondrial reorganization in independently evolved hibernators
abstract_text: The investigation of mammalian hibernation increasingly targets mesoscale physiological mechanisms, as temperature sensitive phase separation of RNA binding proteins and mitochondrial supercomplex reorganization can reprogram cellular respiration without new transcription. To determine if hibernators convergently evolved tunable stress granules and mitochondrial supercomplexes, this project will evaluate comparative genomic resources and transcriptomic datasets using phylogenetic branch site models, biophysical predictors, and time series trajectory analysis. Whole genome assemblies from NCBI, Ensembl, and Zoonomia will be linked to biophysical propensity scores, while RNA seq datasets from SRA and GEO will be harmonized using meta analytic batch correction frameworks. This research will provide a generalizable framework for detecting mesoscale convergence, offering novel insights into torpor evolution with downstream applications for metabolic disease treatment and organ preservation.
full_text: This project investigates hibernation in mammals to determine if convergent evolution alters condensate forming proteins and factors for mitochondrial assembly. The team asks if hibernators convergently evolve mechanisms at the mesoscale level to provide frameworks for preserving organs. The overall design synthesizes data from public sources to test models of convergence and analyze dynamics of expression. The team applies models of phylogenetic branches and biophysical predictors like MobiDB to analyze changes in expression of genes. The project validates results by linking predicted events to changes in expression using data from manipulated cultured fibroblasts. Primary data sources include assemblies of whole genomes from NCBI and datasets of RNA-seq from repositories like GEO. The study integrates these datasets by linking sets of orthologs to scores of propensity and harmonizing transcriptomic records. The team mitigates limitations in depth of sequencing by applying frameworks for batch correction and reporting statistical uncertainty. The proposed project requires extensive collaboration because the broad analytical scope exceeds the capacity of a single laboratory. This complex analysis spans comparative genomics and physiology of hibernation while requiring integrated expertise across multiple distinct scientific disciplines. The team shares primary datasets on Zenodo and publishes open access findings while distributing analytical code through Git. abstract_original: Mammalian hibernation has evolved independently across at least eight lineages—including ursids, sciurid rodents, bats, and even a primate (the fat-tailed dwarf lemur)—yet all hibernators achieve strikingly similar phenotypes: reversible suppression of metabolic rate, translation, and mitochondrial oxidative activity at low body temperature, followed by rapid, damage-free rewarming. While comparative genomic scans have identified candidate genes under selection in hibernators, and tissue-level transcriptomic studies (including our own multi-tissue brown bear resource) have characterized pathway-level shifts in gene expression, little is known about whether convergent evolution acts at the mesoscale—the level of protein assemblies, biomolecular condensates, and organelle architecture that sits between individual gene products and organismal physiology. Emerging evidence in non-hibernator systems shows that temperature- and stress-sensitive phase separation of RNA-binding proteins into stress granules, and reorganization of mitochondrial supercomplexes, can rapidly and reversibly reprogram translation and respiration without new transcription. We hypothesize that hibernators have convergently co-opted or tuned these mesoscale mechanisms as a shared molecular strategy for entering and exiting torpor, and that signatures of this convergence are detectable in existing genomic, transcriptomic, and proteomic datasets. This project will synthesize publicly available whole-genome assemblies and orthology databases (NCBI, Ensembl, Zoonomia), multi-tissue and time-series RNA-seq datasets from hibernating and non-hibernating relatives (SRA, GEO), and proteome-wide intrinsic disorder and phase-separation propensity predictions (e.g., catGRANULE, PScore, MobiDB) to build a cross-species map of condensate-forming and mitochondrial-interacting proteins. We will test for convergent molecular signatures—accelerated evolution, shared amino acid substitutions, or parallel shifts in expression timing—in genes encoding stress granule components, RNA-binding proteins, and mitochondrial supercomplex assembly factors across independently evolved hibernating lineages, using phylogenetic comparative methods that explicitly correct for shared ancestry versus convergence. Where available, we will integrate low-temperature in vitro transcriptomic and metabolic data (e.g., cultured fibroblast time-series data) to link predicted condensate/mitochondrial reorganization events to measured shifts in metabolic and circadian gene expression across torpor-arousal cycles. This effort requires expertise spanning comparative and population genomics, hibernation physiology and multi-tissue transcriptomics, and quantitative biophysical modeling of protein phase behavior and mitochondrial dynamics—capacities that exceed any single lab and necessitate a working group uniting evolutionary genomicists, hibernation biologists, and biophysicists studying condensates and organelle-scale emergence. The synthesis directly targets NCEMS's mesoscale mandate by asking how molecular-scale, temperature-sensitive assembly processes give rise to an emergent, organism-level phenotype (reversible hypometabolism) and whether this emergence follows predictable evolutionary rules. All genomic pipelines, orthology assignments, condensate-propensity scores, and comparative statistical frameworks will be released as open, reusable resources, providing a template for future mesoscale evolutionary synthesis studies and training opportunities for postdocs and graduate students at the interface of genomics, physiology, and biophysics.

title: From Residue Couplings to Circuit Memory: A Cross-Scale Synthesis Linking Coevolutionary Statistics, Allosteric Dynamics, and Phase-Separation Propensity to Regulatory Network Hysteresis
title_norm: from residue couplings to circuit memory a crossscale synthesis linking coevolutionary statistics allosteric dynamics and phaseseparation propensity to regulatory network hysteresis
abstract_text: The molecular biology field studies emergent behaviors like bistability, hysteresis, and irreversible switching in bacterial gene regulatory networks, which require understanding mechanistic links across distinct scales of biological organization. This project will determine if residue level physical architecture predicts irreversible network behavior using a secondary analysis that applies Potts models, graph theoretic descriptors, random forest classifiers, and multivariate regression for feature extraction and cross scale statistical integration. The study will integrate databases including Pfam, UniProt, MDDB, GPCRmd, Dynameomics, DisProt, MobiDB, PhaSepDB, RegulonDB, and EcoCyc by matching identifiers and using structural homology mapping organized within a shared mapping ontology. Establishing this knowledge linking molecular biophysics to network level memory will provide mechanistic explanations for emergent biological behaviors and will directly advance synthetic biology designs and antimicrobial targeting strategies.
full_text: This molecular biology project investigates whether coevolutionary coupling and protein dynamics predict irreversible switching within bacterial networks of gene regulation. Prior studies characterized network memory and properties of proteins independently but lacked mechanistic links across these biological scales. The primary question asks if physical architecture predicts node hysteresis to provide alternative explanations for synthetic biology and antimicrobial targeting. The overall design involves a secondary analysis of public data progressing from dataset curation to cross scale statistical integration. Key methods include statistical coupling analysis and multivariate regression alongside random forest classifiers and information theoretic association measures. The team will validate results using cross validation across families of proteins and permutation testing with rewiring of networks. The project analyzes information from repositories including Pfam and UniProt alongside databases of structures like DisProt and EcoCyc. Researchers will merge datasets by cross referencing identifiers from UniProt and organizing the information through a shared mapping ontology. This shared mapping ontology will mitigate known data limitations like discrepancies in residue numbering and gaps in structural coverage. The proposed timeline spans a multi year period to complete milestones from curation of families to statistical integration. This broad scope requires cross disciplinary collaboration to integrate expertise in biomolecular simulation and dynamics of regulatory networks. The project will share findings and code through open access repositories and executable notebooks to ensure public availability. The proposed team includes postdoctoral researchers and graduate students who will receive cross training in integration of network data.

abstract_original: A central puzzle in molecular and cellular biology is how local, residue-level physical couplings within individual proteins propagate upward to produce circuit-level emergent behaviors such as bistability, hysteresis, and irreversible switching in gene regulatory networks. Existing work has separately characterized (i) coevolutionary statistical couplings among residues using Potts models and statistical coupling analysis across protein families, (ii) dynamic allosteric pathways and temperature- or ligand-sensitive contact networks extracted from molecular dynamics trajectories, (iii) sequence-encoded propensities for intrinsically disordered regions and biomolecular condensate formation, and (iv) network-level dynamical properties of transcriptional regulatory systems, including memory and irreversibility following perturbation. No study has yet asked whether these layers are mechanistically linked: does the architecture of coevolutionary coupling and conformational dynamics within individual regulatory proteins predict which nodes of a transcriptional network will exhibit hysteretic, switch-like, or irreversible behavior? This project proposes a community-scale synthesis to test that hypothesis by integrating four classes of publicly available data that no single lab currently combines: (1) multiple sequence alignments and derived direct-coupling/statistical-coupling matrices for transcription factors and signaling proteins (Pfam, UniProt); (2) publicly deposited molecular dynamics trajectories and contact-network datasets for homologous or orthologous regulatory and allosteric proteins (e.g., MDDB, GPCRmd, Dynameomics-type repositories); (3) curated intrinsically disordered region and condensate-propensity annotations (DisProt, MobiDB, PhaSepDB) for the same protein families; and (4) reconstructed bacterial regulatory network topologies and previously published perturbation-response datasets characterizing irreversibility and hysteresis in transcriptional circuits (e.g., RegulonDB/EcoCyc-derived networks). Using information-theoretic measures of coupling entropy and coevolutionary sector structure alongside graph-theoretic and machine-learning analyses of MD-derived allosteric pathways (including random-forest classifiers previously validated for predicting channel-gating states), we will quantify whether proteins with strong long-range coevolutionary coupling and multistable dynamic ensembles are disproportionately embedded in network motifs associated with hysteresis and irreversibility, and whether disorder/condensate propensity modulates this relationship by providing an additional slow, cooperative mode of regulatory memory. The synthesis will produce an open, versioned, FAIR-compliant multi-scale dataset and analysis pipeline—a public 'coupling-to-circuit atlas'—linking residue-level statistical physics, protein dynamics, mesoscale assembly propensity, and network dynamics for a curated set of well-characterized regulatory systems. This effort requires collaboration across evolutionary systems biology, coevolutionary sequence statistics, computational biophysics/MD, and data infrastructure expertise, exceeding what any single lab's data or toolset can address, and will generate testable, falsifiable predictions about which molecular architectures give rise to emergent network-level memory. Training modules will teach graduate students and postdocs to integrate sequence-based statistical models, trajectory-based dynamics, and network reconstruction within reproducible open-science workflows, directly advancing NCEMS's mission to understand how mesoscale molecular organization gives rise to cellular-scale emergent properties.

title: Flux, Function, and Fitness: A Cross-Species Synthesis Linking Genome-Scale Metabolic Network Architecture to Signatures of Natural Selection
title_norm: flux function and fitness a crossspecies synthesis linking genomescale metabolic network architecture to signatures of natural selection
abstract_text: The fields of population genetics and systems biology examine varying selective constraints and topological structures within genome scale metabolic networks, presenting critical opportunities to understand fundamental patterns of molecular evolution. It is currently not understood how metabolic network architecture dictates whether specific genes experience strong purifying selection or serve as targets for adaptive evolution based on network position. This project will determine if network position and flux metrics predict natural selection across kingdoms by assembling a cross species compendium, performing constraint based modeling, and applying machine learning algorithms including gradient boosted trees. Genomic datasets from repositories including gnomAD and diverse species panels will be integrated with metabolic reconstructions from BiGG and ModelSEED by mapping orthologs through Ensembl Compara into unified per gene tables. This work will yield a predictive framework detailing metabolic evolutionary robustness across kingdoms, providing critical knowledge to identify malleable versus constrained gene targets for advanced metabolic engineering.
full_text: This project integrates systems biology and molecular evolution to understand how networks of metabolism dictate the selection of genes. Previous work mapped topologies of networks and selective constraints independently but never integrated these fields to predict evolutionary outcomes. The proposed study asks if position in a network predicts the strength of selection across kingdoms to guide metabolic engineering. The study uses a synthesis across three phases to calculate metrics of networks and apply machine learning to predict evolution. The team applies modeling based on constraints in COBRApy alongside coalescent simulations and gradient boosted trees with attribution of features. The team will validate results against null distributions based on permutations while controlling for confounders like essentiality and expression. The project analyzes reconstructions of metabolism from BiGG and KBase alongside genomic data extracted from diversity panels and gnomAD. The team will map orthologs using Ensembl Compara and UniProt to combine metrics of networks with statistics of population genetics. The team will mitigate confounding variables with external databases and manage variations in demographics by retraining classifiers on simulations. The timeline of 30 months progresses from construction of compendiums and integrative modeling to final syntheses across kingdoms and publication. This project requires collaboration across disciplines to unite the distinct methodologies of metabolic modeling and inference of population genetics. The team will share data and code through GitHub and Zenodo alongside computational notebooks and publications with open access. The team comprises a postdoctoral researcher and graduate students receiving training across disciplines in systems biology and genomics.

abstract_original: A central puzzle in molecular evolution is why some metabolic genes are under strong purifying selection while others tolerate substantial standing variation, and why certain pathways repeatedly become targets of adaptive selection across independent lineages. We propose that this puzzle can be resolved by treating metabolism as a mesoscale emergent system: the topological and flux-based organization of genome-scale metabolic networks (GSMs)—modularity, flux coupling, redundancy, and control-coefficient distributions—should predict the strength and mode of selection acting on the underlying genes, and conversely, recurrent environmental pressures (diet, temperature, nutrient stress, immune activation) should preferentially reshape specific network modules. This hypothesis has never been tested systematically because it requires integrating two data ecosystems that rarely intersect: curated genome-scale metabolic reconstructions (BiGG, AGORA2, ModelSEED, KBase) and population-genomic diversity/selection datasets (1000 Genomes, HGDP, gnomAD, SNP-chip panels from adaptation studies, and model-organism diversity panels for yeast, Arabidopsis, and maize). Synthesizing these resources demands expertise that no single lab possesses: constraint-based metabolic modeling and flux-variability/flux-coupling analysis, population genetic inference of selection (site-frequency-spectrum statistics, iHS, dN/dS, and simulation-trained deep learning classifiers such as GAN/CNN discriminators), and machine-learning interpretability methods to link network-derived features to genomic signal. Our working group will assemble a cross-species compendium pairing existing GSMs with publicly available selection-scan outputs for the same organisms and genes, computing per-reaction/per-gene topological metrics (centrality, flux control coefficients, module membership, redundancy/backup pathway counts) from steady-state and context-specific models (including previously published macrophage and maize nitrogen-stress GSMs) and aligning them with locus-specific selection statistics. A second aim will extend this framework comparatively across humans, crops, and microbes to ask whether 'evolvability hotspots' in metabolic architecture are conserved across kingdoms or are lineage-specific consequences of network rewiring. This project uses exclusively existing public data, requires collaborative integration of metabolic modeling and population-genomic inference pipelines that individually exist in different communities, and will produce an open, reproducible workflow and annotated cross-species dataset linking network architecture to evolutionary constraint. Beyond resolving a long-standing question about the evolutionary logic of metabolic robustness, the framework offers a predictive tool for metabolic engineering—flagging which reactions are evolutionarily malleable versus constrained—and provides rich training opportunities for graduate students and postdocs to gain dual fluency in systems biology and population genomics, directly building the interdisciplinary, data-savvy workforce NCEMS aims to cultivate.

title: Mesoscale Coordination of Proteome Turnover: Synthesizing Public Degradation Kinetics with Complex, Condensate, and Disorder Architecture to Discover Emergent Proteostasis Modules
title_norm: mesoscale coordination of proteome turnover synthesizing public degradation kinetics with complex condensate and disorder architecture to discover emergent proteostasis modules
abstract_text: Cellular proteostasis research measures protein turnover rates across diverse physiological conditions, but unstandardized datasets currently prevent the evaluation of higher order kinetic coordination within mesoscale structures like protein complexes and biomolecular condensates. The primary objective is to determine if structurally associated proteins degrade at coordinated rates, which this project will assess by applying Bayesian hierarchical modeling and mixed effects regression to map turnover concordance disruptions. The study will integrate kinetic datasets from PRIDE and MassIVE with structural databases like CORUM by recalculating rate constants on a common scale and filtering species matched mappings through gene expression networks. This research will link molecular kinetics to cellular robustness, yielding a novel mechanistic biomarker framework that identifies disrupted turnover coordination in aging and cardiovascular disease.
full_text: This research investigates the domain of cellular proteostasis to determine how spatial organization influences kinetics of protein turnover. Existing datasets capture half lives of proteins across organisms but lack kinetic standardization and integration with structural data. The primary question asks if associated proteins degrade at coordinated rates to establish novel biomarkers for cardiovascular disease. This secondary data analysis harmonizes public protein turnover records to map changes in concordance across various disease states. The analytical approach employs hierarchical Bayesian models and regression techniques within containerized computational workflows to assess statistical significance. The study validates patterns of concordance by analyzing independent turnover datasets from organs of mice and human cells. The project utilizes protein turnover records from MassIVE and PRIDE alongside structural data from CORUM and BioGRID databases. The team integrates these resources by mapping species matched orthologs and standardizing rate constants on a common scale. The study mitigates variance in experimental design by applying hierarchical Bayesian models to account for specific technical differences. The ambitious scope of this proposed project requires combined expertise in models of proteomic kinetics and structural bioinformatics. This necessary cross disciplinary collaboration connects multiple research laboratories to address complex requirements of proteomics within cardiovascular tissues. The team will share derived metadata and containerized code on GitHub to ensure complete transparency of analytical decisions. The research team includes principal investigators and graduate students who will receive cross disciplinary training in structural bioinformatics.
