abstract_original: Protein turnover—the balance of synthesis and degradation—has been measured in hundreds of public datasets using SILAC, dynamic SILAC, 15N/heavy-water metabolic labeling, and pulse-chase mass spectrometry across yeast, mouse tissues, human cell lines, and iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes and endothelial cells. These datasets, generated by dozens of independent labs under different physiological conditions (oxidative stress, hypoxia/hyperoxia, aging, cardiovascular disease models), are rarely integrated with structural and interaction data that describe how proteins are organized at the mesoscale—as stable complexes, transient assemblies, or biomolecular condensates. We propose to build a unified, harmonized turnover atlas that cross-references public half-life datasets with complex membership (CORUM, hu.MAP, BioGRID), intrinsic disorder annotations (MobiDB, IUPred-derived scores), liquid-liquid phase separation databases (PhaSepDB, LLPSDB), and tissue/single-cell expression atlases (Human Protein Atlas, GTEx). Our central question is whether mesoscale organization is a primary determinant of emergent proteostatic behavior: do subunits within stable complexes exhibit coordinated (concerted) degradation kinetics that buffer stoichiometric imbalance, while orphan or condensate-resident proteins show discordant, individually regulated turnover? We hypothesize that loss of this coordination—rather than changes in individual protein half-lives—constitutes an emergent signature of proteostatic collapse in aging and disease, distinguishable only when turnover data are analyzed jointly with structural context rather than protein-by-protein. To test this, we will (1) computationally harmonize turnover rate constants across >30 public datasets spanning organisms, tissues, and physiological perturbations (oxygen tension, replicative and organismal aging, ER/oxidative stress, cardiomyopathy models) using batch-correction and Bayesian hierarchical modeling to place disparate experimental designs on a common kinetic scale; (2) quantify turnover concordance within known complexes and condensates versus size-matched control sets of unrelated proteins, testing whether concordance scales with disorder content, complex stoichiometry, and evolutionary conservation; (3) map how concordance is perturbed under stress and aging conditions already profiled in existing datasets, identifying mesoscale modules whose turnover synchrony breaks down first; and (4) validate cross-tissue generalizability using existing in vivo turnover measurements from heart, lung, and brain under varying oxygen tension and cardiovascular disease models. This effort requires expertise spanning classical proteomic turnover measurement and kinetic modeling, translation and stress-response systems biology, structural/disorder bioinformatics, and cardiovascular tissue-specific proteomics—none of which resides in a single lab, and none of which has previously been assembled at this scale. The project will produce an open, versioned turnover-mesoscale database and reproducible analytical pipeline (containerized, deposited on GitHub/Zenodo), enabling the community to query turnover coordination for any complex, condensate, or disease gene set. Graduate students and postdocs will be trained in cross-lab data harmonization, hierarchical Bayesian kinetic modeling, and structural bioinformatics integration, directly building the data-savvy workforce NCEMS aims to cultivate while addressing a fundamental, previously inaccessible question about how molecular-scale turnover gives rise to emergent, mesoscale proteostatic robustness and its breakdown in aging and disease.

title: From Transcript Counts to Molecular Choreography: A Bayesian Synthesis Framework Linking Spatial Expression Atlases to Single-Molecule Biophysical States of Trafficking Machinery
title_norm: from transcript counts to molecular choreography a bayesian synthesis framework linking spatial expression atlases to singlemolecule biophysical states of trafficking machinery
abstract_text: Cell biology investigates the mesoscale biophysical behavior of copper trafficking and metal homeostasis protein complexes, which is crucial because current quantitative measurements remain disconnected from cellular and tissue transcriptomic contexts. A critical scientific gap is whether the biophysical behavior of protein complexes is predictable from local transcriptomic data, as existing spatial atlases currently lack integration with physical measurements. The primary objective is to determine if single molecule biophysical parameters of metal homeostasis proteins are predictable from spatial expression contexts, which will be achieved by constructing hierarchical Bayesian latent variable models via Markov chain Monte Carlo inference. Single nucleus and spatial MERFISH datasets from the Human Protein Atlas, Allen Brain Atlas, and HuBMAP will be harmonized into a shared embedding space and linked to biophysical parameters through latent variables. This framework will establish how cellular composition determines mesoscale biophysical organization, enabling the direct inference of biophysical functions from single cell gene expression atlases without requiring new experiments.
full_text: Cell biology investigates the mesoscale biophysics of complexes for metal homeostasis (Ctr1 and Atox1) and questions if transcriptomic profiles predict this behavior. Scientists possess quantitative biophysical data but have not integrated these measurements with atlases of tissue and single cell expression. The project asks if spatial expression predicts the biophysics of single molecules to infer functions without new experiments. The research team curates biophysical parameters and integrates atlases of spatial expression via hierarchical Bayesian models using public datasets. Key methods include Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) inference and variational approximations alongside error models for the integration of single cells. Researchers will validate predictive accuracy through cross validation on existing data and posterior predictive checks against held out measurements. Datasets include the Human Protein Atlas and the Allen Brain Atlas alongside spatial MERFISH and studies of single molecule biophysics. The project harmonizes transcriptomic datasets into a shared embedding space to link spatial descriptors with curated biophysical parameters. Hierarchical priors will pool information across cell types to mitigate the limitations of sparse data and cross study heterogeneity. Project milestones include the curation of biophysical parameters and the integration of spatial atlases before finalizing the Bayesian modeling. This research requires cross disciplinary collaboration to combine expertise in the integration of transcriptomic data and the biophysics of copper homeostasis. The team will release an open source database of biophysical parameters and share all modeling code on public repositories. Experts in computational biology and biophysics will mentor one postdoctoral researcher and one graduate student to provide cross disciplinary training.

abstract_original: A central unsolved question in cell biology is whether the mesoscale biophysical behavior of a protein complex—its oligomeric stoichiometry, diffusion coefficient, membrane residence time, or reaction kinetics—can be predicted from the transcriptomic and proteomic context of the cell in which it resides. Decades of single-molecule biophysics have produced quantitative measurements of protein oligomerization, diffusion, and binding kinetics for specific molecular machines (e.g., copper transporters, membrane trafficking complexes, transcription factor–DNA interactions) in isolated cell types and controlled conditions, while single-cell and spatial transcriptomic/proteomic atlases now provide expression and localization maps of these same machineries across hundreds of cell types, tissues, and disease states. These two data universes—molecular-scale kinetic/stoichiometric measurements and cellular-scale expression/spatial context—have never been formally integrated, despite an implicit hypothesis in the field that mesoscale organization (clustering, oligomerization, complex assembly) emerges from, and feeds back onto, the local molecular composition of the cell. We propose to build a public, reusable synthesis framework that curates quantitative single-molecule biophysical parameters (stoichiometry, diffusion, kon/koff, residence times) reported in the literature and repositories for a defined set of trafficking-related and metal-homeostasis machineries (Ctr1, ATP7A/B, Atox1, CCS, and associated chaperones/trafficking regulators), and formally links them, via Bayesian hierarchical latent-variable models, to matched single-cell and spatial transcriptomic/proteomic profiles from public atlases (Human Protein Atlas, Allen Brain Atlas, HuBMAP, and existing brain snRNA-seq/spatial MERFISH datasets) spanning the same or comparable cell types, brain regions, and disease states (e.g., Parkinson's disease, Wilson's/Menkes-related neurodegeneration). The model will treat measured single-molecule parameters as noisy, condition-specific observations governed by latent biophysical state variables, and will estimate how these latent states depend on local expression levels, co-expression neighborhoods, and spatial cellular context, explicitly propagating measurement uncertainty and cross-study heterogeneity using probabilistic inference methods drawn from single-molecule photon-counting statistics. The framework will be validated by predicting biophysical parameters for cell types and conditions where single-molecule measurements do not yet exist but transcriptomic/spatial data do, generating falsifiable, quantitative predictions (e.g., expected oligomeric state of ATP7A in a specific reactive astrocyte subtype) that can guide future targeted experiments. This effort requires collaboration beyond any single lab: computational expertise in spatial transcriptomic integration and cell-state annotation, deep domain knowledge of copper homeostasis and membrane trafficking biophysics, and Bayesian modeling expertise for heterogeneous, noisy single-molecule data. The resulting open-source pipeline, curated biophysical parameter database, and trained hierarchical models will be released under FAIR data principles, providing a template applicable to other molecular machines beyond copper transport, and offering hands-on training for graduate students and postdocs at the interface of quantitative single-molecule biophysics and computational spatial genomics—directly addressing NCEMS's mission to explain how mesoscale molecular organization emerges from and shapes higher-order cellular states.

title: From Chemical Marks to Mesoscale Machines: A Multi-Omics and Molecular Dynamics Synthesis of How tRNA Modification Loss Drives Ribosome Collision Condensates and Translational Stress Phenotypes
title_norm: from chemical marks to mesoscale machines a multiomics and molecular dynamics synthesis of how trna modification loss drives ribosome collision condensates and translational stress phenotypes
abstract_text: Within molecular and cellular biology, tRNA modifications regulate translation speed and fidelity, where modification loss induces ribosome collisions that act as essential nucleation sites for quality control ribonucleoprotein condensates. The quantitative relationship between modification deficient decoding biophysics and condensate nucleation remains uncharacterized, lacking a systematic framework that connects these thermodynamic mechanisms to cellular stress and disease. This project will determine how biophysical signatures predict ribosome collision probability and quality control recruitment by applying molecular dynamics simulations and collision detection pipelines to link structural predictions with sequencing derived pausing scores and proteomic condensate scores. The analysis will integrate MODOMICS, Protein Data Bank, and single cell epigenomic atlases by encoding structural predictions as quantitative features and fusing them via graph based propagation and similarity network fusion clustering. This research will produce a cross scale mechanistic model that connects chemical modification loss to condensate emergence, revealing whether collision triggered condensation drives conserved stress signatures in disease phenotypes.
full_text: The molecular biology research domain lacks a systematic framework connecting modifications in transfer RNA to ribosome collisions and the assembly of condensates. Losing modifications in transfer RNA increases ribosome pausing and the nucleation of condensates but relationships between these events remain uncharacterized. The primary question asks if signatures of transfer RNA predict ribosome collisions to model a novel mechanism across scales for disease. The analytical strategy synthesizes public data to link structural predictions and scores for proteomic condensates when evaluating pathways of disease. Key methods involve molecular dynamics using GROMACS and OpenMM alongside pipelines for Ribo-seq and the imputation of features based on graphs. Workflows for computation will undergo validation against phenotypic outcomes in disease cohorts and benchmarking using held out sets of data. The project uses multiple databases including MODOMICS and Sequence Read Archive alongside epigenomic atlases for single cells from the brain. Integration of data encodes structural predictions as quantitative features for fusion with scores derived from sequencing using feature propagation. Methods for propagation based on graphs will address the sparsity of measurements from single cells through data imputation and denoising. This project incorporates regular monthly meetings of the working group and quarterly synthesis retreats to maintain steady progress. This cross disciplinary collaboration requires simultaneous expertise spanning molecular biology and the integration of data driven by artificial intelligence. The team will distribute findings as preprints while providing data and containerized workflows under licenses for open source software. The team includes multiple trainees at different career stages receiving instruction across genetics in the wet lab and computational biophysics.

abstract_original: A fundamental unsolved question in molecular and cellular biology is how discrete chemical modifications on individual RNA molecules propagate upward to generate emergent, mesoscale ribonucleoprotein (RNP) assemblies that reshape cellular physiology. tRNA modifications (e.g., wobble-position thiolation, dihydrouridine, queuosine) are known to tune translation speed and codon decoding fidelity at the molecular scale, and prior work has shown that loss of these modifications increases ribosome pausing genome-wide. Separately, stalled and collided ribosomes are increasingly recognized as nucleation sites for mesoscale quality-control condensates involving factors such as ZNF598, Pelota/Hbs1, and stress-granule components. Yet no systematic framework connects the biophysics of individual modification-deficient tRNA-ribosome complexes to the assembly thermodynamics of these collision-triggered condensates, nor to their downstream consequences for cellular stress phenotypes, proteostasis, and disease. This project will synthesize four classes of existing public data—(1) curated tRNA modification enzyme and modification-site databases (MODOMICS, bacterial and eukaryotic epitranscriptomic maps) together with comparative genomics of modification enzyme conservation and redundancy; (2) ribosome profiling (Ribo-seq) datasets across bacteria, yeast, and human cell lines under modification-enzyme-deficient versus wild-type conditions; (3) cryo-EM structures of collided/stalled ribosome complexes and quality-control factor assemblies deposited in the PDB and EMDB; and (4) proteomic, single-cell transcriptomic/epigenomic, and condensate-composition datasets (e.g., DrLLPS, PhaSepDB, TCGA/ICGC proteomic subtyping cohorts, and postmortem brain single-cell epigenomic atlases) that report stress-granule/RNP condensate signatures in disease contexts such as leukemia and neurodegeneration. We will use residue-resolution coarse-grained and atomistic molecular dynamics to model how loss of specific tRNA modifications alters codon-anticodon geometry, decoding kinetics, and interface energetics at collided ribosome junctions, generating physically grounded predictions of collision propensity and condensate nucleation likelihood. These structural predictions will be integrated with cross-organism Ribo-seq pausing signatures and condensate proteomic composition using graph-based imputation and similarity-network-fusion clustering to identify conserved “modification–pausing–condensation” axes, and validated against phenotypic outcomes captured in existing multi-omic disease cohorts. This work directly targets NCEMS’ mesoscale mandate: it treats ribosome collision complexes and stress condensates as an intermediate organizational layer between single biomolecule chemistry and cellular/organismal phenotype, an integration no single lab can achieve alone, requiring RNA modification biology, biomolecular simulation, AI-driven multi-omic integration, and clinical proteomic/epigenomic expertise simultaneously. All modeling pipelines, curated datasets, and integrative code will be released as open, reproducible workflows, and the working group will train graduate students and postdocs across wet-lab microbial genetics, computational biophysics, and biomedical data science, producing a new generation of researchers fluent in bridging atomistic simulation with population-scale omics synthesis.

title: Decoding the 'Organelle Signature' Landscape: A Genomic Deconvolution Framework for Discovering Novel Protein- and Lipid-Bounded Compartments Across Bacteria and Archaea
title_norm: decoding the organelle signature landscape a genomic deconvolution framework for discovering novel protein and lipidbounded compartments across bacteria and archaea
abstract_text: The emergence of bacterial and archaeal organelles, including carboxysomes and encapsulins, relies on specific gene clusters that self assemble into functional compartments to organize critical biochemical processes. This project will discover novel prokaryotic organelle systems by applying non negative matrix factorization and topic modeling to extract recurring gene cluster architectures, prioritizing new compartmentalization signatures using AlphaFold and ESMFold structural predictions. The analysis will convert genomic loci from NCBI and GTDB into sparse matrices, integrating the extracted candidate signatures with structural databases and multi omics archives to evaluate condition specific coexpression. This statistically driven framework will replace manual discovery methods, yielding a powerful analytical resource to identify novel prokaryotic organelles and diverse molecular machines across broad genomic datasets.
full_text: This project investigates the emergence of subcellular compartments in bacterial and archaeal organelles where discovery based on homology lacks scale. The study asks if applying matrix factorization to genomic data can identify novel prokaryotic organelles via a statistically driven framework. The overall design extracts loci of gene clusters to decompose encoded vectors via matrix factorization for the prioritization of signatures. Key methods include searches with profile hidden Markov models and topic modeling alongside Bayesian non negative matrix factorization and AlphaFold. Known organelle systems will serve as ground truth anchors to evaluate signature stability across bootstrapped and resampled subsets of genomes. The project utilizes genomic datasets from repositories like GTDB and NCBI alongside public proteomics and structural databases such as AlphaFold. Genomic loci will be converted into feature vectors and integrated with structural predictions to evaluate co expression under specific conditions. Potential statistical noise and lineage specific artifacts will be mitigated by measuring signature reproducibility across resampled subsets of genomic data. Milestones include data assembly and signature extraction followed by the prioritization of candidates and the final synthesis of ranked systems. This cross disciplinary collaboration unites distributed expertise in large scale comparative genomics and organelle biogenesis with methods for structural biology. The team will share analytical pipelines via GitHub and Zenodo alongside preprints and publications with open access to distribute findings. The team features four investigators and two trainees who will gain experience with methods for matrix factorization and microbial physiology.

abstract_original: Bacterial and archaeal organelles—carboxysomes, encapsulins, magnetosomes, ferrosomes, and their atypical relatives—represent striking cases of mesoscale emergence, where discrete sets of genes assemble into compartments with properties (selective permeability, biomineralization, redox control) absent from their individual protein components. Despite decades of discovery, our catalog of prokaryotic organelles remains almost certainly incomplete: current identification relies on manual inspection of gene neighborhoods and homology to a handful of known shell or membrane systems, an approach poorly suited to the scale of modern genomic and metagenomic databases. This project proposes to reframe organelle discovery as a signature-deconvolution problem, adapting mutational-signature-style matrix factorization methods (as used in large-scale cancer genomics) to genomic co-occurrence data. Instead of decomposing mutation spectra into additive processes, we will decompose gene-cluster architectures—shell/membrane protein paralogs, cargo enzymes, transporters, and regulatory genes—across hundreds of thousands of public bacterial and archaeal genomes and metagenome-assembled genomes (IMG/M, GTDB, JGI, NCBI) into a small number of recurring 'organelle signatures.' Known systems (carboxysome, encapsulin, magnetosome, ferrosome, and atypical 'JEEP' loci) will serve as ground-truth anchors to validate the factorization, while residual, previously uncharacterized signatures will be flagged as candidate novel compartments. For each candidate signature, we will integrate structural predictions from AlphaFold/ESMFold databases to assess whether component proteins form shell-like oligomers or membrane-remodeling folds, and will cross-reference public proteomics, transcriptomics, and metabolomics datasets to infer physiological context (e.g., iron/heme handling, cofactor regeneration, anaerobic metabolism) and predict conditions under which candidate organelles are expressed. This directly extends existing team expertise: comparative genomic characterization of magnetosome and encapsulin diversity, mechanistic understanding of iron-storing ferrosomes and heme homeostasis, structural and functional dissection of microcompartment shell proteins and their 'just-enough-parts' atypical loci, and quantitative signature-extraction methodology drawn from large-scale cancer genomic synthesis. No single lab in this consortium possesses the full combination of large-scale comparative genomics infrastructure, organelle biogenesis expertise across iron- and carbon-based systems, and quantitative signature-deconvolution methodology needed to execute this synthesis; the project inherently requires pooling of distinct public data streams (genomic, structural, proteomic) and distinct disciplinary lenses. Deliverables include an open, versioned organelle-signature database and reproducible computational pipeline, a ranked list of candidate novel bacterial/archaeal organelles with predicted structural and functional annotations for community follow-up, and training materials introducing trainees to matrix-factorization approaches for genomic architecture discovery—bridging molecular structural biology, microbial genomics, and quantitative signature analysis. By treating organelle emergence as a generalizable, learnable pattern in genomic architecture rather than a case-by-case discovery, this work aims to substantially expand the known diversity of subcellular compartmentalization in prokaryotes and provide a template method transferable to other classes of mesoscale molecular machines.

title: Circadian Control of Heat-Sensitive Mesoscale Assembly During Plant Cell Division
title_norm: circadian control of heatsensitive mesoscale assembly during plant cell division
abstract_text: Plant cell biology investigates the mesoscale organization of cytokinesis, a process utilizing coordinated cytoskeletal and vesicular machinery that is strongly influenced by heat stress and circadian regulation. This project will determine how circadian phase and heat stress jointly affect plant cytokinesis through a computational data synthesis that applies phase aware regression, molecular networks, image segmentation, and interpretable machine learning. The study will integrate bulk and single cell transcriptomic, proteomic, and microscopic data from multiple databases by establishing a shared metadata schema and connecting molecular network features with image derived cellular phenotypes. This work will reveal the conditions determining cell division robustness, shifting the focus of heat stress biology toward systems level coordination and providing a cellular basis for crop vulnerability.

The project will archive containerized workflows and harmonized metadata in public repositories under licenses for open source software. Plant growth under episodic high temperature depends not only on stress-responsive transcription but also on whether dividing cells can assemble a functional cytokinetic apparatus at the right time. The central question of this synthesis project is: how do time of day and heat stress jointly alter the emergent mesoscale organization of plant cytokinesis, including microtubule arrays, endomembrane trafficking, cell plate formation, and nascent cell wall deposition? We propose that cytokinetic failure under heat is an emergent systems property arising from misalignment among circadian-regulated stress pathways, vesicle sorting capacity, cytoskeletal reorganization, and cell wall biosynthesis, rather than from disruption of any single gene or organelle.

This NCEMS Working Group will use only publicly available datasets to build a cross-scale synthesis of heat-sensitive plant cell division. We will integrate public RNA-seq time courses from Arabidopsis, sorghum, maize, wheat, and other plant systems exposed to temperature perturbations at different times of day; root and shoot single-cell transcriptomic atlases enriched for proliferative tissues; public proteomic, phosphoproteomic, interactome, and subcellular localization resources; and archived fluorescence and electron microscopy datasets containing dividing plant cells, cytoskeletal markers, Golgi/trans-Golgi network markers, cell plate markers, and cell wall biosynthetic reporters. Existing resources such as GEO, SRA, ENA, PRIDE, BioImage Archive, EMPIAR, TAIR, MaizeGDB, Expression Atlas, SUBA, and plant orthology databases will be harmonized into a reproducible analysis framework.

The project has three synthesis aims. First, we will create a shared ontology and data model linking cytokinetic structures, endomembrane compartments, cell wall assembly processes, heat-response regulators, and circadian phase information across plant species and experimental platforms. Second, we will construct confounder-aware, context-specific gene and protein networks that distinguish heat-responsive modules that are constitutive from those gated by time of day, tissue identity, developmental stage, or genotype. These networks will prioritize conserved and lineage-specific modules connecting calcium signaling, heat shock regulation, vesicle trafficking, autophagy-related remodeling, microtubule organization, and polysaccharide deposition. Third, we will apply standardized image-analysis workflows to public microscopy data to extract mesoscale phenotypes such as phragmoplast geometry, cell plate expansion symmetry, vesicle-marker distribution, microtubule array coherence, and spatial relationships among organelles during cytokinesis. Network features will then be linked to image-derived phenotypes to identify candidate molecular configurations that predict robust versus heat-vulnerable cytokinetic assembly.

The expected outcome is an open, community-curated atlas of plant cytokinetic heat sensitivity that connects molecular state, cellular architecture, circadian timing, and species-level variation. This effort requires NCEMS support because it depends on coordination among plant cell biologists, circadian and stress biologists, endomembrane specialists, computational genomicists, image analysts, statisticians, and trainees across institutions. No individual laboratory could assemble, standardize, and interpret these heterogeneous public datasets at the necessary scale. The Working Group will release containerized workflows, harmonized metadata, image-analysis notebooks, network models, and training materials. By synthesizing public molecular and cellular data, the project will reveal how environmental timing reshapes mesoscale cellular organization and will provide a general framework for studying emergent stress sensitivity in eukaryotic cell division.

title: Cross-Scale Synthesis of Emergent Chromatin Microenvironments in Human Brain Cell Types
title_norm: crossscale synthesis of emergent chromatin microenvironments in human brain cell types
abstract_text: Molecular and cellular neuroscience investigates the mesoscale 3D chromatin organization of human brain cells, which is essential because linear genome annotation methods remain insufficient for explaining noncoding brain disorder variants. An integrated understanding of 3D chromatin organization is lacking, leaving it unclear how molecular features form mesoscale structures across brain cell types to influence gene expression and psychiatric disease variants. The primary objective of this research is to define recurrent classes of mesoscale chromatin neighborhoods by applying multiscale graph representations, graph neural networks, and biophysical descriptors to predict structural microenvironments and evaluate heritability enrichment. The study will integrate single cell and bulk chromatin architecture maps, transcriptomic atlases, and epigenetic databases by constructing multiscale graphs where nodes represent genomic elements and edges reflect 3D contacts. This project will yield a cross scale atlas of 3D chromatin structures to evaluate psychiatric disease variants within a spatial regulatory context rather than relying on linear sequence proximity.

A central unsolved problem in molecular and cellular neuroscience is how molecular features of chromatin regulators, transcription factors, histone modifications, and architectural proteins combine to produce mesoscale genome structures that differ across brain cell types and alter cellular phenotypes. We propose a community-scale synthesis project to define the “chromatin microenvironment grammar” of human brain cells: the rules by which local molecular interactions give rise to emergent 3D regulatory neighborhoods, enhancer hubs, and compartmental domains that influence gene expression and psychiatric disease risk. The project will use only publicly available data, integrating single-cell and bulk chromatin conformation datasets, brain single-nucleus RNA-seq and ATAC-seq atlases, epigenomic maps, proteomic resources, transcription factor binding data, genetic association studies, and public annotations of intrinsically disordered regions, multivalent domains, and chromatin-binding proteins.

The working group will address three linked questions. First, which classes of mesoscale chromatin neighborhoods recur across human brain cell types, developmental stages, and disease-relevant genomic loci? Second, can these neighborhoods be predicted from molecular features such as nucleosome positioning, histone marks, CTCF/cohesin occupancy, transcription factor motif density, RNA-binding protein expression, and the disorder or multivalency of chromatin-associated proteins? Third, do psychiatric and neurodevelopmental disease variants preferentially perturb particular emergent chromatin microenvironments rather than individual genes or linear regulatory elements?

To answer these questions, we will assemble a harmonized atlas from public datasets including human and mouse brain single-cell 3D genome maps, PsychENCODE and related brain transcriptomic and epigenomic resources, ENCODE/Roadmap chromatin annotations, public proteomic and protein-domain databases, and genome-wide association summary statistics for schizophrenia, autism, bipolar disorder, major depression, cognition, and neurodegenerative traits. We will develop open computational workflows that align regulatory elements across modalities, infer cell-type-specific 3D regulatory neighborhoods, quantify mesoscale features of chromatin organization, and test whether these features are enriched for disease heritability. A key innovation will be the integration of polymer-inspired and biophysical descriptors—loop density, contact anisotropy, domain compaction, predicted multivalent binding capacity, and disorder-associated interaction potential—with machine learning models trained to predict expression and disease-relevant regulatory disruption.

This project is well matched to NCEMS because it focuses on emergence at the mesoscale: how molecular-scale interactions among DNA, histones, transcription factors, architectural proteins, and disordered chromatin regulators generate higher-order genome structures with consequences for cellular identity and disease. It requires expertise beyond any single laboratory, combining single-cell genome architecture, chromatin structural biology, polymer physics, statistical genetics, proteomics, transcriptomics, and open data engineering. The synthesis will produce a public atlas of brain cell chromatin microenvironments, reusable software for cross-scale genome-structure integration, benchmark datasets for trainees, and testable models for how disease variants alter emergent regulatory architecture. Trainees will participate through collaborative code sprints, reproducibility workshops, and cross-disciplinary analysis teams, gaining experience in public data synthesis, biophysical modeling, and responsible open science.

title: Contamination-Aware Synthesis of Microbiome Functional Modules Linked to Emergent Human Proteome and Metabolome States
title_norm: contaminationaware synthesis of microbiome functional modules linked to emergent human proteome and metabolome states
abstract_text: Within human microbiome ecology, emergent biochemical functions of oral and gut communities critically influence host biology via molecular outputs, despite the poor replication of current disease associations based on taxonomic classifications. It remains unclear whether microbiome host associations are driven by individual microbial taxa with divergent gene content or by mesoscale functional modules emerging from community interactions. To determine if functionally defined microbial modules predict host proteomic and metabolomic states more reliably than taxonomic profiles, this project will synthesize public multi omics data using fast translated alignment, sparse latent factor models, and graph clustering. The study will integrate public shotgun metagenomes, metabolomic repositories, and host proteomic datasets by mapping microbial modules to host molecules through multilevel models and network propagation to prioritize human disease pathways. This work will shift analysis from single taxon correlations to emergent community level biochemical capacities and yield a contamination aware framework for comparing modern and historical human microbiome functions.
full_text: Research into ecology of the human microbiome investigates if emergent functional modules drive interactions with host circulating proteins. Microbiomes influence host biology but associations with taxonomy replicate poorly due to divergent gene content and overlapping functions. This study tests if functional modules predict host states reliably while introducing contamination aware frameworks for historical comparisons. The design synthesizes public data from multiple omics by harmonizing metadata and linking functional modules to host phenotypes. Key methods include fast translated alignment and strain aware profiling alongside sparse latent factor models and network propagation. Results will undergo validation through nested cross validation and held out cohorts alongside tests of randomization and reference subsampling. Data sources include public shotgun metagenomes and databases of metabolomics like MetaboLights alongside reference databases such as UniRef. The team will map functional modules to host proteins and integrate genetic summary statistics to prioritize pathways of disease. To mitigate limitations from damage to DNA and environmental contamination the researchers will calculate provenance scores for sensitivity analyses. The two year timeline includes regular virtual sessions and three meetings in person alongside hackathons and exchanges of trainees. A cross disciplinary collaboration is required to integrate specialized expertise in microbial ecology and algorithms of scalable metagenomics. The team will publish harmonized metadata and code alongside an interactive atlas of functional modules within stable repositories. The group consists of domain experts and trainees who will receive instruction in sequence analysis and open science.

abstract_original: Human-associated microbial communities generate metabolites, antigens, and extracellular molecules that can reorganize host cellular signaling, yet it remains unclear when these effects arise from individual microbial species versus emergent community-level functional modules. This working group will synthesize publicly available metagenomic, metabolomic, proteomic, and genetic datasets to test whether reproducible microbial gene modules across oral and gut ecosystems predict host circulating protein and metabolite states better than taxonomic profiles alone. The central hypothesis is that host molecular phenotypes associated with inflammation, cardiometabolic risk, and immune regulation are coupled to mesoscale microbial community structures: combinations of genes, strains, and biochemical pathways that emerge from microbial consortia and cannot be inferred from single taxa in isolation. We will integrate open shotgun metagenomes from modern oral and gut microbiome studies, public ancient dental calculus datasets that preserve historical oral community functions, paired host metabolomic and proteomic datasets from public repositories, and publicly released proteogenomic and disease-association summary statistics. A major innovation will be a contamination-aware synthesis framework that explicitly models low-biomass and ancient DNA artifacts, batch effects, reference database bias, and cross-study metadata heterogeneity before biological interpretation. Metagenomes will be reprocessed through a standardized protein-level annotation workflow using fast translated alignment, functional binning, strain-aware profiling, and phylogenetic network methods to identify recurrent microbial gene constellations. These modules will then be linked to host proteins and metabolites using multilevel models, network propagation, and genetic triangulation where public pQTL, mQTL, and disease GWAS summary statistics are available. Rather than asking whether a named microbe is associated with a disease, the project asks whether convergent microbial biochemical capacities produce emergent host molecular states across populations, body sites, and time. The project is well suited to NCEMS because it requires coordinated expertise that no single laboratory is likely to possess: scalable metagenomic algorithm development, ancient and low-biomass microbiome quality control, microbial ecology, plasma proteomics, metabolomics, epidemiology, and causal inference. NCEMS support would enable community standards for harmonizing microbiome multi-omics metadata, convene domain experts to evaluate contamination and provenance policies, and train graduate students and postdoctoral fellows in reproducible synthesis workflows spanning sequence analysis, molecular epidemiology, and open science. Deliverables will include an openly documented workflow, reusable contamination and metadata scoring tools, harmonized feature tables, interactive microbial gene-module networks, and a public atlas linking microbial functional emergence to host proteome and metabolome signatures. By combining modern and ancient microbiome data with human molecular phenotype resources, this project will clarify which microbial community functions are stable, recently altered, or disease-linked, and will provide a generalizable strategy for studying emergent molecular phenotypes generated by complex microbial consortia.

title: Predicting Emergent Mesoscale Organization in Bacteria from Public Multi-Omics, Sequence Features, and Cellular Phenotypes
title_norm: predicting emergent mesoscale organization in bacteria from public multiomics sequence features and cellular phenotypes
abstract_text: Bacterial mesoscale organization involves structures like condensates and microcompartments driven by multivalent molecular interactions, which coordinate essential functions and generate emergent cellular states crucial for biological adaptation. Because multi omics and imaging datasets are analyzed in isolation, researchers lack the ability to predict emergent bacterial phenotypes from combined expression and sequence encoded biophysical interaction properties. This project will construct a cross species computational framework to identify latent bacterial organization regimes and link them to phenotypic outcomes, utilizing graph neural networks and multi view learning to synthesize existing sequence derived biophysical features. RNA seq, proteomics, metabolomics, and imaging data from repositories including Gene Expression Omnibus will be integrated by harmonizing cross species annotations via ortholog mapping and transforming inputs into comparable quantitative feature spaces. This framework will establish general predictive principles across species, enabling critical downstream predictions of antibiotic tolerance, virulence activation, engineered circuit stability, plasmid persistence, and evolutionary adaptation.
full_text: This research explores bacterial mesoscale organization and the inability to predict cellular states from isolated datasets of molecular interactions. Bacteria coordinate functions through structures like condensates but extensive datasets remain fragmented without integrating features of biophysical interactions. A cross species framework will identify latent regimes to predict outcomes like tolerance to antibiotics and virulence activation. The synthesis of public data uses computational approaches to infer latent organizational states without generating new experimental data. Methods of analysis include matrix factorization and graph neural networks along with hierarchical Bayesian models and multi view learning. The team will evaluate models through cross validation across studies by utilizing negative controls and propagation of uncertainty. Datasets will incorporate RNA-seq and proteomics and imaging records from repositories like the Sequence Read Archive and Gene Expression Omnibus. Integration of datasets will involve harmonizing cross species annotations via ortholog mapping and converting records into comparable feature spaces. Researchers will mitigate limitations like batch effects and biases of missing data by utilizing hierarchical models and negative controls. Milestones include an initial pilot compendium for Escherichia coli and subsequent expansion to additional taxa to deploy synthesis maps. The broad scope requires a cross disciplinary collaboration to combine expertise in statistical biophysics and machine learning and synthetic biology. Researchers will release code and derived datasets in version controlled repositories alongside interactive maps and persistent identifiers on Zenodo. The team includes data scientists and graduate students who will receive cross disciplinary mentorship through sprints and hackathons.

abstract_original:
Bacteria exhibit coordinated physiological states that cannot be understood from single genes alone: stress bodies assemble, nucleoids compact, secretion and virulence programs switch on, plasmids alter host resource allocation, and quorum-sensing networks synchronize population behavior. Many of these transitions likely depend on mesoscale organization—multivalent protein, RNA, DNA, and metabolite interactions that create spatially and dynamically distinct cellular environments. Yet bacterial transcriptomic, proteomic, metabolomic, genome-variation, and imaging datasets are usually analyzed separately, leaving a central question unresolved: can emergent bacterial cell states be predicted from the combined expression and sequence-encoded interaction properties of their molecular components?

This working group will synthesize existing public data to build a cross-species computational framework for identifying bacterial mesoscale organization states and linking them to phenotypic outcomes such as antibiotic tolerance, virulence, host association, plasmid maintenance, and evolutionary adaptation. We will integrate publicly available RNA-seq, proteomics, metabolomics, Tn-seq/fitness profiling, genome variation, plasmid annotations, and cell-imaging datasets from model bacteria and clinically or ecologically important systems, including Escherichia coli, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Bacillus subtilis, Vibrio species, and insect-associated symbionts where sufficient public data exist. These data will be harmonized with protein sequence features relevant to mesoscale assembly, including intrinsic disorder, charge patterning, low-complexity regions, oligomerization domains, nucleic-acid-binding capacity, predicted interaction networks, and known bacterial compartment or condensate-associated proteins.

The project will ask whether bacterial conditions cluster into reproducible “mesoscale organization regimes” that cut across species and perturbations. For example, do antibiotic stress, efflux-pump disruption, quorum-sensing activation, phage or plasmid carriage, nutrient limitation, and host-associated growth produce common signatures of nucleoid remodeling, RNA-protein granule formation, metabolic compartment use, or envelope-associated assembly? We will develop machine-learning and statistical-physics-inspired models that combine gene-expression modules with sequence-encoded interaction propensities to infer latent organizational states. These states will then be tested computationally for their ability to explain higher-level outcomes: growth-rate tradeoffs, evolutionary repeatability, virulence-factor expression, horizontal gene transfer compatibility, and persistence under stress.

NCEMS support is essential because the project requires coordinated expertise across bacterial evolution, synthetic and plasmid biology, host-microbe systems, biophysics of multivalent assembly, machine learning, omics harmonization, and open-science infrastructure. No new experimental data will be generated. Instead, the working group will create interoperable public resources: a curated bacterial multi-omics compendium, a catalog of predicted mesoscale-organizing proteins and RNAs, reusable workflows for cross-study normalization and uncertainty tracking, and interactive maps linking molecular features to emergent cell-state phenotypes. Trainees will participate in data curation sprints, model-building workshops, and reproducible workflow development.

By connecting bacterial physiology and evolution to principles of mesoscale molecular organization, this project will provide a new synthesis framework for understanding how collective cellular properties emerge from molecular interactions. The resulting resource will help researchers predict when genetic or environmental perturbations are likely to rewire bacterial organization, alter pathogenic potential, destabilize engineered circuits, or constrain evolutionary trajectories.

title: Predicting Emergent Proteostasis Network Rewiring from the Energetic Landscapes of Human Membrane Protein Variants
title_norm: predicting emergent proteostasis network rewiring from the energetic landscapes of human membrane protein variants
abstract_text: Within the domain of molecular and cellular biology, understanding the effects of energetic changes in human membrane protein variants on cellular proteostasis and signaling networks is essential to predict cellular network transitions. However, existing variant and structural data remain fragmented, leaving it unclear how atomic scale energetic perturbations in individual proteins translate into mesoscale cellular phenotypes and network behaviors. To determine if membrane protein variant energetics cross nonlinear thresholds altering cellular behaviors, this project will synthesize public datasets into a multilayer network graph utilizing thermodynamic modeling, structure aware variant prediction, and Bayesian change point analysis. Datasets including ClinVar, AlphaFold, and single cell atlases will be integrated by mapping variants to canonical sequences and structures to construct a multilayer network of physical, genetic, regulatory, and energetic relationships. Identifying these nonlinear thresholds will establish fundamental rules linking molecular variation to cellular phenotypes, which will map tissue specific vulnerabilities and guide future therapeutic hypotheses for membrane protein diseases.

A central unresolved problem in molecular and cellular biology is how small energetic changes in individual proteins propagate into mesoscale cellular outcomes such as altered trafficking, interactome rewiring, stress-response activation, and disease phenotypes. This working group will test the hypothesis that membrane protein variants produce emergent cellular behavior when their effects on folding, translocon insertion, and interaction energetics cross context-dependent thresholds that redirect proteins through the proteostasis and signaling networks. We will address this question entirely through synthesis of public data, integrating molecular biophysics, protein interaction networks, variant interpretation, and single-cell regulatory-state analysis.

The project will focus on human membrane proteins with unusually rich public data: CFTR, GPCRs, potassium and other ion channels, transporters, and disease-associated receptors. We will assemble a harmonized atlas linking ClinVar and gnomAD variants, deep mutational scanning and multiplexed expression datasets, public cell-surface trafficking and abundance measurements, AlphaFold and experimental structures, predicted stability and membrane-insertion energetics, BioPlex/IntAct/STRING protein interaction networks, proteostasis-factor annotations, public drug-response and pharmacological chaperone datasets, and disease- or tissue-relevant single-cell RNA-seq atlases. This integrated resource will allow us to ask when molecular perturbations remain locally buffered and when they instead generate higher-order changes in cellular network state.

Analytically, we will construct a multilayer graph in which nodes represent variants, protein structural regions, proteostasis components, interaction partners, regulatory programs, and cellular phenotypes. Edges will encode physical contacts, predicted energetic coupling, genetic or clinical associations, co-expression, protein-protein interactions, and regulatory relationships inferred from public single-cell data. We will develop open workflows that combine structure-aware variant effect prediction, thermodynamic modeling, network propagation, community detection, and regulon activity inference. A key innovation will be to search explicitly for nonlinear thresholds: regions of sequence and structural space where gradual changes in predicted folding or interaction energy are associated with abrupt changes in trafficking efficiency, interactome connectivity, or activation of stress and inflammatory programs.

This synthesis will produce three major outcomes. First, it will identify general biophysical rules that explain why some variants primarily reduce protein abundance, others alter signaling or channel function without strong expression defects, and others unexpectedly increase surface delivery or network connectivity. Second, it will define tissue- and cell-type-specific vulnerability maps showing where the same molecular defect is predicted to have different consequences because proteostasis capacity, interaction partners, or regulatory circuits differ across cellular contexts. Third, it will nominate classes of variants most likely to be rescued by pharmacological chaperones or other proteostasis-modulating interventions based on energetic mechanism rather than gene identity alone.

The project requires NCEMS support because no single laboratory can integrate the necessary expertise across membrane protein biophysics, disease variant interpretation, large-scale interaction networks, single-cell regulatory analysis, and reproducible data engineering. The working group will include computational and experimental domain experts, trainees, and community contributors who will co-develop open standards for representing energetic variant effects in network models. All curated datasets, analysis pipelines, benchmark tasks, interactive visualizations, and training modules will be released publicly. By connecting atomic-scale energetic perturbations to emergent mesoscale network states, this project will provide a generalizable framework for understanding how molecular variation becomes cellular phenotype.

abstract_original: Biomolecular condensates arise from many weak, context-dependent interactions among proteins, RNAs, and metabolites, yet we still lack a predictive framework for how molecular binding features give rise to mesoscale condensate behaviors and downstream cellular outcomes. This working group will synthesize public datasets to test the hypothesis that distinct classes of cellular condensates are specified by a combinatorial RNA-protein grammar: RNA sequence and structure features tune the effective valency, spacing, and competition among RNA-binding proteins, thereby shaping condensate composition, material state, exchange kinetics, and trafficking connections across the cell. The project will not generate new data. Instead, it will integrate existing eCLIP and related RNA-binding maps, stress granule and nuclear body proteomes, public proximity-labeling datasets, high-content imaging screens, RNA structure probing data, disorder and low-complexity annotations, AlphaFold and experimental structural models, public condensate databases, and transcriptome-wide localization and abundance measurements. The central scientific question is whether mesoscale condensate identity can be predicted more accurately from an integrated RNA-protein interaction network than from protein sequence features or RNA abundance alone. We will build a harmonized atlas connecting RNAs, RNA-binding proteins, condensate-associated factors, subcellular compartments, and perturbation contexts. Computational structural biology will be used to annotate interaction modules, including folded RNA-binding domains, intrinsically disordered regions, short linear motifs, predicted RNA secondary structure, base-composition patterns, and multivalent binding architectures. Network science and machine learning will then identify recurring molecular motifs that distinguish condensates with different behaviors, such as rapid exchange versus persistent retention, nuclear versus cytoplasmic localization, stress-inducible versus constitutive assembly, and trafficking-linked versus compartment-restricted composition. A key innovation is to treat RNAs not simply as clients or scaffolds, but as programmable multivalent polymers whose structural ensemble and binding-site organization can remodel protein interaction networks. The working group will compare candidate grammars across public datasets from human cells, yeast, plants, and disease-relevant perturbations to determine which principles are conserved and which are lineage- or context-specific. We will also evaluate whether disease-associated mutations and repeat expansions alter predicted RNA-protein network topology in ways that favor aberrant mesoscale assemblies. NCEMS support is essential because the project requires coordinated expertise in RNA structure, condensate biophysics, proteomics, imaging, network inference, machine learning, and open data engineering, and because the relevant datasets are fragmented across communities that rarely use common standards. Deliverables will include a public, versioned RNA-protein-condensate knowledge graph; reproducible workflows for dataset harmonization and feature extraction; benchmark tasks for predicting condensate association and dynamic class; and interpretable models that nominate molecular design principles for condensate regulation. Trainees will participate in cross-lab code sprints, data annotation jamborees, and collaborative model-evaluation workshops, gaining experience in reproducible synthesis science. By linking molecular-scale binding determinants to mesoscale condensate properties and cellular routing, this project will provide a general framework for understanding how new cellular behaviors emerge from distributed RNA-protein interaction networks.

title: A Cross-Kingdom Atlas of Sequence-to-Mesoscale Rules for Stress-Responsive Biomolecular Condensates
title_norm: a crosskingdom atlas of sequencetomesoscale rules for stressresponsive biomolecular condensates
abstract_text: The molecular and cellular biology field investigates how environmental stress triggers the reorganization of intrinsically disordered proteins and RNA into stress responsive biomolecular condensates and mesoscale assemblies across diverse organisms. Disconnected datasets and inconsistent terminology currently preclude a quantitative framework to predict how sequence encoded disorder and cellular context dictate the formation of specific mesoscale structures. To determine which combinations of molecular sequence grammar and cellular environment predict condensate spatial organization and material state, this synthesis only project will apply physics informed machine learning models, percolation theory, and automated image analysis. The project will integrate proteome wide disorder annotations, structural databases, and microscopy image repositories by constructing a standardized data model that links computed molecular descriptors with curated cellular mesoscale observables. This research will yield predictive models that establish general principles for how molecular disorder encodes stress adaptation, thereby improving the fundamental understanding of cellular organization and neurodegenerative disease mechanisms.
full_text: The domain of molecular biology lacks a quantitative framework to predict how sequence encoded disorder governs stress responsive condensates. Stress triggers the reorganization of disordered proteins into mesoscale assemblies but existing public data on this process remains disconnected. The primary objective identifies sequence and environmental features predicting condensate states to uncover general principles of cellular stress adaptation. This synthesis project integrates existing public data to analyze relationships between sequence properties and mesoscale behaviors without new experiments. The team will apply physics informed machine learning models alongside associative polymer percolation theory and automated extraction of image features. Results will undergo validation using transparent train test splits alongside the retrospective prediction of transitions induced by cellular stress. The proposed study utilizes AlphaFold annotations alongside in vitro phase diagrams and resources for the binding of ribonucleic acid (RNA). Disparate resources will be integrated into a standardized controlled vocabulary to link molecular descriptors with features from cellular microscopy. Heterogeneous measurements and inconsistent terminology will be mitigated by establishing shared vocabularies and reporting the uncertainty of data explicitly. Milestones include the release of predictive models and community guidelines achieved through data curation sprints and multiple in person meetings. The ambitious scope requires cross disciplinary collaboration spanning simulation of molecules and evolutionary genomics beyond a single laboratory. Data and code will be shared on GitHub while findings will be disseminated via open access publications and preprints. The team comprises diverse computational scientists and trainees who will receive specific training in reproducible coding and statistical validation.

abstract_original: Cells often respond to environmental change by reorganizing disordered proteins, RNA, and multivalent interaction networks into mesoscale assemblies whose properties cannot be inferred from any single molecule alone. Yet the field lacks a unified, quantitative framework for predicting when sequence-encoded disorder produces adaptive condensates, maladaptive aggregates, or spatially organized non-phase-separated assemblies across cellular contexts. This working group will synthesize publicly available molecular, cellular, and biophysical datasets to define generalizable rules connecting intrinsically disordered protein sequence features, RNA context, cellular environment, and emergent condensate properties during stress adaptation. The central question is: which combinations of sequence grammar, interaction valence, charge patterning, expression state, and client composition predict the mesoscale material state, spatial organization, and functional reversibility of stress-responsive condensates across bacteria, plants, yeast, and animals? The project will integrate existing data from condensate and phase-separation databases, proteome-wide disorder annotations, public mutational and saturation-concentration datasets, in vitro phase diagrams, protein-RNA interaction resources, stress-induced transcriptomic and proteomic datasets, AlphaFold-derived structural annotations, public microscopy image repositories, and cryo-electron tomography or volume electron microscopy datasets where available. We will build an open, harmonized data model that links molecular descriptors—stickers, spacers, aromatic and cationic motifs, charge patterning, predicted compaction, folded-domain valence, RNA-binding potential, and post-translational modification sites—to mesoscale observables such as condensate number, size distribution, coarsening behavior, localization, client enrichment, reversibility, and inferred material state. A major analytical innovation will be the development of physics-informed machine learning models that combine associative-polymer concepts, coarse-grained interaction potentials, image-derived condensate phenotypes, and cellular abundance estimates. Rather than treating condensate formation as a binary annotation, the models will infer context-dependent phase behavior and emergent mesoscale regimes: dispersed networks, dynamic droplets, arrested emulsions, gels, fibrillar condensates, and spatially patterned assemblies. Comparative analyses across taxa and stress conditions will test whether evolution repeatedly uses similar disorder-encoded design principles for adaptation, or whether distinct cellular milieus impose different solutions. This synthesis is beyond the scope of a single laboratory because it requires expertise in disordered protein biophysics, molecular simulation, soft matter theory, image analysis, bacterial and eukaryotic cell organization, evolutionary genomics, and FAIR data engineering. NCEMS support would enable a community working group to establish shared vocabularies, benchmark datasets, reproducible workflows, and uncertainty standards for condensate-related data, addressing a current bottleneck in the field: heterogeneous measurements that are difficult to compare or reuse. The anticipated outcomes are an open cross-kingdom atlas of stress-responsive disordered proteins and condensates, validated predictive models for sequence-to-mesoscale behavior, and a set of community guidelines for integrating condensate imaging, biophysical, and omics data. Trainees will participate through collaborative hackathons and model-building sprints focused on reproducible data curation, physics-aware machine learning, and open software development. By synthesizing existing data rather than generating new experiments, this project will reveal how molecular disorder gives rise to adaptive mesoscale organization and will provide a reusable framework for predicting emergent cellular responses from protein sequence and context.

title: Mapping Emergent Drug-Tolerant Cell States from Extrachromosomal DNA and 3D Regulatory Architecture in Cancer Cell Lines
title_norm: mapping emergent drugtolerant cell states from extrachromosomal dna and 3d regulatory architecture in cancer cell lines
abstract_text: Cancer systems biology investigates mesoscale regulatory assemblies, which critically influence transcriptional heterogeneity and drug tolerance by interacting with structural elements like extrachromosomal DNA and rewired 3D chromatin. Current models based on isolated molecular features cannot explain variable transcriptional states, reversible drug tolerance, and adaptive pathway switching in genetically similar cancer cells. To determine how genomic elements assemble into mesoscale structures driving drug responses, this project will synthesize multiomics data into multilayer biological graphs and apply graph neural networks and ensemble machine learning to predict single cell states. Datasets from DepMap, ENCODE, TCGA, and single cell sequencing resources will be harmonized to a common genomic reference and integrated within multimodal biological graphs connecting genes, enhancers, and drugs via physical and regulatory relationships. The resulting multimodal framework will shift cancer drug response prediction from individual biomarkers to evaluating emergent biological properties of mesoscale regulatory structures.
full_text: Cancer systems biology investigates mesoscale regulatory assemblies because isolated molecular features cannot explain variable drug tolerance in cancer cell lines. Current models predict therapy response using individual mutations but interactions with extrachromosomal DNA and rewired chromatin remain incompletely understood. The primary objective determines how mesoscale regulatory structures form to shift the prediction of therapy response toward a multimodal framework. The overall study design filters public data to construct a multilayer biological graph and predict drug sensitivity using machine learning. The project applies graph neural networks and regularized generalized linear models alongside matrix factorization to execute positive unlabeled learning. The team will validate results through comparisons of baseline models and ablation of data layers alongside evaluation of tumor datasets. The proposed study utilizes databases like ENCODE and DepMap alongside public single cell RNA-seq and measurements derived from microscopy. The team will integrate these diverse datasets as interacting layers within a multimodal biological graph after harmonization to a reference. The project will mitigate incomplete labels using positive unlabeled learning and manage batch effects through targeted sensitivity analyses. The project milestones involve defining a data inventory before constructing the biological graph and testing behaviors with single cell data. This cross disciplinary collaboration is necessary because the integration of multiple data modalities exceeds the resources of any single laboratory. The team will release derived datasets and containerized workflows alongside openly published manuscripts and tutorials in public repositories. Experts in machine learning and systems biology will train graduate students and postdoctoral researchers through collaborative data sprints.

abstract_original:
Cancer cell lines with rich public multi-omics profiles provide an unusual opportunity to ask how molecular parts combine into mesoscale structures that generate emergent phenotypes such as transcriptional heterogeneity, pathway plasticity, and drug tolerance. This working group will synthesize existing public data to test the hypothesis that drug response is shaped not only by individual mutations or gene expression programs, but by emergent regulatory assemblies formed through interactions among copy-number amplification, extrachromosomal DNA, enhancer rewiring, 3D chromatin contacts, and protein-coding variant effects. These assemblies can create variable oncogene dosage, altered enhancer accessibility, and heterogeneous single-cell states that are not predictable from any one data modality alone.

The project will integrate publicly available datasets across molecular and cellular scales, including DepMap/CCLE genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, metabolomic, CRISPR-dependency, and drug-sensitivity profiles; public single-cell RNA-seq and Perturb-seq datasets from cancer cell lines; ENCODE, 4DN, and related chromatin accessibility, transcription factor occupancy, enhancer, Hi-C, Micro-C, and promoter-capture resources; TCGA and PCAWG-derived structural variation and amplification calls; public ecDNA and focal amplification annotations from resources such as AmpliconArchitect-based analyses; and available microscopy or image-derived ecDNA measurements where public. The synthesis will focus on well-profiled breast, melanoma, glioblastoma, colorectal, and lung cancer lineages where multi-omics, drug response, and genome-architecture data overlap sufficiently for cross-lineage comparison.

We will develop a multimodal graph-learning framework in which genes, enhancers, variants, regulatory motifs, chromatin contacts, amplified segments, proteins, pathways, metabolites, drugs, and single-cell states are represented as interacting layers. The model will combine supervised, semi-supervised, and positive-unlabeled learning to handle incomplete labels for ecDNA and drug-tolerant phenotypes. It will infer enhancer-gene and amplification-gene relationships, identify 3D regulatory neighborhoods associated with heterogeneous expression, and predict which mesoscale features best explain sensitivity, resistance, or adaptive plasticity across drug classes. Protein-structure and sequence-function annotations will be incorporated for coding variants in amplified or dependency-associated genes, allowing the group to distinguish regulatory dosage effects from altered protein function. Single-cell data will be used to quantify whether predicted mesoscale regulatory assemblies correspond to emergent subpopulations rather than bulk-average expression shifts.

The central scientific products will be: an open atlas of inferred cancer-cell-line mesoscale regulatory assemblies; interpretable models linking these assemblies to drug response and genetic dependency; benchmark datasets for multimodal prediction of emergent cellular phenotypes; and reusable workflows for integrating single-cell, 3D genome, cancer genomics, proteomics, and pharmacogenomic data. The project requires NCEMS support because it spans data types, algorithms, and biological expertise that exceed the scope of a single laboratory: cancer systems biology, 3D genome organization, machine learning, single-cell genomics, protein variant interpretation, and open-science software engineering. Trainees will participate through cross-institutional data-analysis sprints, reproducibility reviews, and open tutorials on multimodal biological graph modeling. By synthesizing existing data rather than generating new experiments, the working group will reveal how mesoscale genome organization and molecular variation combine to produce emergent cancer cell behaviors relevant to therapeutic response.

title: A Public Multimodal Atlas for Predicting Cytoskeletal Control of Cellular Architecture and Ciliary State
title_norm: a public multimodal atlas for predicting cytoskeletal control of cellular architecture and ciliary state
abstract_text: Although individual cytoskeletal components are well studied in molecular and cellular biosciences, understanding how mesoscale cytoskeletal organization generates emergent cell scale architectural outcomes like organelle positioning remains a critical priority. It is currently not understood how localized cytoskeletal interactions collectively predict whole cell architecture, a knowledge gap severely compounded by fragmented biological imaging data across different organisms and modalities. This research will determine whether mesoscale cytoskeletal organization predicts ciliary state and cellular architecture by applying transfer learning image segmentation, graph embeddings, and optimal transport distances to synthesize public imaging datasets and biophysical simulations. The project will integrate fluorescence, electron microscopy, and soft X ray tomography datasets from repositories including the BioImage Archive by extracting standardized geometric features and applying optimal transport methods across modalities. This cross modal framework will test universal quantitative rules linking molecular scale cytoskeletal regulation to emergent cellular morphology, providing a novel resource to synthesize previously isolated biological data.
full_text: Research in molecular and cellular biosciences struggles to explain how localized interactions of the cytoskeleton generate emergent architecture of cells. Individual molecular components of the cytoskeleton are known but their mesoscale interactions cannot yet predict states of whole cells. The proposed study uses a framework across modalities to determine if mesoscale organization of the cytoskeleton predicts architecture of cells. This project for data synthesis curates public datasets and compares empirical features against biophysical simulations without new experiments. The analytical approach applies transfer learning for the segmentation of images alongside embeddings of graphs for comparisons across modalities. Results will be validated using benchmark subsets and mapping of uncertainty alongside cross validation stratified by target organism. The project utilizes public datasets of electron microscopy and imaging of fluorescence from repositories including the Image Data Resource (IDR). These distinct datasets will be integrated by extracting standardized geometric features and applying methods of optimal transport across modalities. The team will mitigate artifacts from varying resolutions of images by computing geometric features at multiple explicit levels of confidence. The proposed timeline encompasses five functional phases spanning initial workshops for scoping through final integration of data and manuscripts. Harmonizing these disparate datasets requires a cross disciplinary collaboration uniting cell biologists with applied mathematicians and computational modelers. The team will release an analysis ready atlas and share containerized code for analysis via public version controlled repositories. The cross disciplinary team includes postdoctoral researchers and graduate students receiving structured mentorship in reproducible curation of open data.
