abstract_original:
A central unresolved problem in molecular and cellular biosciences is how local cytoskeletal interactions generate cell-scale architectural outcomes such as organelle positioning, polarized surface domains, and the presence, length, or loss of cilia and flagella. These outcomes are emergent: they cannot be inferred from any single filament, motor, or organelle, but arise from mesoscale organization across actin, microtubules, septins, centrioles, membranes, and transport pathways. We propose a community-scale synthesis project that will integrate publicly available whole-cell imaging, ciliary and flagellar imaging, cytoskeletal perturbation datasets, and biophysical simulation outputs to determine whether shared quantitative rules link cytoskeletal organization to cellular architecture across organisms and imaging modalities.

The working group will build an open, analysis-ready atlas from public repositories including the BioImage Archive, Image Data Resource, EMPIAR, Cell Image Library, Allen Cell Collection, and published soft X-ray tomography, fluorescence, electron microscopy, and live-cell imaging datasets. We will include mammalian cells with primary cilia or centrosome-associated cytoskeletal structures, Chlamydomonas and related flagellated systems, and non-ciliated model systems such as yeast or dividing animal cells where cytoskeletal networks produce well-defined cellular-scale structures. Rather than treating these systems as separate case studies, we will represent them through common mesoscale features: filament-network anisotropy, cortical versus internal organization, organelle volumes and curvatures, basal body or centrosome position, membrane protrusion geometry, and time-dependent structural transitions.

The project will develop interoperable workflows for segmentation transfer, morphometric feature extraction, and cross-modal comparison. Deep learning models trained on curated volumetric datasets will be adapted to less annotated public images using transfer learning and human-in-the-loop validation. Extracted cellular and subcellular geometries will be represented as meshes, graphs, and time series. We will use optimal-transport-based methods to compare shapes and dynamics across different dimensionalities, sampling rates, and imaging modalities, enabling principled integration of static 3D cellular anatomy with live cytoskeletal dynamics. Agent-based and continuum simulations of actin, microtubule, and motor-driven organization will be incorporated as synthetic reference data, allowing us to ask which physical mechanisms reproduce observed regions of cellular morphospace.

The primary scientific question is whether ciliary state and broader cellular architecture can be predicted from mesoscale cytoskeletal organization. Specifically, we will test whether cells occupy a small number of recurrent architectural regimes defined by cytoskeletal geometry, organelle packing, and centrosome or basal body context; whether transitions among these regimes correspond to events such as ciliogenesis, ciliary shortening, deciliation, cytokinetic ring formation, or large-scale organelle remodeling; and whether perturbations of motors, severing proteins, or cytoskeletal regulators move cells through this shared morphodynamic landscape in predictable ways.

This project requires NCEMS support because no single laboratory can curate, harmonize, and analyze the breadth of public imaging and simulation resources needed to compare mesoscale organization across cell types, organisms, and modalities. The working group will bring together cell biologists, computational modelers, imaging scientists, data curators, applied mathematicians, and trainees. All curated metadata, segmentation workflows, morphometric features, simulation interfaces, and analysis notebooks will be released openly. The outcome will be both a reusable public resource for cell anatomy synthesis and a mechanistic framework for explaining how cytoskeletal organization gives rise to emergent cellular structures.

title: Emergent Regulatory Neighborhoods from Transposable-Element-Derived Transcription Factor Grammar Across Mammalian Cell States
title_norm: emergent regulatory neighborhoods from transposableelementderived transcription factor grammar across mammalian cell states
abstract_text: Within mammalian genomics, transposable elements distribute transcription factor binding sites across genomes to drive human and mouse hematopoietic and immune differentiation, although only a fraction are functionally active. This project will determine how sequence grammars, chromatin states, and spatial clustering form regulatory networks across human and mouse cell states by applying graph based community detection, gradient boosted trees, and domain adaptive neural networks. The study will integrate databases including ENCODE, Cistrome, and single cell atlases by constructing cell state specific graphs that link transposable elements and regulatory regions through shared chromatin states and contact frequency. This framework will establish transposable elements as distributed functional components rather than technical artifacts, providing novel methods to measure emergent mesoscale regulatory behavior across mammalian genomes.
full_text: The proposed study explores whether the regulation of transposable elements during hematopoietic differentiation requires mesoscale chromatin organization or isolated sequences. Transposable elements distribute transcription factor binding sites but current models of sequence affinity cannot predict integration across cell types. The project evaluates transposable elements as functional components by determining how spatial clustering and sequence grammars form regulatory networks. The team links annotations of transposable elements to genomics data and identifies regulatory neighborhoods to compare baseline sequence models. Key methods include the segmentation of epigenomes and the modeling of binding sites alongside domain adaptive neural networks. Results will be validated using statistical null models and permutation tests alongside comparisons against matched standard regulatory regions. The study utilizes databases such as RepeatMasker and Repbase alongside epigenomics repositories including ENCODE and the Human Cell Atlas. The team integrates these datasets by constructing graphs specific to cell states with edges representing genomic distance and shared chromatin. The researchers will mitigate alignment bias through explicit modeling and bypass constraints on data redistribution by providing scripts and checksums. The project timeline spans two years and features three in person synthesis meetings interspersed with regular virtual analysis sprints. Cross disciplinary collaboration is necessary because the integration of datasets requires combined expertise in machine learning alongside comparative genomics. The project will release a regulatory atlas and analysis code alongside documented computational notebooks through public repositories using persistent identifiers. Investigators and graduate students from diverse disciplines will collaborate to provide training in artificial intelligence and open science practices.

The study will integrate databases including ENCODE, Cistrome, and single cell atlases by constructing cell state specific graphs that link transposable elements and regulatory regions through shared chromatin states and contact frequency. This framework will establish transposable elements as distributed functional components rather than technical artifacts, providing novel methods to measure emergent mesoscale regulatory behavior across mammalian genomes.
abstract_original:
Transposable elements (TEs) have dispersed millions of potential transcription factor binding sites across mammalian genomes, yet only a minority become functional regulatory elements in any given cell type. A central unresolved question is whether TE-derived regulatory activity emerges primarily from individual insertions with favorable sequence features, or from collective mesoscale organization in which families of related repeats create dense, chromatin-compatible neighborhoods that recruit transcription factors, nucleosomes, cofactors, and 3D genome contacts in a coordinated manner. This working group will synthesize public epigenomic, genomic, and chromatin conformation data to test the hypothesis that TE families generate emergent regulatory properties when their sequence grammars, chromatin states, and spatial clustering cross cell-type-specific thresholds.

The project will integrate existing datasets from ENCODE, Roadmap Epigenomics, Cistrome, GEO/SRA, 4D Nucleome, FANTOM, and public single-cell atlases, focusing initially on human and mouse hematopoietic and immune differentiation because these systems provide unusually rich transcription factor ChIP-seq, chromatin accessibility, histone modification, transcriptomic, and 3D genome data. We will annotate TE insertions by family, age, conservation, genomic context, motif content, and orthology, then link them to matched chromatin accessibility, nuclease footprints, transcription factor occupancy, histone states, enhancer RNAs, promoter contacts, and nearby gene expression. Rather than treating repeats as nuisance sequence, the analysis will ask when groups of related insertions produce regulatory behavior that cannot be predicted by isolated motif matches alone.

The working group will develop a synthesis framework combining epigenome segmentation, high-resolution binding-site modeling, motif grammar analysis, graph-based chromatin neighborhood detection, and domain-adaptive neural networks that explicitly account for species-specific repeat landscapes. These models will separate three contributions to TE regulatory activity: intrinsic sequence affinity, local chromatin permissiveness, and mesoscale neighborhood effects such as enhancer clustering, contact frequency, and co-occupancy by cooperative transcription factors. Cross-species modeling will determine whether similar regulatory outcomes arise through shared ancestral insertions, lineage-specific TE expansions, or convergent sequence grammars embedded in distinct repeat families.

The expected outcome is an open atlas of TE-associated regulatory neighborhoods across cell states and species, along with predictive models that identify which repeat families are poised to seed new enhancers, insulators, or lineage-specific transcriptional programs. This synthesis will directly address emergence by defining how distributed molecular features—motifs, repeat copy number, chromatin accessibility, nucleosome positioning, and 3D proximity—combine to create higher-order regulatory properties at the mesoscale. The project requires NCEMS-scale coordination because no single lab can uniformly integrate the breadth of public datasets, repeat annotations, machine learning models, chromatin-state maps, and biological expertise needed to compare regulatory emergence across species and cell types. All workflows, harmonized metadata, model outputs, and training materials will be released openly through reproducible computational notebooks and containerized pipelines, with graduate students and postdoctoral researchers trained in collaborative genomic data synthesis, interpretable AI, and open-science practices.

title: A Residue-Resolved Public Data Atlas of Emergent Human Protein Assemblies
title_norm: a residueresolved public data atlas of emergent human protein assemblies
abstract_text: Molecular and cellular biology investigates how local residue level protein contacts form mesoscale assemblies, which is crucial for contextualizing three dimensional protein models and genetic variants within specific biological structures. This project will determine the principles governing higher order cellular assemblies by synthesizing fragmented crosslinking datasets into an integrated knowledge graph using containerized workflows, sequence reconciliation, structural distance filtering, and multilayer network clustering. ProteomeXchange, UniProt, AlphaFold, and Reactome datasets will be integrated into this queryable graph, linking crosslinking evidence with diverse metadata through nodes representing structural features and edges denoting spatial and pathway relationships. The research will produce reusable infrastructure and identify biological rules for protein assembly formation, significantly advancing the interpretation of molecular pathways across distinct genetic and tissue contexts.
full_text: This project in cellular biology investigates mesoscale protein assemblies because public resources lack necessary residue level spatial resolution. The proposed study investigates fundamental principles of assembly formation to uncover structural rules and provide reusable computational infrastructure. This secondary data synthesis project harmonizes public evidence to build an integrated knowledge graph for extensive structural analyses. The team will use containerized workflows for processing of spectra and clustering of networks to generate property graphs. Results will undergo validation by comparing recurrent assembly modules to random networks and benchmarking models against structural baselines. The project will utilize ProteomeXchange alongside distinct repositories for structural data and genetic variants including AlphaFold and ClinVar. Datasets will populate a queryable knowledge graph that links structural evidence with diverse biological metadata through specific nodes. The team will mitigate limitations of ambiguous mappings by retaining uncertain data and generating evidence with explicit error rates. The project executes five work packages that span from the assembly of datasets to the interpretation of biological data. This effort requires cross disciplinary collaboration because the integration of genetics and structural biology demands diverse analytical expertise. All generated datasets and computational code will receive persistent identifiers for deposition into public repositories under permissive reuse licenses. The team features established specialists and early career trainees who will receive extensive instruction in computational graph analysis.

abstract_original:
Mesoscale protein assemblies emerge when many weak, transient, or context-dependent molecular contacts combine to produce cellular functions that cannot be inferred from individual proteins alone. Yet most public interaction resources represent protein relationships as gene-level edges, losing the residue-level proximity information needed to connect molecular interfaces to cellular pathways, tissue specificity, and disease-associated perturbation. This working group will synthesize publicly available crosslinking mass spectrometry, conventional proteomics, structural, pathway, and human genetics datasets to ask: what general principles determine when local protein contacts become higher-order cellular assemblies, and how are these assemblies rewired across tissues, pathways, and disease-relevant sequence variation?

The project will integrate public crosslinking mass spectrometry datasets from ProteomeXchange-associated repositories with curated interaction resources, structural models, tissue proteome maps, Reactome pathway annotations, protein sequence metadata, post-translational modification resources, and human variant datasets. Rather than treating crosslinks only as evidence for isolated protein-protein interactions, we will reanalyze them as residue-level spatial constraints embedded in cellular context. Public raw and processed crosslinking datasets will be harmonized using transparent false discovery criteria, standardized spectrum identifiers, controlled vocabularies, and reproducible workflows. Crosslinks will be mapped to UniProt proteoforms, AlphaFold and experimentally determined structures, pathway reactions, tissue abundance profiles, and known genetic or post-translational modifications. The resulting synthesis will create an open, queryable knowledge graph linking spectra, residue pairs, proteins, complexes, pathways, tissues, and phenotypes.

This atlas will enable three analyses that are difficult for any single laboratory. First, we will identify recurrent mesoscale interaction modules supported by residue-level proximity across independent studies and determine whether they correspond to stable complexes, transient pathway intermediates, or condition-specific assemblies. Second, we will test whether tissue-specific protein abundance and pathway state explain which potential contacts are observed, distinguishing physical compatibility from biological availability. Third, we will map pathogenic, common, and post-translationally modified residues onto crosslink-supported interfaces to ask whether disease-associated perturbations preferentially target emergent assembly hubs rather than individual protein functions.

The project is well suited to NCEMS because it requires coordinated expertise in crosslinking mass spectrometry, proteomics informatics, molecular biophysics, pathway knowledge representation, network biology, structural modeling, and human genetics. It will use only existing public data but will generate new biological insight by integrating datasets that are currently fragmented across repositories, formats, and scales. The working group will also address methodological needs central to synthesis science: benchmarkable crosslink reanalysis, persistent links from conclusions to original spectra, uncertainty-aware interaction scoring, and interoperable data models for residue-resolved cellular networks.

All outputs will be released openly, including reanalysis workflows, standardized metadata templates, confidence-scored crosslink interaction tables, knowledge graph exports, tutorials, and interactive notebooks. Trainees will participate in cross-disciplinary data jamborees focused on reproducible proteomics reanalysis, network modeling, and biological interpretation. The long-term impact will be a community resource and analytical framework for understanding how molecular contacts collectively give rise to emergent cellular organization.

title: Emergent Microbial Chemical Phenotypes from Public Metagenomic, Proteomic, and Untargeted Mass Spectrometry Data
title_norm: emergent microbial chemical phenotypes from public metagenomic proteomic and untargeted mass spectrometry data
abstract_text: Within microbial biochemistry, the emergence of chemical phenotypes from mesoscale molecular structures represents a critical phenomenon, yet abundant mass spectrometry and genomic datasets remain isolated and analytical pipelines routinely discard unannotated biological signals. Current approaches lack essential data integration, analyzing metabolomics without genomic context and leaving researchers unable to explain how consistent microbial chemical phenotypes emerge across environments despite species variations. This research will identify which genetic modules and expressed proteins produce specific metabolite classes by developing a computational framework that applies mass spectrometry pattern querying, alignment free sequence embeddings, and hierarchical Bayesian models to public data. The study will utilize datasets from GNPS, MetaboLights, PRIDE, MGnify, and NCBI SRA, integrating them through standardized metadata, cross modal embeddings, and sample by feature matrices linking spectral motifs, genes, and proteins. This framework will shift the field toward modeling multi component community traits, establishing unannotated metabolites and hypothetical proteins as primary signals for understanding microbial biochemical functions.
full_text: The domain of microbial biochemistry requires data integration to explain how molecular structures produce consistent traits across diverse environments. Public repositories contain abundant datasets but researchers analyze them independently and routinely discard an enormous volume of unannotated signals. This research asks which genetic combinations produce specific metabolites by shifting focus toward modeling traits of complex microbial communities. The team will conduct a secondary analysis of public data to build an open computational framework for statistical modeling. The analytical approach utilizes molecular networking and alignment free embeddings of sequences alongside regularized regression and hierarchical Bayesian models. The team will validate results by comparing combinatorial models against models of single components using permutation tests and negative controls. The proposed study will analyze public datasets from repositories including MetaboLights and PRIDE alongside databases of isolate genomes. The researchers will integrate datasets by standardizing metadata to common vocabularies and creating embeddings across modalities to link diverse features. Researchers will mitigate limitations like batch effects and metadata sparsity by applying sensitivity analyses and validation stratified by environment. The proposed milestones include six sequential work packages spanning harmonization of datasets and extraction of features alongside statistical modeling. This project requires collaboration across disciplines to successfully integrate diverse data types between fields lacking shared analytical standards. The researchers will publish models and negative results under permissive licenses while maintaining portable workflows in public repositories. The research team unites experts and postdoctoral researchers to provide trainees with opportunities to lead specific modules of analysis.

abstract_original: Microbial cells and communities routinely produce chemical phenotypes that cannot be inferred from any single gene, genome, or organism in isolation. These phenotypes emerge from mesoscale organization: co-regulated gene neighborhoods, multi-enzyme pathway fragments, protein complexes, metabolite transformations, and ecological sharing of intermediates. Yet the public record contains the ingredients needed to study this emergence at scale: billions of tandem mass spectra from microbiome-associated metabolomics experiments, thousands of public metagenomes and isolate genomes, and growing proteomics repositories. This working group will synthesize these data to ask a central question: which combinations of microbial genetic modules and expressed proteins reproducibly give rise to emergent metabolite classes across host-associated and environmental microbiomes? We will not generate new experimental data. Instead, we will integrate public datasets from GNPS/MassIVE, MetaboLights, PRIDE, MGnify, IMG/M, NCBI SRA, and public isolate genome resources, prioritizing studies with shared samples, related environments, or compatible metadata. The project will develop an open computational framework that links three layers: (1) spectral evidence for metabolite families and diagnostic chemical substructures from untargeted MS/MS, including reusable query patterns for known and unknown molecular motifs; (2) microbial functional potential from metagenomes and isolate genomes, including gene-neighborhood, operon-like, and pathway-fragment organization rather than only single-gene annotations; and (3) protein-level evidence from public metaproteomics and proteomics datasets where available. The synthesis will combine mass spectrometry pattern querying, molecular networking, alignment-free sequence embeddings, gene-block evolutionary reconstruction, and multilevel statistical models that explicitly test for emergence: metabolite features whose occurrence is better predicted by combinations of genes, taxa, or gene neighborhoods than by any component alone. A key innovation is to treat unknown genes and unknown metabolites as first-class signals. Instead of discarding unannotated spectra or hypothetical proteins, we will create cross-modal embeddings that identify recurring associations between spectral motifs and microbial sequence modules across independent studies. We will then evaluate whether these associations are conserved across environments, enriched in particular microbial lineages, or repeatedly assembled through different taxonomic routes. This will distinguish lineage-specific chemistry from convergent community-level biochemical capacity. The expected outcomes are: a public atlas of microbial gene-module-to-metabolite associations; a ranked set of candidate emergent chemical phenotypes, including metabolite families associated with multi-organism or multi-module genetic configurations; reusable MassQL-style spectral queries and gene-neighborhood search workflows; and benchmark datasets for testing future AI methods in metabolomics-metagenomics integration. The working group requires NCEMS support because the problem spans multiple communities that rarely share standards: mass spectrometry informatics, microbial genomics, metaproteomics, evolutionary bioinformatics, statistics, and data stewardship. NCEMS will enable coordinated metadata harmonization, community curation of reusable feature definitions, collaborative software development, and trainee-led cross-training workshops. All workflows, derived feature tables, models, documentation, and negative results will be released openly. By synthesizing existing public data across molecular and cellular scales, this project will reveal how distributed microbial molecular components assemble into reproducible chemical properties of cells and communities.

title: A Public-Data Atlas of Collective Allosteric State Variables Linking Nuclear Receptor Ligands to Transcriptional Phenotypes
title_norm: a publicdata atlas of collective allosteric state variables linking nuclear receptor ligands to transcriptional phenotypes
abstract_text: Molecular and cellular biology investigates nuclear receptors, where capturing how ligand binding induces allosteric changes that propagate to transcriptional responses is critical because static structures only identify basic conformational changes. Researchers currently do not understand why ligands with similar binding affinities produce different transcriptional phenotypes, as fragmented data fail to explain how diverse ligands alter dynamic receptor ensembles. To identify low dimensional allosteric state variables linking ligand binding to transcriptional outcomes, this project will compute structure based descriptors and integrate functional genomics data to train constrained graph neural networks and hierarchical Bayesian models. Datasets from the Protein Data Bank, AlphaFold, ChEMBL, and Expression Atlas will be harmonized into a graph based knowledge base representing biological entities as nodes and physical binding associations as edges. This research will provide a generalizable framework to clarify fundamental mechanisms of emergent allostery and connect molecular conformational changes to cellular phenotypes for advancements in pharmacology and regulatory biology.
full_text: This project investigates why ligands with similar binding affinities produce different transcriptional phenotypes during allosteric regulation of nuclear receptors. Current static structures describe the contacts of ligands but fail to explain how dynamic ensembles govern tissue specific outcomes. The proposed study identifies conserved allosteric variables to clarify emergent mechanisms and connect molecular changes with cellular phenotypes in pharmacology. Researchers will synthesize public data into a knowledge base to train predictive models for machine learning using structural and genomics information. The analytical approach applies structural alignment and normal mode analysis alongside graph neural networks and hierarchical Bayesian models. The team will validate results by predicting the efficacy of held out ligands and comparing performance against baseline models without data leakage. Datasets include structural resources (Protein Data Bank and AlphaFold) and chemical databases alongside genomics archives (ENCODE and Expression Atlas). Researchers will integrate these diverse datasets into a knowledge base linking biological entities (receptors and ligands) through their documented interactions. The team will mitigate the heterogeneity of data and incomplete structures by deploying uncertainty aware models to report inconclusive results. The timeline spans ontology finalization and benchmark design with progress monitored through monthly virtual sessions and twice yearly in person meetings. This expansive scope demands cross disciplinary collaboration to harmonize diverse datasets across the fields of structural biology and machine learning. The team will distribute all findings and open source computational pipelines through public repositories alongside preprints and open access publications. The cross disciplinary team unites software engineers and domain experts to train early career researchers in the synthesis of public data.

abstract_original:
Nuclear receptors provide a powerful system for understanding emergence in molecular and cellular biology: binding of chemically diverse ligands to a buried pocket produces collective conformational shifts, altered coregulator recruitment, chromatin engagement, and cell-type-specific transcriptional outcomes. Yet a long-standing puzzle remains unresolved: why do ligands with similar affinity for the same receptor often produce distinct efficacy, selectivity, and disease-relevant phenotypes? We propose a community-scale synthesis project to identify the collective allosteric state variables that connect residue-level perturbations in nuclear receptor ligand-binding domains to mesoscale receptor-coregulator-DNA assemblies and downstream transcriptional responses.

This project will use only existing public data. We will integrate structural data from the Protein Data Bank, AlphaFold models, NMR and cryo-EM-derived conformational information, public molecular dynamics trajectories where available, ligand chemistry and activity data from ChEMBL, PubChem, BindingDB, and IUPHAR, protein sequence and evolutionary data from UniProt, OrthoDB, and public phylogenomic resources, coregulator interaction data from BioGRID and IntAct, and cell-level functional data from GEO, SRA, ENCODE, ChIP-Atlas, and Expression Atlas. The resulting resource, NR-AlloState, will harmonize ligands, receptor isoforms, orthologs, mutations, post-translational modifications, coregulator motifs, DNA response elements, chromatin context, and transcriptomic outcomes into a reproducible graph-based knowledge base.

The central hypothesis is that ligand-specific transcriptional phenotypes emerge from low-dimensional, evolutionarily constrained patterns of dynamic coupling rather than from individual contacts alone. We will test this by deriving structure-based flexibility and coupling descriptors from public structures and models, comparing apo, ligand-bound, DNA-bound, and coregulator-bound states across the nuclear receptor superfamily. These descriptors will be integrated with ligand chemical features, mutational effects, disease variants, and transcriptional signatures using uncertainty-aware machine learning and interpretable latent-variable models. The models will be evaluated by their ability to predict held-out ligand efficacy classes, receptor subtype selectivity, coregulator recruitment profiles, and transcriptomic responses across cell types.

The synthesis will address three fundamental questions. First, are there conserved dynamic architectures that explain how nuclear receptors convert ligand binding into regulatory output despite sequence divergence? Second, which residues or residue networks act as evolutionary tuners of ligand sensitivity, partial agonism, or antagonism? Third, when do molecular allosteric changes scale up into predictable cellular transcriptional programs, and when are they overridden by chromatin or coregulator context? By combining evolutionary analysis, protein dynamics, chemical informatics, and functional genomics, the working group will reveal when mesoscale regulatory behavior is encoded in the receptor itself and when it emerges from receptor partnerships in the nucleus.

NCEMS support is essential because the required synthesis spans structural biology, molecular simulation, nuclear receptor pharmacology, evolutionary biophysics, machine learning, and genomics, and depends on harmonizing fragmented datasets that no single laboratory could curate or analyze comprehensively. All curated datasets, code, model outputs, uncertainty estimates, and tutorials will be released openly. Trainees will participate in cross-disciplinary data jamborees and reproducible workflow development, producing both a scientific atlas of nuclear receptor allostery and a generalizable framework for linking molecular conformational ensembles to emergent cellular regulation.

title: From Entangled Proteins to Entangled Genomes: A Synthesis Framework Linking Molecular Topology of Chromatin Regulators to Emergent 3D Genome Organization
title_norm: from entangled proteins to entangled genomes a synthesis framework linking molecular topology of chromatin regulators to emergent 3d genome organization
abstract_text: Within molecular and cellular biology, three dimensional genome organization involves structures regulated by proteins, making the study of how protein physical topology affects mesoscale chromatin architecture critically important for the field. Current models represent chromatin binding proteins as generic binders or loop extruders, leaving the relationship between specific structural topologies and emergent chromosome physical behavior not systematically understood. To determine whether protein topological features provide predictive information about emergent genome organization, this computational synthesis project will apply structural bioinformatics algorithms, machine learning, and polymer physics simulations to test topology aware models. This project will integrate structural databases including the Protein Data Bank and AlphaFold with genomic datasets from ENCODE and GEO, utilizing standardized genome builds, lifted coordinates, and replicate aware normalization matched by metadata. This research will introduce molecular topology as a quantifiable mechanistic variable for genome architecture, linking structural bioinformatics with polymer physics to establish new physical constraints in genomic modeling.
full_text: Current models in cellular biology ignore how physical shapes of chromatin associated proteins constrain three dimensional genome architecture. Scientists know that specific proteins regulate chromosome structures but lack knowledge linking protein topologies to emergent physical behaviors. The team asks whether molecular topology predicts genome organization by bridging structural bioinformatics and the physics of polymers. The computational synthesis project builds a topological atlas of chromatin regulators to test predictive models against standard baselines. Key methods feature algorithms for structural bioinformatics alongside machine learning and simulations based on principles of polymer physics. The researchers will validate models using held out chromosomes and species while benchmarking performance against likelihoods of contact maps. The proposed study uses structural databases like UniProt and AlphaFold alongside genomic datasets from repositories such as ENCODE. The researchers will integrate structural annotations with genomic data by applying standard genomes and normalization techniques designed for experimental replicates. The scientific team will mitigate uncertainties for predicted structures and variable resolution in chromatin by applying explicit confidence scores. The timeline involves biannual meetings and virtual sprints to ensure the successful creation of a public topology atlas. This broad scope requires cross disciplinary collaboration because bridging structural bioinformatics with polymer physics exceeds capabilities of single laboratories. The research team will release all code for analysis under open source licenses while publishing datasets for benchmarking on Zenodo. Diverse personnel including data scientists and graduate students will complete training modules covering structural bioinformatics and modeling of polymers.

abstract_original:
A central unresolved question in molecular and cellular biology is how molecular-scale constraints imposed by chromatin-associated proteins give rise to mesoscale nuclear properties such as chromatin loops, domains, compartments, and chromosome mechanics. Many proteins that act on DNA and chromatin are not simple globular binders: they form rings, clamps, bridged circuits, coiled-coil assemblies, topological traps, or deep entanglements that can constrain polymer motion. Yet current models of 3D genome organization typically represent these proteins as generic binders or loop extruders, without incorporating their structural topology. This Working Group will synthesize public structural, genomic, and biophysical data to ask: do the topological features of chromatin-regulating proteins predict where, when, and how stable mesoscale genome structures emerge?

We will build an open, cross-scale atlas connecting protein topology to chromatin architecture. First, we will annotate the molecular topology of chromatin regulators across eukaryotes and bacteria using existing structures from the Protein Data Bank, AlphaFold Database, model organism proteomes, UniProt, ComplexPortal, and curated chromatin-factor databases. The atlas will classify knots, slipknots, lassos, theta-like circuits, ring-forming assemblies, disulfide- or metal-stabilized closures, coiled-coil bridges, and confidence-scored predicted entanglements. Second, we will integrate these annotations with public Hi-C, Micro-C, ChIA-PET, SPRITE, DamID, ChIP-seq, CUT&RUN, single-cell chromatin conformation, DNA-tracing, and perturbation datasets for cohesin, condensin, CTCF, topoisomerases, histone chaperones, remodeling complexes, and bacterial SMC systems. Third, we will use polymer-physics and maximum-entropy modeling to test whether incorporating molecular-topology-informed constraints improves prediction of emergent chromatin features, including loop lifetime proxies, domain boundary strength, compartmental segregation, mitotic compaction, and inferred mechanical response.

The project’s central synthesis product will be a reusable computational framework that treats chromatin regulators not only by sequence identity or binding location, but by the topological constraints their structures can impose on DNA and chromatin polymers. Comparative analyses across cell types, cell-cycle states, species, and perturbations will identify whether particular protein topologies are associated with recurrent mesoscale outcomes. For example, ring-like and bridged architectures may correlate with persistent loop anchors, topological-clamp-like complexes with boundary insulation, and topologically complex remodeling or chaperone systems with regions requiring high chromatin reorganization. We will also evaluate alternative explanations, including expression level, binding affinity, domain composition, evolutionary conservation, and local chromatin state, to determine when topology adds explanatory power beyond existing molecular annotations.

This effort requires NCEMS-scale support because it combines mathematical topology, structural bioinformatics, chromatin genomics, polymer physics, machine learning, and open-science infrastructure in a way that exceeds the scope of a single laboratory. The Working Group will convene protein topologists, genome modelers, structural biologists, chromatin experimentalists, data scientists, and trainees to define shared standards for representing molecular topology across scales. All annotations, workflows, benchmark datasets, visualization tools, and model outputs will be released openly. By training graduate students and postdoctoral researchers to work across protein structure, genome organization, and mesoscale modeling, the project will create a data-savvy community positioned to explain how molecular entanglement contributes to emergent cellular organization.

title: Emergent Translational Reserve as a Multiscale Determinant of Skeletal Muscle Growth, Repair, and Inflammatory Failure
title_norm: emergent translational reserve as a multiscale determinant of skeletal muscle growth repair and inflammatory failure
abstract_text: In skeletal muscle biology, translational reserve defines the capacity to manage ribosome biogenesis, protein synthesis, and tissue remodeling during stress, which is critical for understanding overlapping molecular pathways that dictate tissue outcomes. An integrative framework remains absent, preventing a cross context synthesis of fragmented datasets to explain why identical stimuli cause adaptive growth rather than maladaptive inflammation or wasting. This project will define and model translational reserve to identify interactions producing adaptive versus maladaptive phenotypes, applying graph neural networks, latent variable models, and differential equations to construct multiscale statistical and dynamic mathematical models. abstract_original:
Skeletal muscle exhibits striking emergent behavior: molecular changes in signaling, chromatin state, ribosome production, autophagy, immune activity, and mechanical response collectively produce higher-order outcomes such as hypertrophy, regeneration, fibrosis, or functional decline. Yet a central unresolved question remains: why do similar anabolic or mechanical cues produce robust growth in some contexts but maladaptive inflammation, impaired repair, or wasting in others? We propose a community-scale synthesis project to define and model an emergent property we call “translational reserve”: the coordinated capacity of muscle cells and their local niche to expand ribosome biogenesis, maintain protein synthesis, buffer proteostatic stress, and support tissue remodeling under mechanical or inflammatory challenge.

This project will use only publicly available datasets to integrate molecular, cellular, and tissue-scale information across human and animal skeletal muscle studies. Data sources will include bulk and single-nucleus RNA-seq from exercise, resistance training, overload, immobilization, aging, muscular disease, rheumatoid arthritis, myositis, and injury models; public proteomics and phosphoproteomics datasets related to mTOR signaling, ribosome assembly, autophagy, and inflammatory pathways; DNA methylation and chromatin accessibility datasets where available; ribosome profiling and translation-associated datasets from muscle and related cell types; and histological or imaging-derived public metadata on fiber size, fiber type, fibrosis, immune infiltration, and functional outcomes. The project will harmonize these heterogeneous resources into a shared cross-species atlas of muscle adaptation states.

The central hypothesis is that tissue-level muscle outcomes emerge from nonlinear interactions among three mesoscale modules: nucleolar/ribosome biogenesis capacity, proteostasis-autophagy buffering, and immune-fibrotic niche signaling. We will test this by developing an AI-driven multiscale integration framework combining graph neural networks, interpretable latent variable models, and mathematical dynamical modeling. The graph representation will connect genes, proteins, pathways, cell states, perturbations, species, disease contexts, and phenotypic outcomes. GPU-accelerated workflows will enable large-scale reanalysis of sequencing and methylation datasets, standardized feature extraction, and scalable model training across many public studies. Mathematical models will then translate learned network structure into dynamic hypotheses about threshold behavior, feedback loops, and tipping points that separate adaptive hypertrophy from maladaptive remodeling.

The expected product is not merely a catalog of exercise-responsive genes, but a predictive synthesis of how molecular and cellular modules combine to generate emergent muscle phenotypes. We will identify conserved and context-specific signatures of translational reserve, determine whether inflammatory disease shifts muscle toward a low-reserve state, and evaluate whether ribosome biogenesis, autophagy, and immune-cell composition jointly predict fiber growth or fibrosis better than any single pathway. Cross-species analyses will distinguish mechanisms conserved between rodent overload models and human training or disease cohorts, while cell-type-resolved analyses will reveal how myonuclei, satellite cells, fibro-adipogenic progenitors, endothelial cells, and immune cells contribute to the emergent tissue response.

NCEMS support is essential because this effort requires coordinated expertise in muscle biology, translational control, inflammation, high-performance computing, graph-based AI, and mechanistic mathematical modeling, as well as community agreement on data standards and reproducible workflows. The working group will release an open atlas, curated metadata schema, analysis pipelines, trained models, and interactive visualization tools. Graduate students and postdoctoral researchers will receive cross-training in muscle physiology, public-data reuse, GPU-enabled bioinformatics, network modeling, and open collaborative science. By synthesizing dispersed public data into a mechanistic, predictive framework, this project will address a fundamental question in molecular and cellular emergence: how molecular-scale control of protein production and stress buffering gives rise to cell- and tissue-scale muscle adaptation or failure.

title: A Public Data Atlas Linking Disordered-Region Sequence Grammar to Emergent Condensate Material States
title_norm: a public data atlas linking disorderedregion sequence grammar to emergent condensate material states
abstract_text: Biomolecular condensates, which form through multivalent interactions involving intrinsically disordered regions and nucleic acids, encompass the material state transitions of RNA binding protein granules, transcriptional and chromatin condensates, and stress responsive condensates. Currently, public data remain dispersed across isolated biological subfields, leaving no framework to link the molecular sequence features of disordered regions to the resulting mesoscale material properties of condensates. This project will determine which combinations of molecular features dictate condensate material states by synthesizing public data through text mining and manual curation to train machine learning models such as gradient boosted trees. Information from diverse databases including LLPSDB, PhaSepDB, DisProt, UniProt, and AlphaFold will be integrated by mapping heterogeneous experimental observations onto a multidimensional condensate material ontology utilizing automated retrieval pipelines. The resulting atlas will map these relationships to distinguish the physical rules governing typical cellular organization from those driving pathological protein aggregation in diseases such as neurodegeneration.

Biomolecular condensates form through multivalent interactions but existing public data remain inconsistently annotated and dispersed across isolated subfields. This project investigates how sequence features dictate material states to distinguish typical cellular organization from pathological protein aggregation. The analytical strategy synthesizes public data using an ontology and machine learning models to predict material state transitions. Key methods include automated text mining and manual curation alongside regularized regression and random forests within containerized workflows. The team will evaluate predictive models using nested cross validation and validate the curation of data through independent double annotation. Datasets include LLPSDB and UniProt and ClinVar alongside confidence profiles from AlphaFold and supplementary data from published literature. Researchers will integrate heterogeneous observations by mapping them onto a multidimensional ontology using retrieval pipelines and manual curation. The team will mitigate data inconsistency and dispersion by quantifying evidence uncertainty and retaining ambiguous or negative cases. Integrating these heterogeneous datasets is feasible through combined expertise in polymer physics and ontology development and artificial intelligence. The extensive project scope requires a cross disciplinary collaboration to encompass condensate biology and neurodegeneration and evolutionary genomics. The project will release curated datasets and predictive models under permissive licenses while maintaining an interactive web interface. The team comprises domain experts and graduate students who will receive training in machine learning and data curation.

abstract_original:
Biomolecular condensates emerge from many weak, multivalent interactions among intrinsically disordered regions, structured domains, nucleic acids, metabolites, and post-translational modifications. Yet the field lacks a synthesis-level answer to a central question: which molecular features determine whether a condensate remains a dynamic cellular compartment, becomes a gel-like regulatory hub, or crosses into aberrant aggregation? We propose a community-scale synthesis project that will integrate public sequence, biophysical, imaging, proteomic, and disease-variant data to build a predictive atlas connecting disordered-region molecular grammar to mesoscale condensate material properties.

The working group will assemble and harmonize existing public data from LLPSDB, PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, DisProt, MobiDB, UniProt, AlphaFold confidence profiles, PhosphoSitePlus, PRIDE, BioImage Archive, Image Data Resource, ClinVar, gnomAD, and published supplementary datasets reporting phase diagrams, FRAP recovery, droplet fusion, viscosity proxies, SAXS/NMR-derived ensemble parameters, turbidity, microscopy phenotypes, and aggregation outcomes. The project will focus on three biologically important condensate classes that are rarely analyzed together: RNA-binding protein granules linked to neurodegeneration, transcriptional and chromatin-associated condensates, and stress- or metabolite-responsive condensates involving polyamines, phosphorylation, oxidation, or other cellular-state variables.

Our central hypothesis is that condensate material state is not encoded by single features such as net charge or aromatic content alone, but by higher-order patterns: sticker valence and spacing, charge blockiness, transient structure propensity, partner valence, nucleic acid context, post-translational modification state, and cellular concentration regimes. These features jointly produce emergent mesoscale properties that can be inferred only by integrating heterogeneous datasets across proteins, organisms, experimental modalities, and disease contexts.

The synthesis will proceed in four coordinated activities. First, we will create an open condensate-material ontology that standardizes experimental descriptors such as liquid-like exchange, viscoelasticity, aging, demixing, gelation, and irreversible aggregation. Second, we will extract quantitative and semi-quantitative material-state labels from public tables, figures, repositories, and curated literature using reproducible text-mining and human-in-the-loop annotation. Third, we will compute interpretable polymer-physics and sequence-patterning features for disordered regions and combine them with PTM, mutation, abundance, localization, RNA-binding, and interaction-network features. Fourth, we will train benchmarked machine-learning and statistical models to predict condensate state transitions and identify conserved physical rules shared across neurodegenerative proteins, transcription factors, histone tails, and synthetic condensate scaffolds.

This project requires NCEMS support because no single laboratory can curate, normalize, and interpret the dispersed data spanning biophysics, cell biology, neurodegeneration, genomics, image analysis, and polymer theory. The working group will bring together experts in intrinsically disordered proteins, condensate physics, chromatin organization, neurodegenerative disease, proteomics, bioimage informatics, evolutionary analysis, and interpretable AI. Deliverables will include an openly licensed database, FAIR workflows, benchmark datasets, interactive visualization tools, and training modules for graduate students and postdocs in reproducible data synthesis. By transforming scattered public observations into an integrated mesoscale atlas, the project will provide a general framework for predicting how molecular disorder gives rise to emergent cellular organization and when that organization becomes pathological.

title: A Comparative Multi-Omics Atlas of Reversible Metabolic Suppression Across Mammalian Hibernators
title_norm: a comparative multiomics atlas of reversible metabolic suppression across mammalian hibernators
abstract_text: Mammalian hibernation requires conserved and lineage specific molecular programs for reversible metabolic suppression and tissue preservation, and detecting shared biological principles among these processes remains critical for evolutionary and physiological research. Current multi omics knowledge remains fragmented by species and tissue, lacking a unified comparative framework to identify how these molecular programs combine across biological scales. This project will build an integrated comparative multi omics atlas to determine how diverse mammals reversibly reorganize cellular energy use without pathological damage, and will apply machine learning alongside evolutionary models to identify tissue specific hibernation modules. The analysis will integrate public bulk and single cell transcriptomic, proteomic, and metabolomic datasets from primary repositories using standardized processing workflows, orthology mapping, and random effects meta analysis. The resulting comparative atlas will evaluate cross scale synthesis, separating true hibernation mechanisms from generic stress responses to reveal whether metabolic suppression relies on conserved pathways or convergent regulatory architecture.
full_text: The broad field of mammalian hibernation lacks a comparative framework to identify conserved programs of reversible metabolic suppression. Existing datasets of multi omics for various mammals remain fragmented and prevent the detection of shared biological principles. The proposed study asks how mammals reversibly reorganize energy use to distinguish mechanisms of hibernation from generic stress. The study design synthesizes public datasets of multi omics to identify conserved modules of hibernation using machine learning. The methodology employs generalized linear models and random forests alongside meta analysis of random effects and neural networks. The proposed study validates results using nested cross validation and sensitivity analyses alongside independent computational reruns by trainees. The team uses public single cell RNA-seq and proteomics datasets from repositories like Gene Expression Omnibus and Zenodo. The project integrates datasets by processing raw reads via standardized workflows and employing meta analysis of random effects. The researchers mitigate known data limitations including batch effects by incorporating control covariates into the applied statistical models. The proposed study demands combined expertise in evolutionary genomics and comparative transcriptomics alongside deep knowledge of hibernation physiology. This extensive project scope exceeds the capacity of a single laboratory and requires cross disciplinary collaboration among experts. The proposed study will release data products under permissive licenses and host software code on platforms like GitHub. The team unites computational biology investigators with graduate students who will receive training in analysis of phylogenetic networks.

abstract_original: Mammalian hibernation is an extreme example of biological emergence: coordinated molecular changes across cells and tissues generate organism-level phenotypes that include profound metabolic suppression, altered insulin sensitivity, muscle maintenance, immune modulation, and reversible shifts in body temperature. Although public transcriptomic, genomic, proteomic, and metabolomic datasets now exist for bears, ground squirrels, bats, hamsters, tenrecs, dwarf lemurs, and laboratory mouse models of torpor, these datasets remain fragmented across species, tissues, seasons, and analytical frameworks. This working group will synthesize existing public data to ask a central question: what conserved and lineage-specific molecular programs allow diverse mammals to reversibly reorganize cellular energy use during hibernation without pathological damage? We will build an open, comparative atlas integrating publicly available bulk RNA-seq, single-cell and single-nucleus RNA-seq where available, proteomic, metabolomic, genome annotation, and regulatory datasets from hibernating and non-hibernating mammals. The project will focus on emergent mesoscale processes that link molecules to cellular and tissue phenotypes, including mitochondrial remodeling, lipid droplet dynamics, endoplasmic reticulum stress responses, circadian-metabolic coupling, extracellular matrix remodeling, and immune-cell state shifts. By mapping orthologous genes and pathways across species and tissues, we will identify modules that repeatedly change during torpor, arousal, winter fasting, and experimentally induced metabolic shifts. We will then test whether these modules show signatures of convergent regulatory architecture across independent hibernating lineages, using comparative genomics, gene regulatory network inference, ancestral-state-aware enrichment analyses, and machine learning approaches that explicitly account for phylogenetic relatedness. A major innovation will be to move beyond lists of differentially expressed genes toward cross-scale synthesis: we will infer how regulatory changes in individual pathways combine into tissue-level and organism-level hibernation states. For example, we will evaluate whether mitochondrial genes, lipid-handling genes, circadian regulators, and inflammatory mediators form conserved cross-tissue network motifs that predict hibernation state better than any single tissue or pathway. We will also compare natural hibernation datasets with public datasets from fasting, cold exposure, obesity, diabetes, muscle disuse, and aging models to distinguish hibernation-specific protective programs from generic stress responses. The resulting resource will provide a mechanistic framework for understanding how reversible metabolic depression emerges from coordinated molecular and cellular changes across tissues. NCEMS support is essential because the project requires a transdisciplinary working group spanning evolutionary genomics, hibernation physiology, comparative transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics, network biology, data harmonization, and phylogenetic statistics. No single laboratory currently has the breadth of expertise or the capacity to curate, standardize, and jointly analyze these diverse public datasets at community scale. Deliverables will include a FAIR hibernation multi-omics atlas, reproducible analysis workflows, orthology-aware gene module annotations, interactive network visualizations, and training materials for graduate students and postdoctoral researchers. By synthesizing existing public data across mammals, this project will reveal how molecular programs combine into emergent cellular and physiological states, while creating a reusable open-science platform for future studies of metabolic resilience.

title: Predicting Condensate-Scale Emergence from Evolutionary and Structural Coupling Networks in Multivalent Proteins
title_norm: predicting condensatescale emergence from evolutionary and structural coupling networks in multivalent proteins
abstract_text: Molecular and cellular biology investigates the emergence of biomolecular condensates from weak molecular interactions in multivalent proteins, a phenomenon critical for explaining condition specific assembly and the influence of distributed coupling networks. Current phase separation predictors lack an integrated framework, leaving researchers unable to predict specific condensate outcomes from sequence encoded features or explain varying assembly behaviors among structurally similar proteins. This project will determine if emergent biomolecular condensate behavior is predictable from evolutionarily conserved networks by synthesizing public data to train machine learning models using direct coupling analysis, Potts statistical models, and graph based structural communication models. The research will integrate resources including UniProt, AlphaFold DB, PDB, LLPSDB, and ClinVar by developing a version controlled knowledge graph linking protein sequences, structural contacts, dynamic ensembles, and condensate phenotypes. This approach will shift the scientific focus from cataloging components to predicting material states using principles of evolutionary constraint, yielding specific protein variants and sites for subsequent experimental testing.

Existing predictors use local features of sequences but lack frameworks to explain the effects of distributed coupling networks. This novel study asks if conserved networks of residues can predict material states of condensates for experimental testing. The design of the study synthesizes public data across six stages to construct models for prediction of condensates. The researchers will apply graph based models of structural communication and algorithms for machine learning to analyze networks. abstract_original:
A central unsolved problem in molecular and cellular biology is how weak, distributed molecular interactions give rise to sharply different mesoscale outcomes, such as liquid-like compartments, gels, aggregates, or dispersed cellular states. We propose a community-scale synthesis project to determine whether emergent biomolecular condensate behavior can be predicted from evolutionarily conserved networks of residue, domain, and motif couplings within multivalent proteins and their interaction partners. The guiding hypothesis is that many condensate-forming systems are regulated by hidden coupling architectures: perturbations at folded domains, intrinsically disordered regions, RNA-binding surfaces, post-translational modification sites, or ion-binding regions propagate through molecular ensembles to alter mesoscale assembly thresholds and material states.

This project will use only existing public data. We will integrate protein family alignments from UniProt, Pfam, MGnify, and model-organism databases; structural models and experimental structures from AlphaFold DB, PDB, SASBDB, and integrative structure repositories; condensate annotations and phase behavior measurements from LLPSDB, PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, PhaSePro, and curated literature-derived datasets; public mutational scans and variant-effect datasets from MaveDB, ClinVar, cBioPortal, and organismal resources; proteomic and phosphoproteomic datasets from PRIDE, MassIVE, and ProteomeXchange; RNA-binding and chromatin-associated interaction datasets from ENCODE and related repositories; and reusable molecular simulation trajectories from public simulation archives where available. These heterogeneous resources will be harmonized into a FAIR, versioned knowledge graph linking sequence features, coevolutionary constraints, structural contacts, dynamic ensembles, modification sites, disease or engineered variants, and observed condensate phenotypes.

Analytically, the working group will combine statistical sequence models, direct coupling and sector-like analyses, information-theoretic measures, graph-based structural communication models, and machine learning on experimentally annotated phase behavior. For each protein family, we will infer conserved coupling networks and map them onto folded domains, disordered regions, short linear motifs, RNA-binding interfaces, and multivalent interaction modules. We will then ask whether particular coupling architectures distinguish proteins that form regulated condensates from homologs that do not, and whether these architectures predict sensitivity to temperature, salt, RNA, phosphorylation, disease mutation, or engineered sequence changes. A major methodological outcome will be an open cross-scale framework that converts evolutionary and structural coupling information into testable predictions of mesoscale assembly propensity and state transitions.

The emergent property addressed here is not any single molecular contact, but the appearance of cellular-scale organization from ensembles of many weakly coupled molecular features. The synthesis is beyond the scope of a single laboratory because it requires expertise in molecular evolution, protein allostery, statistical physics, biomolecular simulation, phase separation, structural bioinformatics, proteomics, RNA biology, and open data engineering. NCEMS support would enable the coordinated curation standards, shared computational infrastructure, trainee-led cross-training, and community benchmarking necessary to make the results reusable.

The project will deliver an open atlas of coupling networks in condensate-associated protein families, reproducible workflows for integrating evolutionary, structural, simulation, and cellular phenotype data, and prioritized predictions for variants or modification sites likely to shift mesoscale organization. By linking molecular information flow to condensate-level behavior, this synthesis will provide a general strategy for understanding how cellular material states emerge from protein sequence, structure, dynamics, and evolution.

title: Evolutionary Discovery of Metabolic Network Modules that Generate Mesoscale Membrane and Organelle Organization
title_norm: evolutionary discovery of metabolic network modules that generate mesoscale membrane and organelle organization
abstract_text: In molecular and cellular biology, understanding how evolutionary changes in genes and metabolic reactions influence mesoscale cellular properties is critical because these features ultimately arise from coordinated metabolic flux. Currently, largely unintegrated public datasets leave a disconnect between evolutionary signals and biochemical flux, lacking a synthesis explaining why specific metabolic network modules repeatedly determine mesoscale cellular organization. This project will identify which metabolic network modules are repeatedly modified by evolution to control mesoscale organization, applying a computational synthesis utilizing interpretable population genetic machine learning and constraint based metabolic modeling. The project will construct a cross species reaction centered knowledge graph to integrate public population genomic data, comparative omic datasets, genome scale metabolic reconstructions, and microscopy phenotypes using standardized identifiers. This synthesis will test the hypothesis of evolutionary convergence within flux controlling metabolic modules, providing a novel framework that mechanistically links genotype, biochemical metabolism, and observable mesoscale phenotypes.

abstract_original:
A central unresolved problem in molecular and cellular biology is how evolutionary changes in genes and metabolic reactions give rise to emergent mesoscale cellular properties such as membrane composition, lipid droplet abundance, mitochondrial remodeling, peroxisome activity, and stress-dependent organelle organization. These properties are not encoded by single genes; they emerge from coordinated flux through lipid, amino acid, redox, and energy metabolism. Yet the public data needed to connect evolutionary pressures, metabolic network architecture, and mesoscale cellular organization now exist across human populations, model organisms, microbes, plants, and immune cell systems. This working group will synthesize these resources to ask: which metabolic network modules are repeatedly targeted by evolution and environmental response because they control emergent mesoscale organization?

The project will integrate only publicly available data: population genomic datasets from humans and other species; comparative genomes and orthology resources; transcriptomic, proteomic, metabolomic, and lipidomic datasets from environmental perturbations including temperature, diet, nutrient limitation, hypoxia, infection, and immune activation; genome-scale metabolic reconstructions from BiGG, ModelSEED, Human-GEM, plant metabolic databases, and organism-specific reconstructions; and public microscopy-derived organelle and cellular morphology datasets from resources such as the Image Data Resource and Cell Painting repositories. We will construct a cross-species reaction-centered knowledge graph linking genes, orthologs, variants, selection statistics, reactions, metabolites, lipid classes, predicted flux states, and mesoscale phenotypes. This graph will allow evolutionary signals and cellular systems measurements to be analyzed in a shared metabolic coordinate system rather than as disconnected gene lists.

Methodologically, the group will combine interpretable population-genetic machine learning with constraint-based metabolic modeling. Deep learning models trained on simulated neutral and selected haplotypes will identify genomic regions whose evolutionary histories are inconsistent with neutrality, while interpretable feature attribution will distinguish selection acting on individual loci from selection on coordinated metabolic modules. In parallel, context-specific genome-scale metabolic models will be reconstructed from public multi-omic datasets to infer flux reorganization under environmental and cellular states. A synthesis layer will then test whether selected genes are enriched not merely in pathways, but in flux-controlling modules predicted to alter mesoscale properties such as phospholipid saturation, sterol balance, acyl-chain remodeling, mitochondrial redox coupling, peroxisomal beta-oxidation, and lipid storage capacity.

The expected outcome is a generalizable atlas of evolutionarily sensitive metabolic modules that generate mesoscale cellular organization across species and conditions. The project will address whether convergent environmental pressures produce convergent metabolic network solutions, whether human adaptive loci disproportionately affect emergent membrane and organelle states, and whether stress-responsive flux modules in cells correspond to modules recurrently shaped by natural selection across populations and taxa. This synthesis requires NCEMS support because it spans population genetics, genome-scale metabolic modeling, lipid metabolism, comparative genomics, machine learning interpretability, and image-based cell phenotyping—expertise and data integration beyond the scope of a single laboratory.

All workflows, harmonized datasets, metabolic model annotations, trained models, and interactive visualizations will be released openly. Trainees will participate in cross-disciplinary hackathons and reproducible analysis teams, gaining experience in evolutionary genomics, metabolic network modeling, public data integration, and interpretable AI for molecular and cellular emergence.

title: Proteome Flux Codes for Emergent Mesoscale Remodeling During Cellular Stress and Disease
title_norm: proteome flux codes for emergent mesoscale remodeling during cellular stress and disease
abstract_text: Cellular biology research investigates the reorganization of mesoscale protein systems and proteome flux during stress and cardiometabolic diseases, a crucial area because static abundance measurements fail to capture rate dependent mesoscale reorganization. It remains unclear how dynamic molecular flux processes combine to produce emergent mesoscale cellular structures and phenotypes because measurements remain fragmented across disparate repositories, technologies, and analytical conventions. This project will define generalizable proteome flux codes by integrating public multi omics datasets into an interoperable atlas, utilizing unsupervised clustering, supervised machine learning, and hierarchical Bayesian models to link molecular flux signatures to cellular outcomes. The analysis will integrate ribosome profiling, RNA sequencing, and single cell transcriptomics datasets from repositories including GEO, PRIDE, and CPTAC, harmonizing turnover and translation measurements via mixed effect models accounting for metadata. This research will produce predictive dynamic models of proteome flux, providing a vital framework to differentiate between reversible adaptive cellular remodeling and persistent pathological restructuring.
full_text: This project in cellular biology investigates how processes of molecular flux produce emergent protein structures during stress and disease. Current knowledge of cellular stress relies on static abundance and misses dynamic reorganization because kinetic measurements remain completely fragmented. The proposed study defines codes of proteome flux through dynamic models to distinguish reversible adaptation from persistent pathological restructuring. This comparative synthesis integrates public datasets to build an interoperable flux atlas and link molecular signatures to cellular outcomes. The analytical approach applies hierarchical Bayesian models and supervised machine learning through managers of reproducible workflows in containerized environments. The team validates results using nested cross validation alongside orthogonal evaluations with unseen datasets and internal challenges of reproducibility. The project extracts records of ribosome profiling and single cell transcriptomics from diverse public databases including the Human Protein Atlas. The team integrates datasets by performing conservative mapping of orthology and harmonizing measurements through hierarchical Bayesian or mixed effect models. The proposed study mitigates heterogeneous identifiers and missing features by establishing shared standards and conducting downstream sensitivity analyses. Project milestones include delivering a public atlas of proteome flux alongside identifying recurrent signatures of flux and generating predictive models. The integration of diverse datasets demands cross disciplinary collaboration because the required specialized expertise exceeds the capacities of single laboratories. The researchers will deposit data in open repositories and maintain version controlled code alongside executable notebooks and tutorials for the community. The diverse team spans multiple career stages to provide training opportunities including code sprints and benchmarking of reproducible workflows.
