abstract_original:
Cells often respond to stress not by changing the abundance of individual molecules alone, but by reorganizing mesoscale protein systems: ribonucleoprotein assemblies, cytoskeletal and nuclear scaffolds, extracellular matrices, metabolic enzyme clusters, and organelle-associated protein communities. A central unsolved question is how molecular flux through the proteome—translation, degradation, post-translational modification, disorder-mediated interaction, and localization—combines to produce these emergent cellular structures and phenotypes. We propose a community-scale synthesis project to define generalizable “proteome flux codes” that predict when changes in protein synthesis and turnover produce mesoscale remodeling across stress, aging, and cardiometabolic disease contexts.

This working group will integrate only publicly available datasets spanning multiple biological scales. Core inputs will include ribosome profiling, RNA-seq, quantitative proteomics, pulse-labeling and protein turnover datasets, phosphoproteomics and other modification maps, protein disorder and structural annotations, subcellular localization resources, protein interaction networks, phase-separation and condensate-associated protein catalogs, and public single-cell or bulk transcriptomic and proteomic datasets from stress models, iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes and endothelial cells, cardiovascular tissues, cancer stress states, and aging-related systems. Rather than treating mRNA, translation, protein abundance, and degradation as separate regulatory layers, we will build harmonized models of protein residence time, production rate, degradation rate, modification state, and mesoscale membership.

The central hypothesis is that emergent mesoscale remodeling is governed by coordinated shifts in proteome flux, especially among proteins with long residence times, intrinsically disordered regions, modification-rich segments, scaffold-like interaction properties, or compartment-specific localization. These features may explain why some cellular responses are rapid and reversible, whereas others become persistent, pathological, or tissue-specific. We will test this through three synthesis aims. First, we will create an interoperable atlas of proteome flux across public datasets, with uncertainty-aware normalization of turnover, translation, and abundance measurements across organisms, cell types, perturbations, and technologies. Second, we will identify recurrent flux signatures associated with mesoscale assemblies, including stress granule-like systems, nuclear lamina and chromatin-associated networks, mitochondrial and metabolic complexes, extracellular matrix remodeling modules, and cytoskeletal or contractile structures. Third, we will develop predictive machine-learning and mechanistic network models that link molecular flux signatures to higher-order cellular outcomes such as stress adaptation, proteostasis collapse, endothelial inflammation, cardiomyocyte dysfunction, and age-associated remodeling.

This project requires NCEMS-scale synthesis because no single laboratory can curate, reconcile, and model the diverse public datasets needed to connect translation dynamics, proteome turnover, structural disorder, post-translational regulation, and disease-relevant cell phenotypes. The working group would bring together experts in proteomics, ribosome profiling, cardiovascular and stem-cell models, structural bioinformatics, stress biology, network science, and open computational infrastructure. Deliverables will include a FAIR public proteome-flux atlas, reproducible workflows, benchmark datasets for turnover inference, interactive visualization tools, and trainee-led tutorials on integrative molecular data synthesis. By focusing on how molecular rates and regulatory layers combine to generate mesoscale biological organization, this project directly addresses NCEMS priorities and offers a new framework for understanding emergent cellular behavior from existing public data.

title: Inferring Conserved Mesoscale Kinetic Programs from Public Spatial Omics and Fluorescence Microscopy Atlases
title_norm: inferring conserved mesoscale kinetic programs from public spatial omics and fluorescence microscopy atlases
abstract_text: While molecular and cellular biology defines cell states primarily by transcript abundance, mesoscale kinetic organization encompassing RNA compartmentalization, protein clustering, and molecular mobility represents a crucial phenomenon for understanding complex biological transitions. The lack of integration between single cell gene expression profiles and subcellular imaging data currently limits the understanding of how emergent mesoscale cellular behaviors function independently of transcript abundance. This project will determine whether diverse cellular transitions follow conserved mesoscale kinetic programs by extracting biophysical features from harmonized public datasets and applying a hierarchical Bayesian multimodal latent state model to identify recurring programs. Single cell transcriptomics, proteomic resources, and fluorescence microscopy datasets will be integrated by mapping heterogeneous measurements into a shared latent representation through probabilistic alignment utilizing cell type, marker genes, and spatial context parameters. This research will establish a spatially grounded biophysical model that shifts cell state definitions, explaining how different biological systems generate similar cellular phenotypes using differing marker genes.
full_text: The field of cellular biology lacks integration of single cell profiles and subcellular images to elucidate mesoscale kinetic organization. This project investigates whether diverse cellular transitions share conserved mesoscale programs to shift toward a spatially grounded biophysical model. This data synthesis study harmonizes public datasets and extracts biophysical features to identify recurring programs across three biological systems. The analytical approach relies on a hierarchical Bayesian multimodal model alongside probabilistic feature extraction and alignment of cell states. The team will validate results using held out datasets and baseline comparisons alongside negative controls with randomized coordinates. Data sources include single cell atlases and the Human Protein Atlas alongside microscopy repositories like the BioImage Archive. These heterogeneous measurements will map into a shared latent representation to probabilistically link image features with transcriptomic states. The model will mitigate variations in optical resolution and batch effects by propagating uncertainty estimates through Bayesian parameters. The proposed timeline spans 18 months and includes milestones for data registries and the release of public manuscripts. The synthesis demands cross disciplinary collaboration to integrate expertise in probabilistic modeling and single molecule biophysics across laboratories. The team will release open source code and a public data registry with persistent identifiers and standard metadata. Graduate trainees and postdoctoral researchers will work alongside principal investigators while receiving cross training in probabilistic modeling techniques.

abstract_original:
Cell states are usually defined by transcriptional profiles, yet many consequential state transitions emerge from mesoscale organization: RNA compartmentalization, protein clustering, membrane localization, molecular mobility, and organelle-associated trafficking. A macrophage-exposed tumor cell, a differentiating neural progenitor, or a stressed neuron may share little transcriptomic identity, but may converge on similar mesoscale kinetic solutions such as altered nuclear export, enhanced membrane-proximal signaling, or increased residence time of regulatory proteins in subcellular compartments. This working group will test the hypothesis that diverse cellular transitions are governed by a small set of conserved mesoscale kinetic programs that can be inferred by synthesizing existing public spatial omics, proteomics, and fluorescence microscopy data.

We will build an open synthesis framework that links three public data classes that are rarely analyzed together. First, we will harmonize single-cell and spatial transcriptomic datasets from public repositories, including brain development and adult brain atlases, tumor microenvironment datasets, MERFISH/seqFISH-style measurements with subcellular RNA localization, and spatial cancer atlases. Second, we will integrate proteomic and immunofluorescence resources such as the Human Protein Atlas, public CODEX/IMC datasets, and subcellular protein localization maps. Third, we will mine public microscopy repositories such as the Image Data Resource and BioImage Archive for live-cell, single-particle, FRAP/FCS, super-resolution, and organelle-tracking datasets that report protein mobility, clustering, stoichiometry, or trafficking dynamics. No new experimental data will be generated.

The central methodological innovation will be a Bayesian multimodal model that translates heterogeneous public measurements into a shared latent representation of mesoscale kinetic state. Rather than treating images as qualitative annotations, the framework will extract probabilistic features including nuclear-cytoplasmic RNA partitioning, local transcript density, protein puncta size and number, apparent oligomeric state, organelle adjacency, membrane enrichment, and effective mobility or residence-time estimates where time-resolved data exist. These features will be linked to matched or harmonized transcriptomic cell states using batch-aware integration and uncertainty propagation. The model will explicitly account for differences in optical resolution, fluorophore sampling, segmentation quality, and assay modality, enabling principled comparison across datasets and laboratories.

We will apply the framework to three biological transitions with abundant public data and strong mesoscale relevance: neural differentiation and maturation, inflammatory remodeling of tumor cells and immune neighborhoods, and cellular stress states involving mitochondrial and membrane-trafficking pathways. Across these systems, we will ask whether transcriptionally distinct cell types reuse common mesoscale programs; whether spatially localized RNAs predict protein compartmentalization or mobility; and whether emergent cellular phenotypes are better explained by inferred kinetic features than by gene expression alone. Expected products include an open atlas of inferred mesoscale kinetic programs, reusable workflows for extracting biophysical features from public microscopy data, benchmark datasets for spatial omics–image integration, and candidate molecular modules linking transcriptional regulation to mesoscale organization.

This project requires NCEMS support because it exceeds the scope of any single laboratory: it demands expertise in single-cell and spatial data integration, statistical optics, Bayesian inference, single-molecule biophysics, image analysis, cell-state biology, and open data engineering. The working group will include trainees as core contributors through hackathon-style data integration sprints, reproducible workflow development, and cross-training modules on spatial omics, microscopy uncertainty, and probabilistic modeling. All curated data links, derived features, code, model outputs, and documentation will be released openly to support community reuse and future synthesis studies of emergent cellular organization.

title: Emergent Chromatin and Immune Cell States from tRNA Modification–Controlled Translation Dynamics
title_norm: emergent chromatin and immune cell states from trna modificationcontrolled translation dynamics
abstract_text: Within molecular biology, chemical modifications to tRNAs affect decoding accuracy and translation elongation, playing a critical role in regulating ribosome traffic, protein complex stoichiometry, and immune phenotypes in human and microbial cells. The scientific field currently lacks a mechanistic model explaining how these localized chemical changes influence proteome remodeling to produce emergent cellular states that are not predicted by transcript abundance. The primary objective is to determine how varying tRNA modification states alter translation dynamics, which this project will investigate through a cross kingdom data synthesis utilizing codon aware statistical models, structural molecular modeling, and interpretable machine learning. The project will integrate MODOMICS, UniProt, AlphaFold, and various single cell datasets by mapping orthology across species, scoring modification sensitive codons, and harmonizing single cell and bulk data through graph based feature propagation. This project will produce a multiscale framework explaining how nucleotide level chemical variations drive identical transcriptomes to develop distinct proteomes and broad immunological changes.
full_text: Within molecular and cellular biology this project investigates chemical modifications of tRNA to address missing mechanistic models of cellular states. Over one hundred tRNA modifications alter translation but the field lacks a synthesis of impacts on emergent cellular phenotypes. This project determines how tRNA modifications alter translation and provides a significant multiscale framework for cells with identical transcriptomes. The overall study design is a cross kingdom synthesis of secondary data across four workstreams without generating experimental data. The team applies statistical modeling and interpretable machine learning alongside structural molecular modeling within containerized computational workflows (Docker and Nextflow). The team validates results by comparing findings against matched null models and testing phenotypic replication across independent datasets. This project utilizes databases including AlphaFold and UniProt alongside single cell RNA-seq data and public microbial pangenome datasets. The team integrates these distinct datasets by mapping orthology across species and harmonizing bulk data through feature propagation. The project mitigates the limitation of data sparsity using graph based imputation and manages batch effects via covariates. The project timeline includes delivering a curated atlas in year one and releasing public manuscripts by year three. This scope requires cross disciplinary collaboration because integrating multiscale data across varied scientific domains exceeds single laboratory capacity. The team deposits harmonized data and code in public repositories like GitHub and publishes findings as open access papers. The multidisciplinary team spans multiple career stages and offers training opportunities through analytical fellowships and reproducible machine learning workshops.

abstract_original:
A central unsolved problem in molecular and cellular biology is how chemical changes on a small number of RNAs produce system-level cell states that are not predictable from transcript abundance alone. This working group will test the hypothesis that tRNA modifications act as mesoscale control points by reshaping ribosome traffic, protein complex stoichiometry, and chromatin-regulatory assemblies, thereby generating emergent epigenomic and immune phenotypes across microbes and human cells. The project will use only publicly available data and will synthesize information across RNA modification biology, ribosome profiling, proteomics, structural modeling, single-cell genomics, and microbial metabolism.

We will build an open, cross-kingdom atlas linking tRNA modification capacity to translation and cellular phenotype. Public resources will include MODOMICS and curated bacterial and eukaryotic tRNA modification enzyme annotations; published tRNA modification mapping datasets; ribosome profiling, RNA-seq, and proteomics from bacteria, yeast, mammalian cells, cancer models, immune perturbation studies, neurodegeneration cohorts, and metabolic stress datasets; public single-cell RNA-seq and single-cell ATAC-seq atlases from tumor, brain, and cardiovascular tissues; microbial genome and metagenome datasets with annotated micronutrient and RNA-modification pathways; and public protein structures from PDB and AlphaFold. No new experimental data will be generated.

The scientific question is deliberately multiscale: when a tRNA modification is lost, altered, or metabolite-limited, which codon contexts experience altered elongation, which proteins become selectively under- or over-produced, and which higher-order cellular structures or regulatory programs are most vulnerable? We will develop a codon-aware synthesis framework that integrates ribosome pausing signatures with transcript abundance, protein abundance, protein complex membership, post-translational modification data, and chromatin accessibility. Graph-based imputation and feature-propagation methods will harmonize sparse single-cell and bulk datasets, while interpretable machine-learning models will identify conserved translation-sensitive modules. Structural and coarse-grained molecular modeling will be used not to create new simulations as primary data, but to contextualize public structures of affected chromatin regulators, RNA-binding proteins, metabolic enzymes, and immune signaling proteins in terms of complex formation, DNA engagement, and mesoscale assembly potential.

The expected outcome is a quantitative map of how nucleotide-scale chemical information propagates to emergent mesoscale organization. We will focus on three synthesis products: first, a conserved catalog of codon- and modification-sensitive translation bottlenecks across organisms; second, a ranked set of chromatin, immune, and metabolic protein complexes whose stoichiometry is predicted to be unusually sensitive to tRNA modification state; and third, a set of cell-state transition models connecting microbial micronutrient availability, host tRNA modification capacity, ribosome pausing, chromatin accessibility, and immune phenotypes. This framework could help explain why similar transcriptional programs diverge into distinct proteomic or epigenomic outcomes, and why microbial metabolites or transporter variation can have unexpectedly broad cellular effects.

NCEMS support is essential because the project requires coordinated expertise in microbial genomics, RNA modification biology, single-cell data integration, proteomics, chromatin biophysics, structural modeling, and AI. The working group will release harmonized datasets, reproducible workflows, interactive network browsers, and training modules for trainees in open, data-intensive molecular synthesis research.

title: A Public-Data Atlas of Emergent Metal-Redox Compartmentalization Across Bacteria and Archaea
title_norm: a publicdata atlas of emergent metalredox compartmentalization across bacteria and archaea
abstract_text: The domain of microbial cell biology recognizes that bacteria and archaea utilize mesoscale prokaryotic compartments, including magnetosomes and encapsulins, to manage metal and redox chemistry and facilitate distinct electron management strategies. Isolated data across class specific databases currently prevents the creation of a synthesis level framework to characterize atypical structures and differentiate compartment forming gene clusters from standard metabolic operons. This project will identify genomic and structural predictors of compartment formation through a data synthesis approach utilizing profile hidden Markov models, RNA seq pseudoalignment, non negative matrix factorization, and interpretable machine learning to develop a predictive scoring model. The pipeline will process genomic, omics, and structural features from repositories including NCBI RefSeq, PRIDE, and the AlphaFold Database into an interpretable machine learning algorithm to calculate unified compartment formation probability scores. This research will establish general design rules for prokaryotic organelle formation and yield a predictive scoring model to direct future experimental research in microbiology and bioengineering.
full_text: This project in microbial cell biology addresses the inability to distinguish mesoscale compartments from standard operons and detect structural convergence. Prokaryotes utilize distinct compartments for metal management but isolated databases leave atypical and distantly related structures inconsistently annotated. The proposed study predicts the formation of these compartments to establish design rules and direct future bioengineering research. This data synthesis project compiles a genomic reference corpus and maps structural data to develop a predictive scoring model. The team will apply profile hidden Markov models and RNA-seq pseudoalignment before utilizing an interpretable machine learning algorithm. The team will validate outputs against experimentally verified compartments and standard operons utilizing taxonomic cross validation and structural alignment. The project draws information from NCBI RefSeq and PRIDE alongside structural repositories like the AlphaFold Database and EMDB. The researchers will process genomic and structural features into an interpretable machine learning algorithm to calculate a probability score. The team will mitigate raw proteomics limitations by harmonizing published abundance tables and manage classification ambiguities with confidence tiers. Project milestones include quarterly meetings and the public release of a compartment atlas alongside a framework of design principles. A cross disciplinary collaboration is necessary because synthesizing multi dimensional data requires specialized expertise beyond a single research group. The project will distribute the final atlas and open source code publicly through version controlled repositories and containerized workflows. The cross disciplinary team features microbial cell biologists and graduate students who will learn reproducible computational methods through tutorials.

abstract_original:
Bacteria and archaea build diverse mesoscale compartments that concentrate metals, redox cofactors, enzymes, membranes, and shell proteins into structures with properties not predictable from any single component. Yet the field lacks a synthesis-level framework for determining when a gene cluster encodes a true organelle-like system, what physiological pressures favor compartment formation, and how different compartment types converge on common solutions for metal storage, oxidative stress control, and metabolic electron flow. This working group will integrate publicly available genomic, metagenomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, structural, and imaging data to define the molecular rules by which metal-redox organelles emerge in prokaryotic cells.

The central question is: what combinations of genes, regulatory programs, protein architectures, ecological contexts, and cellular stress signatures predict the emergence of prokaryotic compartments that manage iron, heme, reactive oxygen chemistry, and cofactor balance? We will synthesize data across known and candidate compartment systems, including magnetosome-like loci, iron-storage organelle loci, encapsulin-associated metalloprotein systems, carboxysome and non-carboxysome bacterial microcompartments, and atypical shell-protein clusters with incomplete or repurposed modules. Rather than treating each organelle class separately, we will ask whether recurrent mesoscale design principles can be detected across independently evolved systems.

The project will use only existing public data. Genome and metagenome assemblies from NCBI, GTDB, IMG/M, MGnify, and public MAG/SAG collections will be mined for shell proteins, membrane remodeling factors, metalloproteins, redox enzymes, transporters, cytoskeletal factors, and regulatory elements. Public RNA-seq and proteomics datasets from pathogens, environmental bacteria, cyanobacteria, anaerobes, and host-associated communities will be reanalyzed to determine when candidate compartment loci are co-regulated with iron limitation, heme exposure, oxidative stress, desiccation, carbon fixation, anaerobic metabolism, or infection-relevant conditions. AlphaFold and structural databases, EMDB/EMPIAR image repositories, and published cryo-electron tomography annotations will be used to connect gene clusters with predicted mesoscale architecture. We will adapt mutational-signature-style decomposition, network community detection, phylogenetic profiling, and interpretable machine learning to identify recurrent “compartment signatures” that distinguish bona fide organelle systems from ordinary metabolic operons.

A major deliverable will be an open, versioned atlas of prokaryotic metal-redox compartmentalization, including standardized locus annotations, confidence scores, ecological metadata, predicted compartment architecture, and links to public omics evidence. We will also develop a reproducible workflow that assigns each candidate locus a quantitative “emergent compartment potential” score based on genomic modularity, co-expression, structural compatibility, taxonomic distribution, and environmental association. This score will allow the community to prioritize unstudied systems for future experimental work while remaining fully grounded in synthesis of public data.

NCEMS support is essential because the project requires coordination among microbial cell biologists, bioinformaticians, structural modelers, metallobiochemists, evolutionary biologists, imaging specialists, and data scientists. The working group will create open tutorials and trainee-led analysis sprints focused on genome mining, public omics reanalysis, structural annotation, and reproducible workflow development. By unifying scattered datasets across organelle biology, metal homeostasis, redox metabolism, and microbial ecology, the project will reveal general principles by which molecular components self-organize into mesoscale cellular structures with new physiological capabilities.

title: Decoding Cytokinetic Resilience: Synthesizing Context-Specific Multi-Omic Networks to Understand Mesoscale Emergence Under Thermal Stress
title_norm: decoding cytokinetic resilience synthesizing contextspecific multiomic networks to understand mesoscale emergence under thermal stress
abstract_text: The research domain of plant cytokinesis examines the resilience of cell plate assembly during high temperature stress, a phenomenon requiring systemic integration of individually mapped circadian responses and endomembrane dynamics. The primary objective is to determine how the circadian clock regulates endomembrane trafficking during heat stress, and the project will apply a data synthesis strategy using transcriptomic processing pipelines, network algorithms, and computational modeling. The project will integrate Sequence Read Archive, Gene Expression Omnibus, PRIDE, and BioImage Archive datasets by mapping transcriptomic networks onto trans Golgi proteomic profiles and correlating these with morphometric cellular imaging changes. This research will establish the biological principles of subcellular structural maintenance under heat stress, providing the foundational knowledge and network data necessary for engineering heat tolerant crops.
full_text: This project investigates plant cytokinesis to understand how circadian rhythms and dynamics of organelles protect cell division during thermal stress. Pathways of formation for cell plates and stress responses are known individually but systemic integration during extreme temperature remains incomplete. The project investigates regulation of cellular trafficking by circadian rhythms to provide foundational data for engineering heat tolerant crops. The researchers will synthesize existing transcriptomic and imaging data across species of plants without the generation of new experimental data. Methods include pipelines for processing of RNA-seq and algorithms to construct networks of genes and models for analysis of images. Predictions of networks for rerouting of machinery for the cell wall will be validated against datasets of vesicle proteomics. The project uses data from the Sequence Read Archive and Gene Expression Omnibus for species of plants including Zea mays. Networks of transcripts will be mapped onto profiles of proteins and correlated with physical changes from images of cells. Rates of false positives from datasets will be mitigated by algorithms to isolate modules specific to the context. The project requires integration of large scale data across domains of computational genomics and chronobiology and cell biology. This extensive integration of heterogeneous data exceeds the computational capacity and the technical expertise of a single laboratory for research. The team will share code via GitHub and deposit data in Zenodo and upload scientific preprints to bioRxiv. The cross disciplinary team provides training in cloud computing and synthesis of data for graduate students and postdoctoral researchers.

abstract_original: Plant cytokinesis represents a profound example of mesoscale emergence. During this transient developmental window, molecular components—including cytoskeletal microtubule arrays, trans-Golgi network-derived vesicles, and cell wall polysaccharides—spatially and temporally self-organize to construct a novel, higher-order structure: the cell plate. This highly dynamic process acts as a severe architectural bottleneck that is exceptionally vulnerable to environmental perturbations, particularly extreme temperature fluctuations and heat waves. While isolated studies have mapped individual components of the cytokinetic machinery or global plant stress responses, a massive knowledge gap remains: how do diurnal signaling rhythms, temporal organelle dynamics, and redundant spatial mechanisms synergize to buffer mesoscale cell division networks against severe thermal stress? Addressing this complex phenomenon requires a scale of inquiry beyond the capacity of any single laboratory. We propose a community-scale data synthesis project, utilizing strictly publicly available data, to decode the emergent properties of cytokinetic resilience. Leveraging vast public repositories—such as the Sequence Read Archive (SRA), PRIDE, and various open-access bioimage databases—we will integrate spatiotemporal transcriptomes, vesicle proteomics, and cellular imaging across diverse plant systems ranging from key models like Arabidopsis to vital crops such as Zea mays, Sorghum, and Rosaceae species. No new experimental data will be generated. Instead, to manage the immense scale and heterogeneity of these multi-omic data, we will deploy massively scalable, containerized computational workflows to process tens of thousands of raw RNA-seq samples uniformly. By applying advanced, noise-aware network construction toolkits, we will generate context-specific gene co-expression networks (csGCNs). These algorithms will filter out confounding cross-dataset variables to isolate distinct regulatory modules that are activated exclusively at the intersection of specific times-of-day and high-temperature stress. We will bridge these transcriptomic network predictions to mesoscale cellular phenotypes by synthesizing public proteomic and image data, applying shape-based computational modeling to evaluate how environmental stress alters division-plane orientation, phragmoplast navigation, and unconventional protein secretion pathways. This transdisciplinary approach uniquely fuses chronobiology, endomembrane cell biology, and computational genomics. We aim to identify how the circadian clock temporally gates the trafficking of essential cell wall components during heat stress, and whether redundant genetic mechanisms reorganize the 4D temporal organellome to prevent catastrophic cell division failure. Supported by NCEMS, this collaborative Working Group will not only answer fundamental questions about subcellular emergence but also serve as a premier training ground. Trainees will gain cutting-edge expertise at the intersection of biological synthesis, AI-driven network analysis, and scalable cloud computing. In strict adherence to open science principles, all resulting multi-omic matrices, context-specific networks, and reproducible computational pipelines will be made fully accessible to the global scientific community.

title: Decoding Mesoscale Emergence in the 3D Genome: Synthesizing Multi-Omic and Polymer Physics Data to Uncover IDP-Driven Chromatin Reorganization in Neuro-Immune Phenotypes
title_norm: decoding mesoscale emergence in the 3d genome synthesizing multiomic and polymer physics data to uncover idpdriven chromatin reorganization in neuroimmune phenotypes
abstract_text: The three dimensional organization of the eukaryotic genome fundamentally governs neuroimmune cellular plasticity, making it critical to connect localized biophysics with global genomic architectures mapped by single cell technologies. Disciplinary isolation of existing datasets prevents translating physical forces into global architectures, leaving an unresolved gap for computational frameworks connecting localized chromatin biophysics to genome wide transcriptional outcomes. This project will determine the biophysical rules governing three dimensional genome architecture by synthesizing existing multiomic data using variational autoencoders and graph neural networks to inform coarse grained polymer physics models and Langevin dynamics simulations. Machine learning frameworks will integrate datasets from the 4D Nucleome Project, Human Cell Atlas, GTEx, PRIDE, AlphaFold, and DisProt into a shared latent space to calculate steric pressures and overlay trait association data. This research will transition genome regulation studies from descriptive mapping to predictive physical modeling, identifying disease associated genetic variants that alter local mechanical genome landscapes and influence neuroimmune transcription.
full_text: This project investigates chromatin architecture and neuro immune plasticity to address missing frameworks that link biophysical forces and transcription. Current datasets remain isolated by discipline and prevent the translation of physical forces into architectures mapped by single cell genomics. The research determines biophysical rules of genome architecture to transition the field toward predictive modeling of disease variants. The proposed study integrates multi omic data via machine learning to extract biophysical parameters for polymer physics models. The team applies variational autoencoders and graph neural networks alongside block copolymer physics modeling and Langevin dynamics simulations. The team validates results by comparing physically constrained machine learning frameworks against purely statistical models using public datasets. The team extracts data from the 4D Nucleome Project and AlphaFold alongside the Human Cell Atlas and PRIDE. Machine learning algorithms map sequence features and expression readouts into a shared latent space to calculate steric pressures. The project addresses the sparsity of single cell data by constructing unified latent representations using graph neural networks. The proposed project requires simultaneous expertise in systems immunology and single cell genomics alongside advanced polymer physics modeling. This broad scientific scope exceeds the technical capabilities of a single laboratory and heavily relies on cross disciplinary collaboration. The research team shares all analytical tools and data pipelines via GitHub and Zenodo following formal hypothesis preregistration. The team includes systems biologists and biophysicists who provide cross disciplinary mentorship to postdoctoral fellows and graduate students.

abstract_original:
The three-dimensional organization of the eukaryotic genome represents a profound emergent phenomenon at the mesoscale. Through the local coordination of epigenetic modifications, structural proteins, and transcription factors, linear DNA spontaneously folds into dynamic 3D architectures, such as loop domains and phase-separated hubs. These mesoscale structures ultimately dictate macroscopic cellular responses. Recent experimental advances have generated vast amounts of publicly available data, including single-cell chromatin conformation maps (e.g., Dip-C, Hi-C), single-cell transcriptomics, proteomics, and transcriptome-wide association studies (TWAS). However, a critical synthesis gap remains: we lack a unified theoretical and computational framework that bridges the physical forces governing mesoscale chromatin architecture—specifically, the entropic and steric pressures exerted by intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) and pioneer factors—with systemic, genome-wide transcriptional outcomes. 

We propose a community-scale synthesis project to decipher the biophysical rules of emergent 3D genome architectures and their cascading effects on neuro-immune cellular plasticity. This working group will entirely leverage existing, publicly available data from the 4D Nucleome Project, the Human Cell Atlas, and GTEx. By integrating single-cell genomics, structural bioinformatics, and deep clinical transcriptomic profiling, our project aims to answer a longstanding mystery: how do local biophysical interactions, such as IDP-driven liquid-liquid phase separation and loop extrusion, generate the highly specific, emergent chromatin topologies required for coordinated cellular responses?

Our transdisciplinary approach is structured around three primary synthesis aims. First, we will utilize machine learning and AI-driven data science to fuse diverse multi-omic datasets (scRNA-seq, ATAC-seq, structural proteomics, and 3D genomics) across diverse human brain and immune cell types. This will create a unified, multi-layered atlas of cell-type-specific 3D genome configurations. Second, we will apply coarse-grained polymer physics modeling and biophysical simulations to these integrated datasets to infer the mechanical transmission and steric pressures exerted by IDPs and pioneer factors at domain boundaries. We hypothesize that biophysical parameters extracted from massive genomic datasets can reliably predict the physical thresholds required for chromatin opening and decompaction. Third, we will map these structural biophysical rules onto complex biological phenotypes, specifically analyzing how systemic perturbations—such as severe infection or neurological stress—remodel the genome's mesoscale architecture to drive maladaptive neuro-inflammatory and psychiatric phenotypes.

This synthesis project fundamentally demands the support of NCEMS, as it surpasses the capacity of any single laboratory by requiring the convergence of systems immunology, single-cell genomics, chromatin biophysics, and polymer physics. In strict adherence to open science principles, all integrated datasets, machine learning models, and polymer simulation pipelines will be made freely available as an open-source "Biophysical 3D-Omics" analytical suite. Furthermore, this working group will deeply integrate trainees, providing postdocs and graduate students with a unique, cross-disciplinary environment to master the synthesis of clinical multi-omics and theoretical biophysics, thereby training the next generation of data-savvy scientists to explore emergent biological complexity.

title: Mapping Emergent Mesoscale Architectures at the Host-Microbiome Interface: A Deep-Time Proteogenomic Synthesis
title_norm: mapping emergent mesoscale architectures at the hostmicrobiome interface a deeptime proteogenomic synthesis
abstract_text: Mesoscale biology investigates structural and functional protein protein interaction networks between human hosts and resident microbiomes, a critical biological phenomenon that remains unmapped across evolutionary time despite well documented independent individual profiles. Current research lacks fundamental understanding of how these cross species protein protein interaction networks assemble and reorganize over evolutionary time or during metabolic stress and disease. This project will determine how host microbiome networks reorganize by conducting a three phase computational synthesis of public multi omic data, utilizing double indexing sequence alignment algorithms, phylogenetic network modeling, and AI based structural prediction. The study will integrate UK Biobank, Human Microbiome Project, ancient DNA, and NCBI nr datasets, applying sequence alignment and genome wide association studies to link microbial interactions to host genetic variants and metabolic states. This research will produce a deep time host microbiome interactome model to identify microbial targets for disease intervention and characterize host microbial coevolution in human physiological adaptation.
full_text: The domain of mesoscale biology investigates networks of proteins between hosts and microbiomes but lacks understanding of assembly across species. Individual profiles of human proteins and microbial metagenomes are documented but architectures of interactions between organisms remain unmapped. This project investigates how networks of microbiomes and hosts reorganize over time to model targets for intervention of disease. The design of the study features a synthesis in three phases to model networks and integrate data of epidemiology. Methods include algorithms for alignment and tools of artificial intelligence such as AlphaFold-Multimer to model networks of phylogenetics. Results will be validated by utilizing computational filters to subtract artifacts of contamination and verifying pipelines with test datasets. The project utilizes the UK Biobank and the Human Microbiome Project alongside archives of ancient DNA and protein databases. Datasets will be integrated through alignment of sequences to map metagenomes and artificial intelligence to model interactions of proteins. The team addresses limitations of contaminant DNA by deploying algorithms and mathematical filters to remove artifacts of contamination. The proposed milestones encompass three phases consisting of data assembly and network modeling alongside integration of proteogenomic information. Cross disciplinary collaboration is required because analyzing vast volumes of data demands combined expertise in ecology and computational biology. The team will share findings through open access journals and publish pipelines on platforms of open science including GitHub. The team includes experts and postdoctoral researchers who will train students in disciplines of artificial intelligence and algorithmic optimization.

abstract_original:
The unexpected appearance of new biological properties often occurs at the mesoscale, where distinct biomolecules assemble into complex functional modules. While mesoscale organization within individual cells is increasingly well-characterized, the emergence of cross-species mesoscale architectures—specifically, the structural and functional protein-protein interaction networks between human hosts and their resident microbiomes—remains a profound mystery. Understanding how these emergent host-microbiome interfaces assemble and evolve is critical to deciphering human systemic adaptations, yet it has been severely limited by computational bottlenecks, the prevalence of uncharacterized 'dark' microbial taxa, and the historic siloing of human proteomics and microbial metagenomics.

We propose a multidisciplinary Working Group to conduct a community-scale synthesis of publicly available multi-omic datasets, answering fundamental questions about the evolutionary emergence of mesoscale host-microbe protein networks. Our project integrates massive, disparate public databases: high-resolution human genomic and plasma proteomic cohorts (e.g., UK Biobank, providing data on thousands of circulating human proteins and their genetic regulators) alongside vast repositories of modern and ancient human metagenomic data (e.g., the Human Microbiome Project, ancient dental calculus, and paleofeces databases). We will not generate new experimental data; rather, we will deploy a novel, transdisciplinary analytical strategy using AI and data science to synthesize these existing resources.

To overcome the immense computational challenge of cross-kingdom alignment, we will leverage state-of-the-art, ultra-fast protein sequence alignment algorithms and advanced phylogenetic network modeling to process massive short-read datasets at a fraction of traditional computational costs. This infrastructure will map millions of microbial sequences—including those from understudied and ancestral microbial lineages—into a functionally annotated protein space. Crucially, by applying rigorous, gold-standard computational bio-filters derived from low-biomass microbiome research protocols, we will systematically exclude environmental contamination, ensuring that the inferred cross-species interactomes represent genuine biological interfaces.

We will then utilize AI-driven structural predictions and proteogenomic integration frameworks, such as cis-anchored protein mapping and Mendelian randomization, to model how these microbial proteins physically and functionally interact with the host systemic proteome. By comparing these proteogenomic networks across deep evolutionary time (ancient vs. modern humans) and diverse metabolic states (e.g., caloric restriction, multi-disease outcomes), we will uncover how emergent mesoscale properties—such as multi-protein metabolic sinks, host-mimicking immune complexes, and novel signaling hubs—have appeared and reorganized under evolutionary and environmental pressures.

This synthesis requires the unique collaborative infrastructure of NCEMS, as it operates at a scale far beyond the capacity of any single laboratory. By bridging algorithmic phylogenetics, rigorous microbial ecology, and large-scale epidemiological proteomics, our Working Group will establish a new paradigm for studying biological emergence. The project strictly adheres to open science principles, committing to the FAIR release of all analytical pipelines, canonical network models, and integrated databases. Importantly, this initiative will cross-train a diverse cohort of trainees, equipping the next generation of data-savvy scientists with the transdisciplinary expertise required to navigate complex multi-omic integration, algorithmic optimization, and rigorous contamination control.

title: Mapping the Emergent Bacterial Condensome: Synthesizing Transcriptomic and Biophysical Data to Predict Mesoscale Organization in Pathogenesis and Stress Adaptation
title_norm: mapping the emergent bacterial condensome synthesizing transcriptomic and biophysical data to predict mesoscale organization in pathogenesis and stress adaptation
abstract_text: The mesoscale organization of bacterial cells relies on biomolecular condensates formed through liquid liquid phase separation, which govern crucial biological functions in cellular organization and stress response. However, knowledge remains incomplete regarding how in vivo monomer concentrations, stoichiometric ratios, gene expression fluctuations, and evolutionary mutations interact with structural biophysics to regulate condensate formation. To construct a bacterial condensome atlas and predictive computational platform, this research will apply artificial intelligence driven biophysical models and associative polymer theory to map sequence encoded interaction potentials against condition specific monomer concentrations. The project will integrate AlphaFold DB structural predictions with Gene Expression Omnibus RNA sequencing and PRIDE proteomics data, converting transcript abundances into monomer concentrations mapped onto critical concentration thresholds for phase separation. This framework will link genetic variance and transcript expression levels to concentration thresholds, enabling the direct prediction of biophysical phenotypes from standard sequencing data without requiring experimental assays.
full_text: This research explores the mesoscale organization of bacteria to understand how genetic variations control phase separation of biomolecular condensates. Bacteria form condensates during stress but the regulation of phase separation by monomer concentrations and structural biophysics remains incomplete. The study asks how transcriptomic changes induce phase separated networks to predict biophysical phenotypes directly from standard sequencing data. This computational synthesis maps sequence encoded potentials and overlays monomer concentrations to predict condensate formation from existing public datasets. The team applies artificial intelligence and associative polymer theory alongside machine learning algorithms within tools such as Nextflow. Results will be validated computationally through statistical methods and artificial intelligence protocols as well as error propagation models. Datasets include structural predictions from AlphaFold and RNA sequencing data from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) alongside proteomics from PRIDE. Proteomics data will convert transcript abundances into monomer concentrations to map onto critical concentration thresholds for phase separation. The limitations of inferring concentrations from transcriptomic data alone will be resolved by establishing translation rate scalars from proteomics. The successful execution of this demanding project requires combined expertise in the fields of bacterial evolutionary genomics and bioinformatics. This cross disciplinary collaboration integrates soft matter biophysics and associative polymer modeling to solve the required computational challenges. The team will publish open access results and share machine learning models through platforms like GitHub and Zenodo. The team includes biologists and data scientists alongside postdoctoral scholars receiving cross disciplinary mentoring in high performance computing.

abstract_original:
The mesoscale organization of bacterial cells represents a critical frontier in molecular and cellular biosciences. While eukaryotic cells heavily rely on membraneless organelles and biomolecular condensates formed via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), the role of these emergent mesoscale structures in bacteria is only beginning to be recognized. Recent evidence suggests that bacteria utilize transient biomolecular condensates to coordinate stress responses, compartmentalize RNA-protein networks, and regulate host-microbe interactions. However, a major puzzle remains: how do dynamic fluctuations in gene expression and evolutionary mutations act as biophysical switches to trigger or dissolve these mesoscale assemblies? Addressing this requires integrating the principles of soft matter biophysics with systems-level bacterial genomics.

We propose to form an NCEMS Working Group that synthesizes massive, publicly available transcriptomic, proteomic, and structural datasets to construct the first comprehensive atlas of the "bacterial condensome." This project strictly utilizes existing data, integrating thousands of bacterial RNA-seq datasets (from GEO and SRA) covering diverse physiological states—including antibiotic exposure, host colonization, and quorum sensing—with genome-wide structural predictions from AlphaFold DB and intrinsically disordered protein (IDP) databases. 

By leveraging AI-driven biophysical models and associative polymer theory, our cross-disciplinary team will computationally map the sequence-encoded interaction potentials of bacterial proteomes. We will then overlay dynamic monomer concentrations derived from publicly available transcriptomic and proteomic data. Because the internal architecture and formation of condensates are highly sensitive to instantaneous monomer concentrations and specific stoichiometry, combining expression flux data with biophysical phase-separation thresholds will allow us to predict the emergence of mesoscale structures across distinct bacterial cell states. 

Our synthesis approach will focus on three key objectives: (1) Answer novel questions regarding how global shifts in transcriptomic states drive the systems-level emergence of phase-separated networks during bacterial stress adaptation. (2) Solve long-standing puzzles regarding pathogenic evolution by analyzing how specific mutations—such as those altering virulence factors or disrupting multidrug efflux pumps—reprogram internal condensate architecture or stoichiometry to enhance pathogenesis. (3) Develop an open-source, reproducible computational platform that bridges evolutionary genomics and soft matter physics, allowing researchers to predict phase-separation events directly from RNA-seq and genomic isolate data.

This community-scale synthesis project fundamentally requires NCEMS support, as it transcends the capabilities of any single laboratory. It necessitates a deep transdisciplinary integration of bacterial evolutionary genomics, RNA-seq bioinformatics, and polymer biophysics. In adherence to open science principles, all resulting atlases, predictive AI models, and analytical pipelines will be freely distributed. Furthermore, the Working Group will provide intensive cross-training for postdocs and graduate students, cultivating a new generation of data-savvy scientists uniquely fluent in both complex population-level genomics and the biophysical principles of mesoscale cellular emergence.

title: Emergent Mesoscale Dynamics from Molecular Thermodynamics: Synthesizing Protein Mutational Landscapes and Single-Cell Interactomes
title_norm: emergent mesoscale dynamics from molecular thermodynamics synthesizing protein mutational landscapes and singlecell interactomes
abstract_text: Within computational systems biology and protein biophysics, mesoscale protein protein interaction networks and localized energetic perturbations represent crucial biological phenomena for interpreting extensive large scale interaction and cell type specific transcriptomic datasets. Biological models currently utilize static binary connections, leaving how localized thermodynamic changes propagate through cellular systems to alter network topology and emergent phenotypes entirely unresolved. To determine how mutational free energy changes alter network topology and how local expression buffers these thermodynamic defects, this project will simulate continuous thermodynamically weighted networks using graph theory, mass action modeling, and machine learning. The project will combine MaveDB and Protein Data Bank datasets to calculate variant specific free energies, applying these quantitative weights to STRING networks before overlaying Human Cell Atlas single cell transcriptomic data. This research will output dynamically weighted thermodynamic models incorporating cellular context, providing a quantitative mechanism to explain context dependent phenotypic variation and incomplete penetrance.
full_text: This computational systems biology project investigates how local thermodynamic perturbations of proteins alter network topology and cellular phenotypes. Existing databases document static protein protein interactions and fail to incorporate quantitative thermodynamic affinities within variable cellular environments. The study evaluates how mutation induced energetic changes alter interaction networks to explain context dependent variations of phenotypes. This in silico study calculates variant thermodynamic parameters to construct weighted networks and simulate context specific cellular behaviors. The team will apply graph theory via Python alongside mass action modeling and computational simulations of network dynamics. The team will validate analytical robustness through extensive statistical modeling and machine learning classifications of the simulated networks. The project utilizes mutational scans from MaveDB alongside structural models and single cell transcriptomics from the Human Cell Atlas. Researchers will calculate energetic weights from mutational data to construct networks before overlaying single cell transcriptomic expression profiles. This comprehensive data integration establishes functional mass action models based on local transcript abundances across distinct cell types. The proposed project executes three sequential phases encompassing thermodynamic parameterization and network construction alongside single cell functional contextualization. This extensive scope necessitates cross disciplinary collaboration to successfully integrate specialized expertise across protein biophysics and computational biology. The researchers will publicly release all synthesized databases via Zenodo and distribute open source analysis code through GitHub. The diverse collaborative team unites structural biophysicists and network biologists to provide cross disciplinary training for graduate students.

abstract_original:
A central challenge in the molecular and cellular biosciences is bridging the gap between single-molecule biophysics and systems-level cellular behavior. While the thermodynamic constraints governing the biosynthesis, folding, and trafficking of individual proteins—such as G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) and ion channels—are increasingly well-characterized, we lack a predictive understanding of how these molecular-level energetic properties scale up to shape mesoscale protein-protein interaction (PPI) networks. The unexpected appearance of new biological system properties, such as robust cellular homeostasis or the sudden collapse into pathological states like misfolding diseases and senescence, often originates at this poorly understood mesoscale level. 

This proposed NCEMS Working Group will synthesize three previously disconnected domains of publicly available data to uncover the thermodynamic rules governing mesoscale network emergence. Specifically, we will integrate (1) large-scale Deep Mutational Scanning (DMS) and biophysical datasets capturing sequence-to-function thermodynamic landscapes; (2) structural interactome repositories including AlphaFold-predicted multimeric interfaces and public PPI databases; and (3) cell-type-specific transcriptomic atlases derived from single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq). Our collaborative, transdisciplinary approach will proceed in three phases. First, we will aggregate and harmonize public DMS datasets with structural models to calculate how specific sequence variations alter the folding and binding free energies of membrane and intracellular proteins. Second, we will leverage advanced network science methodologies to map these energetic parameters onto mesoscale protein complexes. Rather than treating PPI networks as static binary connections, we will construct dynamically weighted, "energetic networks" that model the thermodynamic coupling between interacting proteins. Third, we will contextualize these biophysical networks using public scRNA-seq data. By applying gene regulatory network inference and cell-type-specific co-expression data, we will evaluate how the buffering capacity of different cellular environments modulates the penetrance of thermodynamic defects—explaining, for example, why identical mutations cause membrane supertrafficking in one cell type but induce targeted degradation or inflammatory stress responses in another.

This project requires the unique support of NCEMS, as it demands a synthesis of expertise in protein biophysics, structural biology, evolutionary dynamics, and computational systems biology that far exceeds the capabilities of a single laboratory. The Working Group will adhere strictly to open science principles, releasing a novel, open-source analytical framework capable of predicting emergent cellular behaviors from primary sequence variation. Furthermore, the project will serve as a premier training ground for the next generation of data-savvy scientists, providing postdocs and graduate students with cross-disciplinary expertise in synthesizing molecular thermodynamics, machine learning, and single-cell systems biology.

abstract_original:
Biomolecular condensates represent a canonical example of mesoscale emergence in biology, where non-stoichiometric assemblies of RNAs and proteins phase separate to form dynamically regulated, membraneless organelles. While the compositional landscape of condensates—such as stress granules and nuclear speckles—is increasingly well-documented, a fundamental mechanistic gap remains: we lack a predictive understanding of how atomic-scale RNA-protein interactions and protein sequence determinants scale up to dictate emergent, mesoscale material properties like viscoelasticity, interfacial tension, and dynamic subcellular trafficking. Currently, a massive amount of disconnected, publicly available data exists across diverse domains. These include high-resolution structural repositories (PDB, EMDB) capturing RNA-protein complexes, high-throughput pooled imaging datasets linking protein sequences to condensate phenotypes, and extensive dynamic spatial proteomics (e.g., BioID, APEX, and proximity-labeling networks) tracking proteome trafficking. 

We propose an NCEMS Working Group to synthesize these disparate, multi-modal datasets into a unified, predictive computational framework of mesoscale condensate emergence. Relying entirely on existing publicly available data, our transdisciplinary team will bridge computational structural biology, RNA modeling, soft matter physics, and cellular proteomics. First, we will leverage advanced macromolecular modeling (e.g., Rosetta-based frameworks) and deep learning algorithms to extract high-confidence structural signatures—such as RNA-protein interaction interfaces, multivalent valency maps, and RNA folding architectures—from existing cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) maps and structural databases. Second, we will map these structural metrics onto dynamic, spatial interactomes derived from public proximity-labeling proteomics datasets. This synthesis will allow us to reconstruct the precise spatiotemporal trafficking networks of phase-separating proteins and their RNA scaffolds across varying cellular conditions, such as oxidative stress and environmental fluctuations.

Finally, we will integrate soft matter physics principles to correlate these derived structural networks with the tunable, emergent material properties documented in public high-throughput imaging screens. By identifying the underlying "grammar" of multi-component condensate networks, we aim to solve long-standing puzzles regarding how specific sequence properties and chaperone interactions dictate the assembly, maintenance, and dissolution of these mesoscale compartments. 

This synthesis project requires the unique collaborative environment of NCEMS, as it extends beyond the computational or biological capacity of a single lab. It will yield an open-access, integrated database and predictive analytical pipeline linking atomic structures to emergent cellular phenotypes. Furthermore, it will directly address the NCEMS mission by developing a new analytical strategy for understanding mesoscale biological systems, while providing a rich, collaborative training ground for postdocs and graduate students in the integration of structural bioinformatics, AI-driven macromolecular modeling, and spatial omics data.

abstract_text: This research domain investigates the mesoscale spatial organization of biomolecular condensates and the physical properties of phase separating intrinsically disordered proteins, phenomena critical for understanding binary liquid liquid phase separation outcomes. This project will construct a predictive computational framework that maps primary sequences to emergent structural properties by applying natural language processing, transformer neural networks, equilibrium field theory, and coarse grained molecular dynamics simulations to existing public datasets. Data from PhaSepDB, DisProt, AlphaFold DB, EMDB, and the Protein Data Bank will be extracted and standardized into a single relational database aligning primary protein sequences with physical measurements using a common ontology. This framework will provide a novel method to quantitatively calculate soft matter physics profiles and structural behaviors of condensates based on sequence data rather than qualitative observations.

Biomolecular condensates represent a primary mode of mesoscale spatial organization across all domains of life, governing processes ranging from eukaryotic stress adaptation to bacterial subcellular compartmentalization. While recent years have seen an explosion of data cataloging phase-separating proteins, predicting the emergent physical properties of these assemblies—such as ultrastructural organization, emulsion stability, and tunable viscoelasticity—from primary sequence remains a critical frontier. Current efforts largely focus on binary predictions of liquid-liquid phase separation, failing to capture the intricate biophysical rules that dictate how condensates dynamically respond to environmental fluctuations, resist coalescence, and maintain complex multiphase architectures within the crowded cellular milieu.

This working group proposes a community-scale synthesis project to decode the pan-domain molecular grammar underlying condensate ultrastructure and mesoscale emergence. By aggregating and synthesizing disparate, publicly available datasets—including curated phase-separation databases (PhaSepDB, CD-CODE), intrinsically disordered protein (IDP) sequence repositories (DisProt), structural data (AlphaFold DB, EMDB for cryo-ET maps), and thousands of published in vitro biophysical measurements (phase diagrams, zeta potentials, and rheological parameters)—we will construct a unified, predictive framework of condensate physics. In strict adherence to the NCEMS mandate, our approach relies entirely on the integration of existing multi-omics, structural, and biophysical data, requiring no new experimental generation.

To achieve this, we will combine artificial intelligence with physics-driven multiscale computational modeling. First, we will develop a machine-learning pipeline to mine sequence features, specifically mapping the 'stickers-and-spacers' valency and electrostatic charge patterning of IDPs across diverse biological kingdoms. We will correlate these specific sequence grammars with documented emergent behaviors, such as RNA-induced conformational switching, multiphase coexistence, and hydration-dependent structural transitions. Second, we will leverage these synthesized datasets to parameterize high-throughput, sequence-dependent coarse-grained molecular models. This will allow us to simulate mesoscale phenomena—such as long-ranged electrostatic repulsion, surface charge-driven size control, and fusion propensity—at an unprecedented scale. By triangulating these physical simulations with published ultrastructural readouts, we will determine how localized structural transitions and net charge within dense phases dictate higher-order cellular functions.

This transdisciplinary effort uniquely bridges structural biology, computational biophysics, and soft matter physics. The project requires the NCEMS infrastructure to facilitate the large-scale integration of highly heterogeneous data types (from atomic coordinates to rheological values) and to support the collaborative computational demands of parameterizing pan-domain physical models. Ultimately, this synthesis will solve long-standing puzzles regarding how intrinsically disordered sequences encode mesoscale architecture, generating predictive tools that map the physical rules of cellular adaptation. Furthermore, the project will train a diverse new generation of data-savvy biophysicists equipped to navigate the intersection of machine learning, polymer physics, and structural biology, fully embracing open science principles by releasing all analytical workflows, trained AI models, and coarse-grained parameters to the global community.

title: AI-Driven Synthesis of Mesoscale Chromatin and Protein Networks to Decode Emergent Cellular Plasticity and Immune Evasion
title_norm: aidriven synthesis of mesoscale chromatin and protein networks to decode emergent cellular plasticity and immune evasion
abstract_text: Cancer plasticity, therapeutic resistance, and tumor immune evasion depend upon mesoscale cellular structures like 3D chromatin architectures and protein protein interaction networks, though vast multi omics datasets remain isolated across disciplines. How distributed genetic sequence variations alter mesoscale assemblies remains poorly understood because genomic structural variations, protein complex stability, and immunological single cell profiles are rarely modeled together. This data synthesis project will build a computational framework linking 1D genetic sequence variations to cellular immune escape by predicting chromatin reorganization and protein dynamics using deep learning, graph neural networks, and statistical learning. The study will integrate ENCODE, TCGA, and single cell transcriptome repositories via graph neural networks to merge genomic, transcriptomic, and deep mutational scanning data into comprehensive 3D chromatin and protein network models. The resulting computational framework will explain cancer adaptation and immune checkpoint variability by characterizing systems level mesoscale networks rather than analyzing isolated single molecules.
full_text: This project investigates cancer plasticity to understand how distributed genomic variations and secondary modifiers alter mesoscale cellular structures. Extensive omics data exist but remain isolated without connecting structural variations of genomes to stability of protein complexes. The proposed study builds a computational framework to model cancer adaptation by analyzing mesoscale cellular structures instead of isolated molecules. This data synthesis project maps chromatin reorganization from genomic variations to predict dynamics of protein complexes and immune escape. The analytical strategy utilizes statistical learning alongside deep learning for image analysis and models of graph neural networks. Results will undergo validation in silico using ensemble scoring functions and machine learning frameworks without de novo experiments. abstract_original: The emergence of complex cellular phenotypes—such as tumor immune evasion and rapid therapeutic resistance—is fundamentally driven by interactions at the mesoscale. Rather than arising from isolated molecular events, these adaptive traits emerge from the dynamic reorganization of 3D chromatin architectures (e.g., enhancer-promoter hubs and extrachromosomal DNA assemblies) and the subsequent rewiring of mesoscale protein-protein interaction networks. Despite the sheer volume of public multi-omics data, understanding how distributed genetic variations and secondary genetic modifiers synergistically perturb these mesoscale assemblies to drive variable disease expressivity remains a long-standing mystery. This Working Group proposes a community-scale synthesis project to decode the multiscale mechanisms underlying cancer plasticity and immune-checkpoint efficacy. By synthesizing vast, publicly available datasets—including ENCODE, TCGA, CCLE/DepMap, DICE, and large-scale CRISPR/Cas9 cellular screens—we will build an AI-driven computational framework that connects 1D sequence variation to emergent cellular outcomes. Importantly, this project relies exclusively on existing data and requires a transdisciplinary integration of machine learning, computational structural biology, 3D genomics, and tumor immunology. Our synthesis approach is structured across three integrated aims. First, we will map how primary driver mutations and secondary genetic modifiers dictate lineage-specific 3D genome organization. By leveraging single-cell transcriptomics, single-cell eQTL data, and 3D chromatin conformation maps, we will employ advanced sequence-to-function statistical learning to model the assembly of mesoscale regulatory hubs. We will specifically focus on how extrachromosomal DNA and structural variants override traditional topological boundaries to drive oncogenic and immunosuppressive transcriptional programs. Second, we will bridge the gap between 3D chromatin dysregulation and mesoscale protein complex dynamics. Using positive-unlabeled (PU) machine learning and ensemble-based scoring functions for protein-protein docking, we will predict how altered gene expression profiles and variant-driven misfolding events reshape protein interaction networks. This will allow us to map the hierarchy of protein complex stability and identify interaction nodes that act as functional hubs during cellular adaptation. Finally, we will link these mesoscale reconfigurations to emergent cellular outcomes, specifically the variable expressivity of immune escape in T cell subsets and breast cancer models. By analyzing transcriptomic and structural tumor-immune interaction networks, we will pinpoint the epigenetic and structural determinants that curtail targeted therapy and immunotherapy efficacy. This project directly aligns with the NCEMS mission to investigate emergent mesoscale phenomena through AI and data synthesis. The collaboration merges expertise in single-cell regulatory genomics, precision oncology, evolutionary genetic modifiers, and computational structural biology—a synergy beyond the scope of any single laboratory. Adhering to gold-standard open science practices, all predictive models, ensemble classifiers, and annotated multiscale networks will be distributed via public web portals. Furthermore, this Working Group will provide rigorous, cross-disciplinary training for a diverse cohort of trainees, equipping the next generation of data-savvy scientists to lead multiscale biological synthesis.

title: Uncovering Emergent Rules of Mesoscale Organelle Remodeling by Integrating Volumetric Imaging Atlases and Stochastic Biophysical Models via Optimal Transport
title_norm: uncovering emergent rules of mesoscale organelle remodeling by integrating volumetric imaging atlases and stochastic biophysical models via optimal transport
abstract_text: Understanding cytoskeleton driven organelle remodeling, including centriole symmetry breaking and ciliary deciliation, is critically important within mesoscale cellular architecture to connect cataloged microscale molecular constituents with whole cell structural and dynamic datasets. This project will determine how microscale cytoskeletal interactions dictate mesoscale organelle remodeling using a computational pipeline that extracts three dimensional morphometrics to constrain stochastic agent based biophysical simulations via Markov Chain Monte Carlo parameter estimation. This approach will integrate whole cell volumetric imaging and live cell time series from EMPIAR and the Allen Cell Observatory using deep learning auto segmentation and Gromov Wasserstein algorithms to generate unified consensus trajectories. This generalized methodology will formally link macroscopic cellular imaging data to microscopic biophysical parameters, providing a foundational framework to evaluate complex processes like organelle shedding and biogenesis site selection.
full_text: This project mathematically integrates heterogeneous biological datasets to determine how microscale cytoskeletal interactions control macroscopic organelle architecture and remodeling. The primary objective determines how microscale interactions dictate organelle remodeling by formally linking macroscopic imaging to microscopic parameters. The computational pipeline extracts morphometrics from static images and aligns temporal data to constrain agent based biophysical simulations. Key methods include segmentation of images via deep learning and modified Gromov-Wasserstein metrics alongside Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) estimation. The team will validate simulation outputs by reproducing empirical Fused Gromov-Wasserstein consensus trajectories derived from public biological datasets. Data sources include volumetric imaging of whole cells and live cell time series from EMPIAR and the Allen Cell Observatory. Deep learning algorithms extract morphometrics from static images while optimal transport algorithms align heterogeneous temporal data into unified trajectories. The team resolves differences in spatial resolution and temporal frequency by applying modified Gromov-Wasserstein algorithms to align state spaces. The ambitious methodology spans computer vision and optimal transport mathematics alongside agent based biophysics and organelle cell biology. This broad integration of diverse scientific disciplines exceeds the expertise of any single laboratory and requires collaboration across disciplines. The researchers will share harmonized datasets via Zenodo and deposit code with permissive licenses within Docker containers on GitHub. The diverse team includes organelle biologists and computational mathematicians while providing training across disciplines for postdoctoral scholars and graduate students.
