The emergence of mesoscale cellular architecture—such as the dynamic assembly, architectural scaling, and targeted shedding of organelles—relies on the continuous reorganization of underlying cytoskeletal networks. While the molecular constituents, such as actin, microtubules, and motor proteins, are heavily studied, the biophysical rules dictating how these stochastic microscale interactions scale up to control whole-organelle structural decisions (e.g., centriole symmetry breaking, rapid ciliary deciliation, and cytokinetic ring compaction) remain deeply elusive. The recent explosion of publicly available volumetric imaging atlases and multidimensional live-cell time-series datasets presents an unprecedented opportunity to solve this long-standing puzzle. However, these repositories are highly heterogeneous in spatial resolution, temporal frequency, and imaging modality, preventing traditional analytical approaches from extracting unifying biophysical principles. 

This Working Group proposes to uncover the emergent properties of cytoskeleton-driven organelle remodeling through the community-scale synthesis of existing, publicly available whole-cell imaging and time-series datasets (such as those from EMPIAR, the Allen Cell Observatory, and systematically curated cell anatomy literature databases). We will not generate new experimental data; rather, we will bridge the gap between static, high-resolution structural snapshots and complex, dynamic live-cell trajectories. 

To achieve this synthesis, our transdisciplinary team will integrate AI-driven image analysis with advanced mathematical modeling. First, we will deploy deep learning auto-segmentation pipelines to extract quantitative 3D morphometrics—such as surface curvature, volume, and cytoskeletal network connectivity—from vast datasets of whole-cell soft X-ray and electron tomograms. Second, to synthesize dynamic temporal data across varying experimental platforms, we will implement scalable Gromov-Wasserstein optimal transport metrics. This innovative mathematical framework allows us to align unequally spaced, multidimensional biological time series into a unified state space, calculating barycenters that represent consensus trajectories of mesoscale organelle remodeling.

These generalized structural trajectories will subsequently serve as rigorous empirical constraints for stochastic, agent-based biophysical models. By simulating the intricate interactions between cytoskeletal filaments and diverse motor protein populations, we will computationally test competing hypotheses regarding organelle biogenesis and disassembly. To efficiently explore the vast parameter space of these constrained models, we will utilize Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) parameter estimation, directly linking computational outputs to the synthetic optimal transport trajectories derived from public data. This closed-loop analytical strategy will reveal how specific microscale parameter shifts (e.g., altered motor binding kinetics or localized substrate depletion) spontaneously trigger macroscopic morphological changes like whole-cilium shedding or single-site centriole biogenesis.

Addressing these fundamental questions of mesoscale emergence requires the unique collaborative infrastructure of NCEMS, as this synthesis spans computer vision, optimal transport mathematics, agent-based biophysics, and organelle cell biology—a scope far beyond the capabilities of any individual laboratory. Adhering strictly to open science principles, all integrated datasets, optimal transport algorithms, and parameterized biophysical models will be published openly. Finally, this project will provide immersive cross-disciplinary training for graduate students and postdocs, preparing a new workforce of data-savvy scientists capable of interrogating biological emergence through the integration of AI and complex systems mathematics.

title: Decoding the Emergence of Mesoscale Regulatory Networks Driven by Transposable Elements through Cross-Species Epigenomic Data Synthesis

abstract_text: Transposable elements supply transcription factor binding sites that shape mammalian mesoscale chromatin structures and regulatory networks, making their computational epigenomic analysis vital for understanding evolutionary biology in systems like multi lineage hematopoiesis. However, extreme sequence divergence and sequence repetition prevent existing comparative genomic models from explaining how species specific transposable element insertions transition into coordinated mesoscale chromatin regulatory networks. To discover how grouped transposable elements form enhancer clusters driving lineage specific phenotypes, this project will synthesize harmonized public data using domain adaptive neural networks with adversarial training and epigenomic segmentation algorithms to reconstruct regulatory networks. Epigenomic datasets sourced from ENCODE, the Sequence Read Archive, and the Gene Expression Omnibus will undergo standardized processing and multi track segmentation to generate a unified registry of cross species regulatory elements. This research will provide a novel computational method for cross species epigenomic imputation, establishing transposable elements as collaborative structural components of genome evolution determining hematopoietic cellular phenotypes.

The synthesis of fragmented data from public repositories demands extensive computational infrastructure to process information on a large scale. The scope of this project requires cross disciplinary collaboration to provide combined expertise in machine learning and evolutionary biology. The researchers will share all datasets and processing code under open source licenses on platforms such as Zenodo. The team includes specialists of artificial intelligence and graduate students who will receive cross disciplinary instruction in deep learning.
rephrased_abstract: Transposable elements supply transcription factor binding sites that shape mammalian mesoscale chromatin structures and regulatory networks, making their computational epigenomic analysis vital for understanding evolutionary biology in systems like multi lineage hematopoiesis. However, extreme sequence divergence and sequence repetition prevent existing comparative genomic models from explaining how species specific transposable element insertions transition into coordinated mesoscale chromatin regulatory networks. To discover how grouped transposable elements form enhancer clusters driving lineage specific phenotypes, this project will synthesize harmonized public data using domain adaptive neural networks with adversarial training and epigenomic segmentation algorithms to reconstruct regulatory networks. Epigenomic datasets sourced from ENCODE, the Sequence Read Archive, and the Gene Expression Omnibus will undergo standardized processing and multi track segmentation to generate a unified registry of cross species regulatory elements. This research will provide a novel computational method for cross species epigenomic imputation, establishing transposable elements as collaborative structural components of genome evolution determining hematopoietic cellular phenotypes.
abstract_original:
Emergence in biological systems frequently stems from the spatial and functional organization of individual molecular interactions into higher-order mesoscale architectures. In molecular biology, the clustering of transcription factor (TF) binding events within dynamic chromatin landscapes forms robust regulatory domains that control cell-type identity. A long-standing mystery in cellular sciences is how these complex mesoscale regulatory networks emerge evolutionarily to drive genomic innovation. Transposable elements (TEs)—highly repetitive DNA sequences that mobilize throughout genomes—are increasingly hypothesized to be primary engines of this emergence, functioning as distributed, ready-to-use TF binding modules that nucleate new regulatory hubs. However, the collective mechanism by which species-specific TEs collaboratively rewire chromatin at the mesoscale remains critically under-explored.

A major barrier to understanding TE-driven emergence is methodological: sequence divergence and the repetitive nature of TEs severely confound cross-species alignment and predictive modeling. Individual research groups lack the diverse expertise and computational infrastructure required to synthesize the vast arrays of fragmented, publicly available epigenomic data necessary to resolve this puzzle. To address this, our Working Group proposes a community-scale synthesis of ultra-high-resolution, publicly available epigenomic datasets—spanning ChIP-seq, ChIP-exo, ATAC-seq, and DNase-seq—across multiple mammalian lineages. 

By uniting experts in computational epigenomics, evolutionary biology, and machine learning, this NCEMS-supported collaboration will deploy advanced domain-adaptive neural networks to synthesize these diverse datasets. These sophisticated AI architectures are specifically designed to correct for evolutionary domain shifts caused by species-specific repeats, enabling accurate, cross-species prediction and imputation of TF binding and chromatin states. Applying integrative state annotation algorithms across these standardized datasets, we aim to answer three fundamental questions: (1) How do coordinated arrays of TEs collectively nucleate emergent mesoscale chromatin structures, such as robust enhancer clusters? (2) What are the specific sequence and chromatin determinants that allow a newly transposed element to transition along a continuum—from an isolated molecular binding event to an integrated, cooperative node within a cell-type-specific regulatory network? (3) How do these mesoscale structural innovations dictate higher-order cellular outcomes, using well-profiled systems like multi-lineage hematopoiesis as our model framework?

This project fully embraces the NCEMS mandate for open science and reproducible synthesis. Our pipelines will be embedded within flexible, web-based bioinformatics management platforms (e.g., Galaxy-integrated environments) to ensure rigorous quality control and full reproducibility across thousands of public datasets. Furthermore, the Working Group will serve as an essential training incubator. By embedding graduate students and postdoctoral researchers in a collaborative, transdisciplinary ecosystem, we will train a diverse, data-savvy workforce. Trainees will gain unparalleled hands-on experience at the intersection of artificial intelligence, high-throughput epigenomics, and evolutionary theory, ultimately equipping the next generation of scientists to decode the emergent properties of the cell.

title: Mapping Emergent Mesoscale Architectures by Synthesizing the Global Crosslinking Mass Spectrometry and Genetic Interactome Archives
title_norm: mapping emergent mesoscale architectures by synthesizing the global crosslinking mass spectrometry and genetic interactome archives
abstract_text: Mesoscale biology investigates the structural architecture and dynamic interactions of multi protein assemblies, rendering abundant physical distance constraints from crosslinking mass spectrometry datasets essential for advancing structural systems biology. Current systems biology models lack spatial constraints and structural techniques lack cellular context, while existing mass spectrometry datasets remain highly fragmented and rely on inconsistent error estimation models. The primary objective is to synthesize crosslinking mass spectrometry data into a three dimensional tissue specific interactome; computationally, this project will extract constraints using sequence search engines, integrate AlphaFold2 Multimer predictions, and apply network propagation algorithms. Standardized crosslinking measurements from ProteomeXchange and PRIDE will be merged with tissue specific abundance atlases and Reactome databases, paired with structural predictions, and overlaid with UK Biobank genome wide association data. This research will output standardized methodologies for structural multi omics integration, providing a mechanistic explanation for how pleiotropic genetic variants disrupt physical architecture and cause cellular dysfunction.

abstract_original:
The transition from individual biomolecules to functional organelles is governed by emergent mesoscale properties, which are largely driven by dynamic protein-protein interactions (PPIs) and multi-protein assemblies. While traditional systems biology has mapped cellular networks, these models often lack the spatial resolution required to understand the physical constraints and architectural emergence of mesoscale complexes. Over the past decade, Crosslinking Mass Spectrometry (XL-MS) has emerged as a powerful technique to capture direct physical distance constraints within and between proteins in their native cellular environments. Thousands of such datasets currently reside in public repositories. However, these datasets remain severely fragmented, lacking harmonized error estimation, standardized metadata, and integration with broader cellular networks, thereby obscuring our view of mesoscale biology.

We propose a community-scale synthesis project to systematically re-process, harmonize, and integrate the global public archive of XL-MS data to uncover the structural architecture of emergent mesoscale assemblies. By leveraging standardized frameworks such as the Universal Spectrum Identifier (USI) and the Proteomics Standards Initiative Extended FASTA Format (PEFF), our transdisciplinary working group will extract and validate high-confidence, spatially resolved PPIs from billions of mass spectra deposited across global repositories like ProteomeXchange. We will synthesize these structural distance constraints with existing tissue-specific proteomic atlases and curated pathway knowledgebases to build a comprehensive, 3D-informed interactome of the human cell.

This synthesized structural interactome will allow us to address long-standing questions regarding mesoscale emergence: How do localized protein interactions dynamically scale to form stable multimeric complexes and organelle contact sites across different human tissues? To connect these biophysical properties to human health, we will integrate our structural networks with genome-wide association study (GWAS) data. Using network-propagation analysis, we will map how disease-associated and highly pleiotropic genetic variants specifically perturb the physical architecture of these mesoscale assemblies, altering their emergent properties and downstream cellular outcomes.

This project perfectly aligns with the NCEMS mission. It relies entirely on the synthesis of existing, publicly available data, bypassing de novo experimental data generation. The massive computational scale of re-analyzing disparate XL-MS archives, combined with the required cross-disciplinary fusion of biophysics, bioinformatics standardization, and network genetics, makes this endeavor impossible for a single laboratory. By leveraging NCEMS support, we will assemble a diverse team of structural biophysicists, data scientists, and systems biologists. In strict adherence to open science principles, all harmonized datasets, spatial networks, and programmatic pipelines will be disseminated via public REST APIs and integrated into community resources. Furthermore, the project will serve as a premier training ground, equipping early-career researchers with advanced skills in multi-omics integration, structural modeling, and big data harmonization, ultimately training the next generation of data-savvy scientists to explore the frontiers of mesoscale biology.

title: Uncovering Mesoscale Emergence in Microbial Dark Matter through AI-Driven Synthesis of Metagenomic and Mass Spectrometry Data
title_norm: uncovering mesoscale emergence in microbial dark matter through aidriven synthesis of metagenomic and mass spectrometry data
abstract_text: In microbial ecosystems, operons encode mesoscale multi enzyme protein complexes that generate specialized metabolites, representing an important biological phenomenon that yields extensive public omics data from uncultured organisms. The current scientific gap is the inability to connect novel microbial protein structures to their chemical products because of isolated datasets and restricted culture biased reference databases. This project will build a reference free computational network connecting uncultured microbiome genetic sequences to biochemical outputs by synthesizing datasets using alignment free neural networks, evolutionary reconstruction models, and machine learning association models. The research will integrate Sequence Read Archive metagenomes with PRIDE spectra by applying machine learning and large scale co occurrence analyses to paired multi omic metadata. This project will produce a reference free computational network that maps unannotated genetic information directly to chemical phenotypes, enabling the identification of previously unrecognized biological and chemical data.
full_text: The study of microbial ecosystems struggles to connect uncharacterized protein complexes and specialized metabolites across separated datasets and restricted databases. Abundant omics datasets reveal multi enzyme complexes and metabolites but culture biased reference databases leave uncultured biological structures unidentified. The proposed study builds a reference free computational network to map unannotated genetic sequences directly to novel chemical phenotypes. This computational synthesis analyzes public metagenomic and mass spectrometry datasets before integrating them via machine learning and joint occurrence analyses. The team applies alignment free neural networks and machine learning association models alongside evolutionary reconstruction frameworks and query languages. The team will benchmark computational models against characterized biosynthetic gene clusters and known mass spectrometry spectra using statistical bootstrapping. Datasets include metagenomes from the Sequence Read Archive and MG-RAST alongside spectra from Global Natural Products Social Molecular Networking. The project integrates these datasets using machine learning models and large scale occurrence analyses of paired multi omic metadata. The team mitigates culture dependent database biases by deploying alignment free deep learning models and reference free pattern matching languages. Project milestones include a genomic discovery phase and a mass spectrometry pattern mining phase before multi omic synthesis. Cross disciplinary collaboration is necessary because dataset integration requires combined expertise in microbial ecology and artificial intelligence alongside software engineering. The project will share open source code on GitHub and deposit FAIR compliant data into Zenodo while providing virtual workshops. Graduate students and postdoctoral fellows will join ecologists and bioinformaticians to receive cross disciplinary training in genomics and artificial intelligence.

abstract_original: Microbial communities exhibit remarkable emergent properties, orchestrating complex biochemical dialogues that shape host and environmental systems. These behaviors emerge primarily at the mesoscale, where diverse operons dictate the assembly of multi-enzyme protein complexes. These mesoscale structures subsequently synthesize heavily modified, highly diverse specialized metabolites. However, the vast majority of this biochemical repertoire remains hidden as biological "dark matter," largely because traditional analytical approaches rely on heavily biased reference databases. Consequently, our understanding of how novel mesoscale complexes emerge and drive chemical diversity remains fundamentally fragmented. To solve this long-standing puzzle, we propose the Working Group for Multi-Omic Synthesis of Mesoscale Emergence. This project will execute a community-scale synthesis of massive, publicly available but currently siloed datasets: uncultured metagenomic sequences and billions of untargeted mass spectrometry (MS/MS) proteomics and metabolomics spectra. Because this synthesis requires advanced cross-disciplinary data science spanning microbial evolutionary genomics and computational mass spectrometry, it fundamentally necessitates the collaborative environment and computational infrastructure provided by NCEMS. Our working group will pioneer a reference-free computational ecosystem to link the genetic blueprints of uncultured microbiomes to their emergent mesoscale assemblies and resulting chemical outputs. First, we will utilize alignment-free deep learning architectures—such as Siamese neural networks—to analyze global public metagenomes. This will enable the identification of shared functional domains and the evolutionary reconstruction of complex ancestral operons, bypassing the limitations of known functional annotations. Second, we will deploy expressive pattern-matching algorithms and mass spectrometry query languages to mine over a billion public MS/MS spectra. This computational search will identify structural patterns of uncharacterized metabolites and peptide fragments produced by these previously hidden operon-encoded assemblies. By synthesizing these independent multi-omic data streams, the working group will construct a unified "Genomic-to-Chemical Mesoscale Graph." This integrated network will answer fundamental questions regarding how novel multi-protein structures emerge across microbial lineages and how variations in these mesoscale assemblies translate into unappreciated chemical diversity, such as complex lipid or polyamine modifications. This synthesis will directly link primary molecular sequence data to emergent community-level biochemical phenotypes. The working group is entirely committed to open science principles; all unified data structures, predictive neural network models, and MS/MS querying workflows will be published as open-source computational tools. Furthermore, this initiative emphasizes vital workforce development, providing dedicated training for a diverse cohort of postdocs and graduate students at the intersection of computational multi-omics, deep learning, and mesoscale biology. By bridging disparate biological disciplines, this project will reveal the structural and chemical emergence of microbial ecosystems while maximizing the latent value of public omics data.

title: Evolutionary Origins of Mesoscale Signaling: An AI-Driven Synthesis of Exascale Dynamics and Ancestral Allosteric Networks
title_norm: evolutionary origins of mesoscale signaling an aidriven synthesis of exascale dynamics and ancestral allosteric networks
abstract_text: Molecular biology research focuses on mesoscale emergence and allosteric regulation in modular signaling hubs, specifically nuclear receptors and Src family kinases, to unite large isolated biological datasets. This computational data synthesis project will integrate phylogenomic, structural, and functional data using maximum likelihood phylogenetics, Markov State Models, and Graph Neural Networks to map evolutionary dynamic coupling networks and predict emergent cellular phenotypes. The project will synthesize datasets from UniProt, Pfam, and Protein Data Bank by mapping molecular dynamics metrics onto structural ensembles to construct dynamic network graphs that predict ChEMBL and GEO functional data. This novel framework will shift protein modeling from static structures to dynamic networks, providing a predictive resource that directly advances downstream synthetic biology, protein engineering, and pharmacology.
full_text: Abundant datasets of structural sequences remain isolated and lack a unified framework to connect atomistic dynamics with mesoscale phenotypes. The primary question maps dynamic networks to predict cellular phenotypes and provide a novel framework for engineering of proteins. This computational synthesis project reconstructs ancestral structures and extracts network metrics to train models for predictions of cellular phenotypes. Key methods combine AlphaFold2 with Markov State Models and Graph Neural Networks to analyze the dynamics of protein assemblies. Results will be validated using methods for quantification of uncertainty including Bayesian neural networks to generate confidence intervals for predictions. The project will utilize datasets from the Protein Data Bank (PDB) and UniProt alongside functional information from GEO and ChEMBL. Distinct datasets will be integrated by mapping network metrics onto structural ensembles to create graphs for neural network predictions. The absence of empirical structures will be mitigated using algorithms for structural prediction alongside techniques for quantification of uncertainty. Synthesizing atomistic dynamics with functional genomics demands extensive computational resources and specialized personnel across multiple domains of scientific expertise. This expansive scope requires a cross disciplinary collaboration because the necessary technical capabilities exceed the capacity of single laboratories. The team will share data on Zenodo and publish open source code on GitHub using standard frameworks for containerization. The team includes three postdoctoral fellows and three graduate students who will receive advanced training in models of machine learning.

abstract_original: The unexpected emergence of complex cellular behaviors from biomolecular interactions remains a central challenge in molecular biology. At the mesoscale, modular signaling hubs—such as nuclear receptors (NRs) and multi-domain kinases—translate diverse metabolic and environmental cues into precise transcriptional cascades. Although the community has generated vast amounts of isolated structural and functional data, the dynamic mechanisms by which atomic-scale ligand binding allosterically dictates the recruitment of massive, multimeric co-regulator complexes at the mesoscale remain obscured. We hypothesize that this mesoscale emergence is governed by conserved, dynamic 'wiring diagrams' sculpted over evolutionary time. Currently, thousands of static structures, petabytes of open-access exascale molecular dynamics (MD) trajectories, and deep phylogenomic sequence alignments exist across disparate public repositories. However, they have never been systematically integrated. This Working Group will synthesize public structural data (PDB), open-source MD trajectories (leveraging distributed computing repositories like Folding@home), and expansive phylogenomic databases to elucidate the evolutionary and dynamic origins of mesoscale signaling. We will construct a transdisciplinary, AI-driven pipeline that maps atomic-level conformational fluctuations to emergent cellular transcriptional outputs. Our project is structured around three integrated synthesis aims. First, we will fuse phylogenomic databases with structural ensembles to reconstruct the ancestral sequence space of key modular proteins, including nuclear receptors and Src-family kinases. Leveraging machine learning models, we will synthesize open-access structural data to predict ancestral conformational ensembles, bridging evolutionary history with structural biophysics. Second, we will mine distributed computing datasets to calculate network-based dynamic metrics, specifically adapting the Dynamic Flexibility Index (DFI) and Dynamic Coupling Index (DCI), across these evolutionary trajectories. This massive data synthesis will reveal how functionally critical rigid hinges and flexible active sites migrate, couple, and co-evolve to support novel ligand specificities and enable mesoscale complex formation. Third, we will develop machine learning models that link these dynamic coupling architectures directly to publicly available transcriptomic and high-throughput functional assay datasets (e.g., GEO, ChEMBL). This framework will predict how specific mutation- or ligand-induced shifts in allosteric networks cascade into emergent phenotypic states, such as metabolic reprogramming or disease pathologies. This community-scale synthesis relies exclusively on existing, publicly available data, bypassing de novo experimental generation in strict accordance with the NCEMS mandate. By bridging evolutionary protein dynamics, receptor pharmacology, and exascale computational biophysics, this project demands a transdisciplinary collaboration far surpassing the capacity of any single lab. The initiative champions open science by committing to publish all AI models, dynamic network maps, and synthesized phylogenetic trajectories in robust, open-access portals. Furthermore, it addresses the NCEMS mission by providing rich cross-training opportunities for a diverse cohort of graduate students and postdocs, equipping the next generation of researchers with essential skills in data science, generative AI, and multi-scale biological synthesis. Ultimately, this work will solve long-standing puzzles regarding the structural basis of evolution and establish a predictive framework for allosteric emergence in cellular systems.

title: Emergent Topologies at the Mesoscale: Synthesizing Protein Entanglement and 3D Genome Architecture through AI and Polymer Physics
title_norm: emergent topologies at the mesoscale synthesizing protein entanglement and 3d genome architecture through ai and polymer physics
abstract_text: The field of cellular biophysics studies the mesoscale organization of the three dimensional genome, emphasizing how protein level topological entanglements influence chromosomal architecture and macromolecular complexes under mechanical stress. This project will determine how protein level entanglements dictate viscoelastic genome properties using a three phase computational synthesis that integrates artificial intelligence cataloging, maximum entropy coevolutionary modeling, and coarse grained polymer physics simulations including MiChroM and MEGABASE. Structural data from AlphaFold, the Protein Data Bank, large scale sequence alignments, and high resolution chromosomal contact maps will be integrated using machine learning to assign biophysical parameters to specific chromatin interacting nodes. This research will introduce a novel physics based framework to analyze chromosomal compaction, providing essential knowledge to understand genome structural stability and mesoscale cellular organization under axial stress.
full_text: The cellular biophysics domain studies genome organization to reveal how protein level topology affects mechanics of mesoscale chromatin networks. Current polymer physics models treat proteins as trivial nodes and overlook their integration into macromolecular complexes under mechanical stress. This physics based study synthesizes genomic data to answer how protein entanglements determine viscoelastic properties of the genome. The study uses a three phase synthesis to combine artificial intelligence cataloging with coarse grained polymer physics simulations. Key methods include convolutional neural networks and statistical machine learning alongside molecular dynamics and MiChroM polymer physics models. The investigators validate and filter all structural predictions of protein topology by evaluating AlphaFold prediction confidence (pLDDT) scores. Datasets utilized include the Protein Data Bank (PDB) and AlphaFold Protein Structure Database alongside high resolution Hi-C maps. Statistical machine learning links structural topology data with genomic loci to assign biophysical parameters into polymer physics simulations. The team mitigates prediction artifacts within structural datasets by filtering information using convolutional neural networks and confidence scores. Proposed project milestones include completion of three distinct computational phases and creation of the comprehensive MesoTopo Atlas database. The cross disciplinary project demands expertise from structural biologists and mathematicians to integrate knot theory and polymer physics. The researchers will share software code via GitHub and publish open access articles alongside publicly hosted Zenodo databases. The diverse team includes postdoctoral fellows and graduate students receiving dual mentorship in structural topology and genomic modeling.

The physical organization of the mesoscale—the critical nexus between single biomolecules and large-scale organelles—relies on complex topological constraints to drive emergent biological functions. A long-standing puzzle in cellular biophysics is how intricate entanglements at the individual protein level (such as knots, slipknots, and theta-curves) scale up to influence the mesoscale architecture and mechanical properties of massive cellular assemblies like the 3D genome. While recent advances in deep learning have unveiled thousands of previously uncharacterized knotted proteins across the human proteome, and data-driven polymer physics models have successfully mapped chromosomal loop extrusion by multi-protein SMC (Structural Maintenance of Chromosomes) complexes, these domains of study have largely remained isolated. We propose a community-scale synthesis project to construct the first unified framework of biological topology, from individual polypeptide entanglements to macroscopic chromatin networks.

By integrating vast, publicly available datasets—spanning the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database, the Protein Data Bank (PDB), high-resolution Hi-C chromosomal contact maps, and large-scale coevolutionary sequence alignments—our multi-disciplinary Working Group will trace the flow of topological information across biological scales. First, we will develop and deploy advanced topological algorithms and convolutional neural networks to comprehensively catalog entanglements, theta-curves, and pierced lassos specifically within chromatin-associated proteins, condensin/cohesin complexes, and mesoscale phase-separated condensates. This structural synthesis will yield a comprehensive, genome-wide map of protein entanglement in the nucleus, classifying structures based on predicted topological complexity, chaperone-dependency, and coevolutionary constraints.

Next, we will fuse these topological structural maps with data-driven, coarse-grained polymer physics models to understand mesoscale emergence. Utilizing maximum entropy approaches and large-scale conformational sampling, we will simulate how topologically complex protein hubs mechanically interact with chromatin arrays. We seek to test the hypothesis that intricately folded proteins and highly constrained topological motifs act as specialized architectural ratchets and viscoelastic anchors. By acting as topological roadblocks or highly stable scaffolding hubs, these proteins may fundamentally direct the emergent 3D spatial organization, loop-extrusion dynamics, and mechanical stress responses of interphase and mitotic chromosomes.

This project strictly leverages existing open-access data, requiring no new experimental generation, but instead relying on the transdisciplinary synthesis of physical knot theory, structural bioinformatics, machine learning, and computational genomics. Support from NCEMS is critical, as mapping the interplay between structural topology and genomic organization far exceeds the capacity of isolated labs. The initiative will culminate in the 'MesoTopo Atlas,' an open-access AI-driven platform integrating protein entanglement data directly with genomic architecture models. Adhering strictly to FAIR open-science principles, this Working Group will also provide unparalleled training opportunities, equipping the next generation of data-savvy biophysicists with the computational and theoretical tools necessary to explore the frontier of multi-scale biological topology.

title: Deciphering the Mesoscale Emergence of Skeletal Muscle Adaptation: A GPU-Accelerated Multi-Omic and Mathematical Synthesis of Ribosome Dynamics under Competing Stresses
title_norm: deciphering the mesoscale emergence of skeletal muscle adaptation a gpuaccelerated multiomic and mathematical synthesis of ribosome dynamics under competing stresses
abstract_text: Within the domain of skeletal muscle plasticity, the formation, assembly, and regulation of the ribosome represent critical biological phenomena that orchestrate known signaling cascades involving mTORC1 and systemic immune factors. This project will build a computational model explaining how stressors alter ribosomes and muscle dimensions by synthesizing data via parallel partitioning algorithms on multiple graphics processing units, graph neural networks, and partial differential equations with free boundary conditions. Data from the Gene Expression Omnibus, Sequence Read Archive, Proteomics Identifications Database, and Protein Data Bank will be standardized, aligned, and mapped into network nodes to yield translation rates for cell size projections. The resulting framework will connect conflicting physiological signals to physical muscle changes, establishing a unified model that accelerates network reconstruction and applies novel free boundary mathematics in biology.
full_text: This project studies regulation of ribosomes in skeletal muscle plasticity to understand how physical and immune inputs dictate cell size. abstract_original:
Skeletal muscle plasticity—specifically its capacity to undergo hypertrophy or atrophy—is an emergent cellular property strictly governed by mesoscale phenomena: the dynamic assembly, biogenesis, and regulatory control of the ribosome. While individual molecular pathways (e.g., mTORC1 signaling) and systemic influences (e.g., inflammatory cytokines) are well documented, a fundamental mystery remains regarding how competing systemic signals—such as mechanical overload from exercise and systemic inflammatory stress from rheumatic conditions—spatiotemporally integrate at the mesoscale translational machinery to drive opposing phenotypic outcomes. Although individual transcriptomic, translatomic (Ribo-seq), and proteomic studies have profiled these states in isolation, the resulting vast repositories of publicly available data remain fragmented.

We will integrate transcriptomic, Ribo-seq, phosphoproteomic, and structural data across healthy exercise cohorts and patients with inflammatory conditions. Because aligning and synthesizing such divergent, high-dimensional multi-omic datasets is computationally prohibitive for traditional bioinformatics pipelines, we will develop ultra-fast, GPU-accelerated algorithms and Graph Neural Network (GNN) frameworks. These AI-driven tools will efficiently align divergent sequences, reconstruct dynamic translational networks, and predict the interaction structures of mesoscale molecular assemblies in real time.

To bridge the gap from GNN-derived molecular networks to emergent cellular phenotypes, we will couple our AI frameworks with advanced mathematical modeling. We will construct spatiotemporal systems of partial differential equations (PDEs) with free boundaries to model the physical expansion of the muscle fiber cross-sectional area (hypertrophy) as a direct mathematical consequence of mesoscale ribosome biogenesis and translational output. This hybrid AI-mathematical framework will allow us to simulate how localized mechanical stimuli promote ribosomal assembly, and precisely how inflammatory stress acts as a molecular roadblock to dampen this translational capacity.

This transdisciplinary approach perfectly aligns with the NCEMS mission. The project relies entirely on the computational synthesis of existing public repositories, generating no new experimental data. It demands the integration of three distinct scientific domains—high-performance GPU computing, continuous mathematical modeling, and molecular exercise physiology—a synergy fundamentally beyond the capabilities of any single laboratory. All developed GPU-accelerated pipelines, GNN architectures, PDE models, and integrated datasets will be open-sourced, adhering to the highest standards of reproducible team science. Furthermore, our Working Group will cross-train a new generation of data-savvy postdocs and graduate students at the intersection of AI, computational mathematics, and cellular biology. By decoding the mesoscale logic of translational control under competing biological stresses, this synthesis will uncover profound insights into the emergent nature of cellular growth and adaptation.

title: Deciphering the Grammar of Emergence: Predicting Mesoscale Condensate Properties from Evolutionary Constraints and Polymer Physics in Intrinsically Disordered Regions
title_norm: deciphering the grammar of emergence predicting mesoscale condensate properties from evolutionary constraints and polymer physics in intrinsically disordered regions
abstract_text: Mesoscale cellular biology investigates biomolecular condensates formed by the liquid liquid phase separation of intrinsically disordered regions of proteins, where amino acid valence and patterning control critical stability and viscoelasticity properties. Current knowledge lacks a universal biophysical understanding of how evolutionary pressures constrain sequence grammar to maintain condensate fluidity and how missense mutations disrupt this balance to cause pathological aggregation. The primary objective is to develop a physics informed machine learning framework linking sequence constraints to mesoscale properties through an in silico analysis utilizing profile Hidden Markov Models and unsupervised representation learning regularized by scaling theories. Protein sequences from DisProt, MobiDB, PhaSepDB, CD-CODE, SASBDB, BMRB, ClinVar, gnomAD, and Pfam will be integrated to anchor verified phase separation behavior to structural ensemble measurements and clinical variants. This project will yield a physics informed machine learning method to predict condensate properties, providing a critical foundation for identifying neurodegenerative therapeutic targets and rationally designing synthetic biomolecular condensates.
full_text: This project in mesoscale cellular biology investigates how mutations disrupt liquid liquid phase separation of intrinsically disordered protein regions. Current models of polymer physics explain condensate stability but isolated studies prevent a universal understanding of phase separation. This research builds a physics informed machine learning framework to predict condensate properties and identify targets for neurodegenerative diseases. This in silico analysis of public datasets harmonizes information to build models and predict effects of pathological mutations. The team will use profile Hidden Markov Models and physics informed machine learning guided by theories of scaling. The predictive performance of the model will be rigorously benchmarked against existing algorithms that are driven purely by data. The proposed study leverages public genomic databases including ClinVar and gnomAD alongside biophysical repositories such as PhaSepDB and SASBDB. Relevant protein sequences will be cross referenced with phase separation behavior and structural measurements and clinical variant data. The team will overcome the fragmentation of isolated repositories by harmonizing these disparate sources into a single framework. Proposed milestones for this project include distinct methodological phases for harmonization of data and model training and predictive mapping. This cross disciplinary collaboration is essential because integrating artificial intelligence and polymer physics exceeds capabilities of single laboratories. The project will share datasets via Zenodo and code via GitHub while publishing findings in open access journals. The collaborative team of principal investigators and students will provide cross disciplinary mentorship and host annual virtual hackathons.

abstract_original:
Biomolecular condensates represent a fundamental paradigm of mesoscale emergence in cellular biology, transitioning from individual biomolecular interactions to functional, non-stoichiometric organelles with highly tunable material properties. Central to this liquid-liquid phase separation are the intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) of proteins. Theoretical frameworks rooted in polymer physics—such as the sticker-and-spacer model—have established that the valence and patterning of specific amino acids (e.g., aromatics, charged residues) govern the thermodynamic stability and viscoelasticity of these condensates. However, a major long-standing puzzle remains: how do evolutionary pressures constrain the sequence grammar of highly flexible IDRs to maintain optimal mesoscale emergence, and how do missense mutations disrupt this delicate balance to trigger pathological solid-like aggregation, as seen in neurodegenerative diseases? 

To address this compelling scientific question, our proposed NCEMS Working Group will execute a community-scale synthesis of publicly available genomic, biophysical, and clinical datasets. This transdisciplinary project strictly utilizes existing data, moving beyond the traditional single-protein focus to uncover universal rules of phase separation. We will integrate and harmonize diverse public data sources, including IDR sequence databases (DisProt, MobiDB), condensate repositories (PhaSepDB, CD-CODE), large-scale biophysical archives containing Small-Angle X-ray Scattering (SAXS) and Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) structural ensembles (SASBDB, BMRB), and comprehensive clinical mutation registries (ClinVar, gnomAD). 

Our primary objective is to develop a physics-informed machine learning framework that bridges the gap between molecular sequence constraints and emergent mesoscale material properties. By synthesizing deep evolutionary sequence alignments with structural and biophysical data, we will map the multidimensional functional constraints placed on IDRs. First, we will train predictive models to decode the universal 'grammar' of conserved disorder, quantifying how specific patterns of hydrophobic clustering, electrostatics, and transient helicity are preserved across millions of years to maintain optimal condensate fluidity. Second, we will project thousands of clinical mutations onto these physical landscapes to predict which uncharacterized variants induce aberrant phase transitions, such as intra-condensate demixing or pathological fibrillization. 

This project requires NCEMS support to facilitate the necessary cross-disciplinary collaboration, bringing together experts in polymer physics, neuro-pathogenesis, computational structural biology, and artificial intelligence. The resulting synthesis will not only answer fundamental biological mysteries but also pioneer innovative analytical strategies by embedding polymer scaling laws directly into machine learning architectures. These insights will have transformative implications across disciplines, from identifying novel therapeutic targets in neurodegeneration to advancing synthetic biology by enabling the rational design of IDRs for engineered gene circuits. 

In strict adherence to Open Science principles, all harmonized databases, physics-informed AI models, and reproducible analysis pipelines will be released publicly through an interactive, open-source web portal. Furthermore, this working group will provide vital training for the next-generation workforce, immersing graduate students and postdoctoral researchers in a highly collaborative environment that bridges statistical mechanics, biophysics, and advanced data science.

title: Evolutionary Synthesis of Multi-Omics Data to Uncover Mesoscale Emergence in Mammalian Metabolic Suppression
title_norm: evolutionary synthesis of multiomics data to uncover mesoscale emergence in mammalian metabolic suppression
abstract_text: Mammalian metabolic suppression during hibernation and torpor requires the coordination of mitochondrial remodeling, energy partitioning, and circadian metabolic interactions, representing an important biological phenomenon with molecular components documented in specific species. This project will reconstruct pan mammalian gene regulatory networks and evaluate latent suppression pathways in non hibernating primates through an in silico synthesis, applying approximate Bayesian computation and multi layer graph neural networks to model evolution. Whole genome, bulk RNA, and single cell transcriptomic data from Ensembl and NCBI repositories will undergo processing via containerized pipelines to standardize sequence alignment and quantify transcripts into a single integrated database. Identifying these dormant metabolic suppression networks will address fundamental evolutionary questions regarding trait retention and will provide biological targets for treating metabolic disorders and preserving ischemic organs.
full_text: This project examines the suppression of metabolism in mammals during hibernation to determine if the genetic architecture is ancestral. Researchers understand specific molecules for metabolic adaptation in certain species but the systemic mechanisms of evolution remain completely unidentified. The proposed study models latent networks of metabolic suppression in primates to address evolutionary questions and discover therapeutic targets. This computational project compares multi omics data from hibernators and outgroup species without generating any new experimental data. The team uses Approximate Bayesian Computation (ABC) integrated with neural networks to model the evolution of metabolic suppression. The analytical approach also applies graph neural networks with multiple layers to infer networks of gene regulation from sequences. The project utilizes sequencing data of whole genomes and single cells from the Sequence Read Archive (SRA). Pipelines in containers will process these diverse datasets to standardize quality control and alignment of sequences into one database. This unified database will integrate distinct profiles of transcriptomes by mapping orthologous regions of genomes across all evaluated species. Project milestones include the harmonization of data and modeling of evolutionary genomics followed by the integration of systems. Integrating datasets on a large scale requires a cross disciplinary collaboration to combine expertise in evolutionary genomics and machine learning. The researchers will host code under open source licenses on GitHub and archive data alongside model weights in Zenodo. The team includes principal investigators and trainees who will receive cross disciplinary instruction in chronobiology and ecological physiology.

abstract_original:
The ability of mammalian cells to drastically suppress metabolism and endure extreme physiological stress—such as during hibernation or torpor—represents a profound example of biological emergence. While isolated studies have documented the molecular components of these adaptations, it remains a long-standing puzzle how genomic variation and transcriptomic plasticity coordinate to produce emergent mesoscale properties, such as dynamic mitochondrial network remodeling, subcellular energy partitioning, and circadian-metabolic coupling. To bridge this gap, we propose an integrative, community-scale synthesis of publicly available multi-omics data to uncover the shared evolutionary and molecular mechanisms governing mammalian metabolic suppression.

Our working group will synthesize massive, multi-tissue transcriptomic (bulk RNA-seq, single-cell RNA-seq, and time-series data) and high-coverage whole-genome sequencing datasets across a diverse array of mammalian lineages. This phylogenetic spectrum will include obligate and facultative hibernators (e.g., ursids, rodents, bats) alongside non-hibernating outgroups, notably diverse primate species. By contrasting extreme metabolic adaptors with non-hibernators, we aim to resolve whether the genetic architecture for cellular metabolic flexibility represents a deeply conserved ancestral state, arose convergently, or was shaped by archaic introgression and structural variation.

Methodologically, we will leverage advanced Artificial Intelligence (AI) and data science frameworks to integrate these disparate data types. Drawing on computational modeling approaches, we will employ Approximate Bayesian Computation integrated with Neural Networks (ABC-NN) to trace the evolutionary history and demographic architecture of key metabolic regulatory nodes. Concurrently, we will train multi-layer Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) on integrated cross-species transcriptomes to infer dynamic, pan-mammalian gene regulatory networks (GRNs). This approach will allow us to pinpoint how molecular-level signals—specifically upstream metabolic regulators and circadian clock transcription factors—govern mesoscale subcellular outcomes. We will specifically focus on identifying the synchronized transcriptomic shifts that enable organelle-level survival during hypothermia, such as the regulation of mitochondrial ATP production and the buffering of cellular oxidative stress.

This project strictly utilizes existing open-access multi-omics data, fulfilling the NCEMS mandate for synthesis research without generating new experimental datasets. By uniting experts in evolutionary genomics, ecological physiology, chronobiology, and machine learning, our cross-disciplinary team will transcend the capabilities of individual labs to determine if latent transcriptomic pathways for extreme metabolic suppression remain intact in non-hibernating mammals.

In strict alignment with NCEMS goals, our working group is committed to open science principles. All integrated data, AI models, and analytical pipelines will be distributed through public, reproducible repositories. Furthermore, this project prioritizes workforce development by deeply embedding graduate students and postdoctoral researchers in our collaborative workflows, providing them with critical, cross-disciplinary training at the nexus of evolutionary genomics, mesoscale biology, and advanced data science.

title: Synthesizing Evolutionary and Biophysical Landscapes to Predict the Emergence of Mesoscale Biomolecular Condensates
title_norm: synthesizing evolutionary and biophysical landscapes to predict the emergence of mesoscale biomolecular condensates
abstract_text: In cellular biology, primary protein sequences determine the capacity for liquid liquid phase separation, which forms biomolecular condensates and membraneless organelles that play critical roles under varying physiological conditions. Current knowledge lacks a complete understanding of how atomic level sequence coevolution and allosteric gating control the exact thermodynamic properties required for mesoscale droplet formation across different cellular environments. The primary research objective is to determine how coevolutionary constraints encode phase separation propensity, and this project will execute a three tiered computational synthesis applying Direct Coupling Analysis and deep learning architectures to analyze structural molecular dynamics models. Sequence derived coevolutionary constraints from Pfam and UniProt will map onto three dimensional AlphaFold and MoDEL structural ensembles, providing energetic potentials as features for deep learning models trained on LLPSDB and PhaSePro phenotypic data. This research will produce a predictive machine learning framework that links atomic level fluctuations to cellular behaviors, elucidating how genetic changes and environmental stress drive pathological states.
full_text: This cellular biology project studies how sequence coevolution and allosteric gating control thermodynamic properties for liquid liquid phase separation. Primary protein sequences dictate phase separation capacity but the exact evolutionary pathways and allosteric mechanisms under physiological conditions lack clarity. The primary question asks how coevolutionary constraints encode phase separation to build a predictive framework connecting atomic fluctuations to pathology. The study design involves a three tiered computational synthesis of public data to map coevolutionary constraints onto biophysical networks. The analytical approach applies random forest algorithms and deep learning architectures alongside models of direct coupling analysis and graph theory. Researchers will benchmark the results through techniques of cross validation against phenotypic phase behavior data from the LLPSDB database. The project gathers sequence data from Pfam and UniProt alongside phenotypic phase separation records from PhaSePro and LLPSDB. The team also acquires three dimensional structural ensembles from the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database and MoDEL trajectory databases. Integration occurs by mapping constraints of sequence evolution onto structural ensembles to extract features for models of deep learning. The broad project scope demands cross disciplinary collaboration to integrate computational biophysics and structural biology with machine learning. This extensive integration requires collective expertise because the required knowledge exceeds the resources of a single research laboratory. The investigators will publish results in open access journals and share computational pipelines through a dedicated web portal. The diverse team trains graduate students and postdoctoral scholars in evolutionary bioinformatics and standardized practices of data management.

abstract_original: The unexpected assembly of mesoscale biological structures, specifically biomolecular condensates and membraneless organelles, represents a quintessential emergent phenomenon in cellular biology. These condensates, driven by liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), govern critical subcellular processes ranging from gene regulation to cellular stress responses. While the physical chemistry of LLPS is increasingly studied, a long-standing puzzle remains: how do evolutionary constraints at the atomic scale—specifically sequence coevolution and intrinsic allosteric gating—dictate the thermodynamic parameters required for mesoscale droplet formation across varying cellular environments? To answer this, our Working Group proposes a community-scale synthesis project that bridges molecular evolution, computational biophysics, and structural biology. Currently, investigations into protein phase separation remain siloed. However, there is an unprecedented volume of publicly available data ready for integration. We will synthesize massive multiple sequence alignments (MSAs) from genomic databases (e.g., Pfam, UniProt), predicted structural ensembles from the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database, public molecular dynamics (MD) trajectories, and curated phenotypic databases of phase-separating proteins (e.g., PhaSePro, LLPSDB). No new experimental data will be generated; instead, we will leverage these public resources to build a unified predictive model of mesoscale emergence. Our multidisciplinary team will employ a three-tiered computational strategy. First, leveraging information theory and statistical models of coevolutionary sequence information (Potts models, Direct Coupling Analysis), we will extract evolutionary constraints and coupled networks within intrinsically disordered regions and RNA-binding domains of condensate-forming proteins. Second, we will map these coevolutionary constraints onto structural ensembles and public MD trajectories. By applying multi-ensemble contact analysis, graph theory, and random forest machine learning, we will uncover how these evolutionary linkages encode temperature-sensitive and stress-responsive allosteric switches. Finally, we will integrate these atomic-level biophysical networks with macro-level phase separation databases to identify the generalized rules governing how localized molecular changes propagate into mesoscale phase transitions. This ambitious synthesis requires NCEMS support to facilitate collaboration across labs that traditionally operate in distinct domains. Beyond compelling scientific questions, our Working Group is deeply committed to open science and workforce development. Guided by the principles of Discipline-Based Diversity Research (DBDR), we will deliberately recruit and train a diverse cohort of graduate students and postdocs. Trainees will be cross-trained in evolutionary bioinformatics, AI-driven biophysics, and FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) data management practices. All developed analytical workflows, machine learning models, and integrated databases will be published as open-source resources. Ultimately, this project will reveal the evolutionary and allosteric ontology of biomolecular condensates, solving fundamental questions about how mesoscale properties emerge from sequence-level information, while cultivating the next generation of data-savvy, diverse biological scientists.

title: Emergent Metabolic Landscapes: Synthesizing Deep Learning and Genome-Scale Modeling to Decode the Evolutionary Rewiring of Cellular Metabolism
title_norm: emergent metabolic landscapes synthesizing deep learning and genomescale modeling to decode the evolutionary rewiring of cellular metabolism
abstract_text: Evolutionary genomics and systems biology investigate the mesoscale organization of metabolic networks, an important field where population genetics and mathematical models predict how environmental pressures shape emergent cellular metabolic phenotypes. Current metabolic models rely on a single reference cellular state and lack a mechanistic understanding of how distributed population level genetic variations synergize to alter network level metabolic properties. To determine how polygenic adaptations cause flux rerouting in specialized cells, this project will apply neural networks, coalescent simulations, and flux balance analysis to construct context specific genome scale metabolic models from multi omic data. The study will integrate 1000 Genomes Project and archaic hominin datasets with GTEx data to constrain reaction bounds, subsequently cross referencing computational predictions against matched transcriptomic and metabolomic profiles from public databases. This framework will replace the single reference paradigm with models accounting for genetic diversity, yielding findings that inform computational strain design and explain population specific susceptibilities to metabolic diseases.
full_text: This project in evolutionary genomics and systems biology investigates how distributed genetic variations alter properties of metabolic networks. Current models predict metabolic fluxes but rely on a single reference state without incorporating variations from population genetics. The proposed study investigates how polygenic adaptations reroute fluxes to explain susceptibilities to disease and inform metabolic engineering. The study design features a computational synthesis of data to infer evolutionary signatures and validate predictions of models. The analytical approach applies generative adversarial networks (GANs) and convolutional neural networks (CNNs) alongside metabolic models and coalescent simulations. The team validates metabolic predictions by comparing distributions of fluxes against profiles from single cell transcriptomics and metabolomics. The project uses datasets including the 1000 Genomes Project and Human Cell Atlas alongside the BiGG Models database. The team identifies evolutionary signatures in genomic data to constrain bounds in models and generate predictions of metabolism. The resulting predictions of metabolism are evaluated against matched profiles of transcriptomics to ensure rigor of the study. The project proceeds through consecutive phases of evolutionary inference and modeling of metabolism before culminating in data validation. This cross disciplinary scope requires collaboration across multiple laboratories to integrate deep learning with models of systems biology. The team shares containerized code on GitHub and deposits weights of models in Zenodo for access by researchers. The project supports postdoctoral fellows and graduate students who receive cross training in computer science and systems biology.

The transition from individual genetic variations to complex cellular phenotypes is governed by the mesoscale organization of metabolic networks. While decades of population genetics have identified thousands of loci under natural selection or archaic introgression—often linked to diet, climate, and pathogen response—we lack a fundamental understanding of how these distributed, population-level genetic changes synergize to produce emergent metabolic properties at the cellular level. Simultaneously, systems biology has developed robust tools to model cellular metabolism, but these frameworks rarely incorporate the rich evolutionary history of human populations. This project proposes a massive, community-scale synthesis of publicly available genomic, transcriptomic, and metabolomic data to bridge this gap, unifying evolutionary genomics and systems biology through the lens of artificial intelligence.

Our collaborative working group will synthesize data from global genomic repositories (e.g., 1000 Genomes Project, Simons Genome Diversity Project, archaic hominin genomes) with multi-omic physiological databases (e.g., GTEx, Human Cell Atlas, and Metabolomics Workbench). We will tackle this synthesis in three integrated phases. First, we will deploy interpretable deep learning architectures, including Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), to perform high-resolution inference of natural selection and archaic introgression across global populations. These AI models will be trained on extensive neutral coalescent simulations to identify complex evolutionary signatures specifically within genes encoding metabolic enzymes, transporters, and regulatory networks.

Second, we will map these evolutionarily divergent haplotypes onto context-specific Genome-Scale Metabolic (GSM) models of highly specialized cell types, such as adipocytes and macrophages. By integrating expression quantitative trait loci (eQTL) data to constrain reaction bounds in the GSMs, we will employ optimization-based stoichiometric modeling to simulate how selected genetic variants collectively rewire metabolic fluxes. This will allow us to predict emergent mesoscale phenomena, such as the spontaneous reorganization of lipid biosynthesis pathways in extreme climates or metabolic polarization shifts in immune cells.

Finally, we will validate these in silico metabolic predictions by synthesizing matched public single-cell transcriptomics and mass spectrometry-based metabolomics datasets, cross-referencing population-specific metabolic profiles with our GSM-derived flux distributions. 

This project directly addresses the NCEMS mandate to explore mesoscale emergence by demonstrating how independent mutations interact within complex stoichiometric networks to yield novel biochemical phenotypes. By leveraging only existing public data, this collaboration merges deep learning, population genetics, and genome-scale modeling—a synthesis beyond the capacity of any single laboratory. Adhering to open science principles, all trained AI models, context-specific GSMs, and reproducible analytical pipelines will be hosted publicly. Furthermore, this working group will train a new generation of interdisciplinary postdoctoral fellows and graduate students, equipping them to navigate both generative AI and mechanistic systems biology to solve long-standing puzzles in molecular evolution.

title: Mapping the Emergent Collapse of Mesoscale Proteostasis Networks in Aging and Stress
title_norm: mapping the emergent collapse of mesoscale proteostasis networks in aging and stress
abstract_text: Investigating mesoscale proteostasis networks under environmental stress and cardiovascular aging is critical because the complex regulatory networks that buffer macromolecular assemblies like sarcomeres and stress granules remain poorly understood. The primary objective is to map mesoscale proteostasis networks and determine complex collapse thresholds; this project will synthesize existing data using automated harmonization pipelines, ordinary differential equation modeling, bifurcation analysis, and random forest algorithms. The project will integrate single cell transcriptomic, proteomic, and structural datasets from public repositories by applying batch correction algorithms and mapping kinetic parameters onto predefined mesoscale assemblies to construct unified analytical matrices. This work will produce a predictive computational framework for mesoscale biological stability, identifying systemic molecular vulnerabilities in cardiovascular aging and shifting the field toward a dynamic systems perspective.
full_text: This project investigates cardiovascular mesoscale assemblies (including sarcomeres) to uncover kinetic thresholds where the maintenance of structural stability fails. Researchers have identified isolated microscale kinetic rates but the complex regulatory networks that buffer mesoscale assemblies remain poorly understood. The team will determine mathematical thresholds of complex collapse to establish a novel predictive framework for systemic molecular vulnerabilities. The overall study design combines dynamic systems modeling with machine learning to identify kinetic signatures of complex collapse. Key methods include ordinary differential equation modeling and machine learning algorithms alongside specific batch correction tools and containerization software. The resulting machine learning models will be validated against human plasma proteomic data to verify systemic clinical signatures. The project utilizes structural protein data and RNA-seq datasets from the Gene Expression Omnibus and Proteomics Identifications Database. Researchers will integrate these distinct datasets by mapping kinetic parameters onto mesoscale assemblies to construct unified data matrices. The team will mitigate technical variations across disparate studies by applying batch correction algorithms within an automated harmonization pipeline. The proposed study is structured into three integrated phases and incorporates biannual synthesis sprints to accomplish project goals. The project requires cross disciplinary collaboration to successfully integrate systems biology with cardiovascular disease modeling and computational biophysics. The researchers will publish findings in open access journals and share version controlled code through a public repository. The team features principal investigators alongside postdoctoral fellows and graduate students receiving cross disciplinary instruction in dynamic systems modeling.

abstract_original:
Cellular survival during physiological stress and aging depends on the delicate balance of protein synthesis, folding, and degradation. While the kinetic rates of individual biomolecules are increasingly characterized, a critical long-standing puzzle remains: how do these microscale dynamics integrate to determine the emergent stability and function of mesoscale macromolecular assemblies, such as the nuclear lamina, sarcomeres, and stress granules? Traditional single-lab approaches often treat transcriptomics and proteomics in isolation, failing to capture the discordant, dynamic buffering—governed by translation rates and protein turnover—that sustains these mesoscale structures under duress. 

To address this gap, we propose a community-scale data synthesis Working Group to map the emergent properties of mesoscale proteostasis networks under environmental stress (e.g., hypoxia, metabolic perturbation) and biological aging. This project will strictly utilize the vast repository of publicly available multi-omics datasets, generating no new experimental data. We will integrate transcriptomics (bulk and single-cell RNA-seq), translatomics (ribosome profiling), global proteomics, in vivo protein turnover rates (pulsed SILAC and dynamic SILAM), and structural databases quantifying protein disorder. By harmonizing disparate datasets across mammalian tissues, induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) models, and large-scale biobanks, we will build a unified computational framework to decode how multi-level regulation dictates mesoscale structural integrity.

Our collaborative synthesis will employ machine learning and dynamic systems modeling to answer fundamental questions about molecular emergence. Specifically, we will test the hypothesis that the intrinsic structural disorder of component proteins and their highly regulated turnover rates act as a buffer during the Integrated Stress Response (ISR). We will mathematically model how the uncoupling of mRNA and protein abundances reaches a “tipping point” where this buffering capacity fails, leading to the abrupt pathological disassembly or aggregation of mesoscale complexes. We will focus our analytical pipelines on cardiovascular and vascular aging models, using LMNA-linked cardiomyopathies and stress-induced endothelial dysfunction as prototypical examples of mesoscale failure translating to cellular collapse.

This project requires the unique transdisciplinary environment provided by NCEMS. The synthesis demands a fusion of expertise spanning translation dynamics, protein misfolding, cardiovascular disease modeling, systems biology, and big data precision medicine—perspectives perfectly aligned with our team’s background. By moving beyond isolated analyses of transcript-protein correlations, our Working Group will uncover the universal network principles governing protein turnover dynamics and mesoscale complex stability.

In strict adherence to NCEMS open science principles, all unified databases, AI-driven predictive models, and analytical workflows will be open-source and freely disseminated to the community. Furthermore, this initiative will serve as a premier training ground for the next generation of data-savvy scientists. Postdoctoral and graduate trainees integrated into the Working Group will receive cross-disciplinary mentorship in multi-omics integration, computational biophysics, and reproducible team science, equipping them to lead the future of synthetic biology and molecular data science.

title: A Bayesian Synthesis Framework for Predicting the Emergence of Mesoscale Ribonucleoprotein Compartmentalization from Public Spatial Transcriptomic and Single-Molecule Datasets
title_norm: a bayesian synthesis framework for predicting the emergence of mesoscale ribonucleoprotein compartmentalization from public spatial transcriptomic and singlemolecule datasets
abstract_text: Molecular and cellular biology investigates how mesoscale ribonucleoprotein condensates and membrane less organelles form from single molecule interactions, requiring integrated kinetic and steady state spatial data to explain structure formation. Currently, the field lacks analytical models that connect single molecule interaction kinetics with whole cell spatial transcriptomic data to explain the physical mechanisms of RNA compartmentalization. This project will construct a computational model to predict ribonucleoprotein compartment spatial distribution by extracting kinetic parameters, co embedding variables with spatial transcriptomics, and generating thermodynamic probability landscapes via Bayesian reaction diffusion modeling and non equilibrium statistical mechanics. Datasets from SMTracker, Zenodo, NIH 4D Nucleome Data Portal, SpaceTx, and Brain Initiative Cell Census Network will be integrated by modifying dimensionality reduction algorithms to map kinetic variables onto spatial RNA density coordinates. This novel computational framework will calculate dynamic biophysical properties from static genomic imaging data, bridging nanometer scale tracking with micrometer scale transcriptomic maps to predict ribonucleoprotein compartment distributions.
full_text: The study investigates the formation of ribonucleoprotein condensates by addressing the absence of models linking kinetics and spatial transcriptomics. Single molecule tracking and spatial transcriptomics capture distinct dynamics but remain unintegrated for the explanation of mesoscale structure formation. This project asks how computational models can predict condensate distribution by linking nanometer scale tracking and micrometer scale maps. The study employs a three phase computational workflow to extract kinetic parameters and generate thermodynamic probability landscapes of condensates. The methods incorporate single molecule reaction diffusion models and adapted embedding algorithms within software containers using multiple programming languages. The computational models will undergo validation using withheld datasets and benchmarking against independent multiplexed immunofluorescence and transcriptomic data. The project utilizes data from SMTracker and Zenodo alongside repositories from the SpaceTx consortium and other public databases. The team will integrate these sources by modifying dimensionality reduction algorithms to map variables onto a shared embedding space. The team will mitigate data heterogeneity across diverse biological states through standardized quality control metrics and algorithmic frameworks. The timeline includes the organization of a community training workshop during the second year of the proposed study. The broad scope requires a cross disciplinary collaboration to provide concurrent expertise in computational genomics and probabilistic modeling. The team will upload datasets to Zenodo and host open source software on GitHub under an MIT license. The team includes principal investigators and trainees who will receive cross disciplinary instruction regarding computational genomics and biophysics.
