abstract_original:
The unexpected appearance of mesoscale biological properties—such as the formation of localized subcellular translational hubs and membrane-less ribonucleoprotein (RNP) condensates—bridges the critical gap between stochastic single-molecule interactions and deterministic cellular phenotypes. Despite vast amounts of publicly available data at both ends of this spatial spectrum, our understanding of mesoscale emergence remains deeply fragmented. Single-molecule biophysical studies capture the high-resolution kinetic, stoichiometric, and reaction-diffusion properties of multivalent protein-RNA and protein-DNA interactions. Conversely, highly multiplexed spatial transcriptomics maps the subcellular compartmentalization of thousands of RNA species across whole cells and tissues. Currently, these two disjoint data modalities are rarely synthesized, leaving a crucial analytical blind spot in the molecular and cellular biosciences.

This proposed NCEMS Working Group will synthesize publicly available single-molecule tracking (SMT), single-molecule localization microscopy (SMLM), and multiplexed spatial transcriptomics (e.g., MERFISH, seqFISH) datasets to elucidate the biophysical rules governing the emergence of mesoscale RNP compartmentalization. We propose to develop a transdisciplinary predictive framework that merges rigorous Bayesian single-molecule inference with large-scale spatial multi-omics integration algorithms. Our collaborative approach strictly leverages existing public data to solve the long-standing puzzle of how transient, multivalent microscale interactions scale up to form stable mesoscale structures across diverse physiological and disease states, such as neurodevelopment and cancer microenvironments.

Our methodology proceeds in three integrative phases. First, utilizing advanced probabilistic modeling and Bayesian inference tools originally designed for single-photon and single-particle tracking, we will extract fundamental kinetic parameters, dissociation constants, and multivalent stoichiometric profiles of key RNA-binding proteins from public biophysical data repositories. Second, we will embed these microscale biophysical priors into a unified, scalable predictive algorithm—extending existing embedding and integration frameworks like Harmony—to analyze broad public spatial transcriptomic datasets. Third, we will calculate in situ thermodynamic probability landscapes to model how dynamically forming multivalent complexes drive specific RNAs into mesoscale compartments, effectively mapping single-molecule reaction-diffusion kinetics onto whole-cell spatial transcriptomic coordinates.

This community-scale synthesis relies fundamentally on NCEMS support, as it goes far beyond the scope of a single laboratory. It demands the deep integration of diverse scientific domains: computational multi-omics, single-molecule tracking, statistical optics, and biophysical chemistry. By bringing together researchers across these fields, we will deliver an open-source computational platform that uncovers how localized molecular biophysics dictates higher-order cellular architecture.

In strict adherence to open science principles, all harmonized multi-scale datasets, Bayesian models, and deep integration pipelines will be made freely available. Furthermore, the Working Group is deeply committed to training the next generation of data-savvy scientists. Trainees will receive cross-disciplinary mentorship, learning to bridge the analytical divide between the physics of photon-arrival statistics and the computational scale of genome-wide spatial omics. Ultimately, this project will pioneer innovative analytical strategies to decode the physical emergence of mesoscale biological organization from publicly available data.

title: Synthesizing Multi-Omic and Structural Data to Decode the Emergent Mesoscale Organization of Epigenetic and Epitranscriptomic Networks
title_norm: synthesizing multiomic and structural data to decode the emergent mesoscale organization of epigenetic and epitranscriptomic networks
abstract_text: Mesoscale biological research focuses on how epigenetic and epitranscriptomic modifications affect higher order chromatin clutch organization and translational ribonucleoprotein complex assembly to respond to environmental and metabolic factors. This computational project will determine how coordinated epigenetic and epitranscriptomic modifications drive mesoscale organization to control cellular state transitions by harmonizing multi omic data to parameterize residue resolution coarse grained molecular dynamics simulations. Data from the Human Cell Atlas, Gene Expression Omnibus, and Protein Data Bank will be integrated via single cell bi level feature propagation and similarity network fusion clustering to combine multi omic profiles. This research will establish a unified framework of biological emergence across different physical scales to link atomistic molecular interactions with mesoscale structural dynamics and cellular state transitions.
full_text: This project investigates mesoscale biological phenomena to determine how combined epigenetic and epitranscriptomic modifications remodel architectures and influence cellular heterogeneity. The study asks how coordinated modifications drive cellular transitions to establish a unified framework of biological emergence across physical scales. This computational synthesis project harmonizes multi omic data to parameterize simulations of mesoscale structures before mining the cellular outputs. Key methods include single cell feature propagation and network fusion clustering alongside coarse grained simulations and intercellular interactome mapping. The team will evaluate results by comparing simulated instabilities of complexes with observed translation deficits in public omic datasets. Data sources include the Human Cell Atlas and Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) alongside structural databases and collections of ligand receptors. The team will combine multi omic profiles via network fusion clustering to parameterize molecular dynamics simulations from structural databases. The researchers will mitigate the technical sparsity of single cell sequencing data by imputing missing values through feature propagation. The project entails sequential phases of data harmonization and molecular simulations before concluding with interactome and phenotypic data mining. This scope demands cross disciplinary collaboration to provide concurrent expertise in structural biophysics and single cell artificial intelligence algorithms. The project will share data through public repositories and distribute code via containers while publishing findings in open access journals. The team includes principal investigators and graduate students alongside postdoctoral researchers who will receive cross disciplinary computational training.

abstract_original:
Mesoscale biological phenomena—such as the higher-order organization of chromatin clutches and the coordinated assembly of translational ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes—emerge from dynamic networks of molecular-level modifications. While specific epigenetic and epitranscriptomic marks (e.g., histone acetylation, lysine lactylation, and tRNA modifications) are known to respond to metabolic and environmental cues, the rules governing how these multi-layered modifications collectively interact to remodel mesoscale architectures and drive cellular-level phenotypic heterogeneity remain a critical unknown. This NCEMS Working Group proposes a community-scale data synthesis project to answer a fundamental question: How do coordinated epigenetic and epitranscriptomic modifications cooperatively drive the emergent mesoscale organization of chromatin and translational machineries to control cellular state transitions?

To solve this long-standing puzzle, our team will synthesize massive amounts of publicly available data, including single-cell transcriptomic and epigenomic atlases (e.g., Human Cell Atlas, GEO), multi-omic disease and aging cohorts (e.g., TCGA), epitranscriptomic maps, and structural databases (PDB, EMDB). Because interpreting this multi-layered data transcends the capabilities of a single discipline, we will integrate diverse expertise in structural biophysics, single-cell AI algorithms, multi-omic proteomics, and RNA bioinformatics.

Our methodological strategy comprises three integrated phases. First, we will employ advanced AI and graph-based analytical strategies—specifically bi-level feature propagation and similarity network fusion clustering—to harmonize, impute, and integrate highly sparse single-cell epigenomic, transcriptomic, and proteomic data. This will allow us to define distinct, multi-omic cellular states and map concurrent alterations in chromatin marks and RNA modifications across diverse biological conditions, such as aging and metabolic stress. Second, the extracted modification profiles will serve as boundary conditions to parameterize residue-resolution, coarse-grained molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. By bridging atomistic details to the mesoscale, these simulations will model how specific combinations of modifications alter electrostatic and thermodynamic landscapes, thereby dictating chromatin fiber destacking, nucleosome interactomes, and the structural coupling of RNP networks. Third, using extensive bioinformatic data mining and interactome mapping, we will link these emergent mesoscale structural states to downstream cellular functional outputs. Specifically, we will decode how modified chromatin architectures and RNP assemblies influence translation dynamics—such as global ribosome pausing—and ultimately rewire intercellular ligand-receptor communication networks.

Aligned with the core mission of NCEMS, this project relies exclusively on the integration and synthesis of existing public datasets without generating new experimental data. The transdisciplinary nature of coupling single-cell multi-omic AI imputation with coarse-grained structural modeling necessitates a highly collaborative Working Group approach. We are committed to open science principles; all generated multi-omic interactome maps, AI frameworks, and MD simulation pipelines will be deposited in public repositories with reproducible workflows. Furthermore, this initiative will prioritize the training of a diverse, next-generation workforce of data-savvy scientists, equipping postdocs and graduate students with highly interdisciplinary skills at the intersection of AI, computational biophysics, and systems biology. By revealing how molecular modifications percolate upward to dictate mesoscale structure and cellular fate, this synthesis will yield novel, transformative insights into the fundamental principles of biological emergence.

title: Synthesizing the Global Repertoire of Microbial Mesoscale Compartments: Emergence, Pathogenesis, and Bioengineering Potential from Public Omics Data
title_norm: synthesizing the global repertoire of microbial mesoscale compartments emergence pathogenesis and bioengineering potential from public omics data
abstract_text: Prokaryotic biology features organized mesoscale compartments such as lipid bounded ferrosomes and protein bounded encapsulins that isolate toxic intermediates, concentrate substrates, recycle cofactors, and biomineralize trace elements. Current knowledge is restricted to a small number of model organisms, leaving the global distribution, structural assembly principles, and evolutionary origins of these bacterial organelles fundamentally uncharacterized. This project will systematically map the genetic diversity, biophysical self assembly rules, and physiological functions of microbial compartments using machine learning genomic classifiers, three dimensional structural modeling with AlphaFold Multimer, and host pathogen RNA seq meta analysis. Genomic, structural, and transcriptomic data from the NCBI Sequence Read Archive, JGI Integrated Microbial Genomes and Microbiomes, and Protein Data Bank will be synthesized into an interactive relational database named the Mesoscale Compartment Atlas. This comprehensive resource will define the evolutionary progression of bacterial organelles, identify their role in pathogen survival, and provide structural templates for synthetic biology and nanoparticle drug delivery applications.
full_text: This study in prokaryotic biology investigates mesoscale compartments because cultivation dependent methods obscure their structural assembly and origins. Prokaryotes use compartments to isolate toxic intermediates and concentrate substrates but current knowledge remains restricted to model organisms. The primary objective maps genetic diversity using public omics data to identify roles of compartments in pathogen survival. This computational synthesis project links compartment expression with pathogen survival through structural modeling and meta analysis of RNA-seq data. The analytical approach applies deep learning classifiers and Hidden Markov Models and AlphaFold-Multimer for calculations of structural properties. The team will benchmark predictions by training machine learning algorithms on the known genetic loci of established organelles. Utilized datasets include the Protein Data Bank and the Sequence Read Archive alongside public host pathogen RNA-seq data. The proposed study integrates structural models and transcriptomic correlations into an interactive platform called the Mesoscale Compartment Atlas. The limitation of low sequence homology requires mitigation through the definition of multigenic signatures based on operon structures. The integration of disparate structural and transcriptomic data sources necessitates extensive expertise in bacterial cell biology and pathogenesis. This extensive project scope requires cross disciplinary collaboration because the large scale computational genomics exceed a single laboratory. The team will deposit underlying datasets in Zenodo and share all research findings as open access bioRxiv preprints. The collaborative team includes principal investigators and graduate students who receive cross mentorship and training in structural modeling.

abstract_original:
The emergence of organized mesoscale structures—such as lipid-bounded ferrosomes, magnetosomes, and protein-bounded bacterial microcompartments (BMCs)—from individual molecular components represents a critical evolutionary leap in prokaryotic biology. These structures allow bacteria to achieve localized metabolic reactions, sequester toxic metabolites, facilitate electrochemical cofactor recycling, and resist host immune clearance. While experimental studies have elucidated a handful of these bacterial organelles, the vast diversity of mesoscale compartmentalization remains hidden within fragmented public databases. Our multidisciplinary working group proposes a large-scale data synthesis project to map the genetic, structural, and functional landscape of prokaryotic organelles. This project brings together expertise in bacterial cell biology, structural modeling, host-pathogen dynamics, and large-scale computational genomics to synthesize publicly available metagenomic, transcriptomic, and structural datasets.

First, we will apply advanced machine-learning algorithms to mine public genomic and metagenomic repositories (e.g., MG-RAST, NCBI SRA) for novel loci encoding structural shell proteins, cytoskeletal elements, and membrane-remodeling factors. Leveraging approaches analogous to genomic signature analysis used in complex disease profiling, we will develop "compartment signatures" to identify both canonical assemblies and atypical, minimal functional loci. Second, we will integrate these genomic sequences with public structural databases (PDB) and predictive tools (AlphaFold-Multimer) to model the emergent self-assembly of these newly discovered components into enclosed mesoscale architectures. We will specifically focus on identifying structural features that enable targeted molecular gating and cofactor recycling, extracting design principles for programmable metabolic functions.

Third, to understand the physiological impact of these mesoscale phenomena, we will synthesize dual host-pathogen RNA-seq data and clinical microbiome datasets. By correlating the expression of mesoscale compartment genes with pathogen survival metrics in host environments, we will uncover how these structures provide emergent stress responses—such as desiccation tolerance and evasion of host nutritional immunity via trace metal sequestration—and how their dynamic regulation contributes to chronic infection pathogenesis.

This purely computational, synthesis-driven approach leverages existing data to solve long-standing puzzles about the evolutionary origins and biochemical necessities of bacterial compartmentalization. The primary deliverable will be a publicly accessible "Mesoscale Compartment Atlas" detailing genetic signatures, structural models, and predicted functional states. Furthermore, by characterizing these bacterial organelles as natural analogues to therapeutic nanoparticle delivery systems, our synthesis will directly inform downstream synthetic biology and translational drug delivery efforts. Supported by NCEMS, this collaborative project will cross-pollinate structural microbiology, pathogenesis, and data science, providing a robust, transdisciplinary training ground for a new generation of scientists focused on multi-scale biological emergence.
